outcomes.statement: Apply injury prevention principles to ensure safe work performance in the autobody trade.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 1A: Injury Prevention (Core) · Suggested Time: 2-4 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify industry standard personal protective equipment (PPE), including dust masks, approved respirators, coveralls, chemical resistant gloves, eye and hearing protection and footwear.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify, label, store and handle hazardous materials according to Workplace Hazardous Materials Information System (WHMIS 2015).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Assess the fire plan for the work area, including components such as fire alarms, fire extinguishers, exits and procedures, and make recommendations for improvements.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Assess hazards and apply appropriate safety procedures when working in a confined space.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Disconnect batteries and other power sources prior to undertaking autobody repairs where appropriate.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Describe ways to reduce personal injury or material and equipment damage as a result of unsafe work acts or environments.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Explain the proper procedures to follow to report a workplace injury.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Apply safe and fair work practices, including freedom from violence, harassment and bullying.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Assess the ergonomic design of the work space and implement appropriate procedures to ensure safety.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Implement a plan for a safe and healthy classroom and shop environment.

outcomes.statement: Examine the evolution and characteristics of automobile design.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 2: Automobile Design (Core) · Suggested Time: 4-6 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Research the history of automobile design from various eras and places and discuss characteristics of selected models.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify major (e.g., roof, floor, quarter panels, cowl section and rocker panels) and minor (e.g., front fenders, hood, trunk lid, door and splash pans) exterior automobile body components.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Compare body-on-frame, unibody and modified unitized automobile body construction.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explain how different types of glass (e.g., laminated and tempered) are designed to prevent injuries to automobile occupants.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Research required qualities and skills necessary to design automobiles.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Examine how financial considerations can impact automobile design.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Explore the effect of relevant federal legislation and regulations (e.g., safety) on automobile design.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Create, using drawing skills, computer-aided design programs or model-making, an innovative automobile body considering factors such as safety, fuel efficiency, occupant comfort and ride, ergonomics, automobile use and styling.

outcomes.statement: Use and maintain autobody hand tools and equipment following safe procedures.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 3: Hand Tools (Core) · Suggested Time: 4-6 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Describe how to use hand tools such as wrenches, screwdrivers, pliers, body hammers, chisels, dolly blocks, files, pulling tools, picking tools and hand cutting tools safely.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Perform correct procedures for a specific autobody repair using appropriate hand tools.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Inspect hand tools before use and tag for repair as required.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Maintain and store hand tools and equipment appropriately.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Research the cost of purchasing hand tools to enter the autobody trade.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Assess the design and organization of the workspace to prevent work-related injuries from the improper use of hand tools.

outcomes.statement: Use and maintain autobody power tools and equipment following safe procedures.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 4: Power Tools (Core) · Suggested Time: 4-6 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Describe how power tools such as grinders, drills, drill presses, nibblers, die grinders, cut-off wheels, files, featheredgers, ratchets and impact wrenches safely.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Perform correct procedures for a specific autobody repair using appropriate power tools.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Inspect power tools before use and tag for repair as required.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Maintain and store power tools and equipment appropriately.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Research the cost of purchasing power tools to enter the autobody trade.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Assess the design and organization of the workspace to prevent work-related injuries from the improper use of power tools.

outcomes.statement: Use gas metal art welding (GMAW) equipment to complete specified autobody welds.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 5A: Welding in Autobody (Core) · Suggested Time: 10-12 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Demonstrate knowledge of GMAW equipment such as nozzles, contact tips, liners, wire rolls, gauges and flow meters, amperage adjustment and voltage adjustment.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explain the importance of employing correct start-up and shut-down procedures for GMAW equipment including checking and cleaning up the work station.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Compare various types of wire and shielding gases used for GMAW.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Disassemble, clean and reassemble GMAW welder components.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Identify metals and perform preparation and assembly tasks prior to welding.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Perform and analyze a variety of specified welds, including plug weld, spot weld, butt weld and lap weld.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Identify the purpose and proper use and fit of personal protective equipment (PPE) required for welding, including eye protection (lens shades), clothing, hearing protection and footwear while identifying the hazards from which they protect individuals.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Ensure all PPE is cleaned appropriately.

outcomes.statement: Assess damaged areas and carry out repairs to straighten metal.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 6: Metal Straightening (Core) · Suggested Time: 20-30 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Modules 3

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Research the range of corrective work procedures required to straighten metal.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Estimate technical measurements to prepare a surface for repair.

indicators.label: c
d
indicators.text: Examine metal to detect how stretched areas feel and look, and determine how to shrink the areas.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Examine the metal to know where to shrink and how much to shrink, and use appropriate tools to shrink the areas.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Research, estimate and compare the repair cost to straighten metal versus replacement.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Assess the design and organization of the workspace to prevent workplace injuries when straightening metal.

outcomes.statement: Assess damaged areas and carry out repairs to body fill.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 7: Body Filling (Core) · Suggested Time: 8-12 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Prepare cost estimates of the materials used to repair damaged surfaces.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Estimate how much body filler and hardener is needed to repair damaged surfaces.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Rough areas to be filled with disc sanders using a 60-or 80-grit disc to ensure the body filler will adhere to the metal.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Demonstrate how to spread body filler over damaged areas with putty knives to create a smooth appearance similar to finished panels.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Apply appropriate sanding techniques to prepare surfaces for refinishing and to obtain true panel contours.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Examine damaged areas for smoothness and adjust as necessary to obtain true panel contours.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Practise proper safety procedures by wearing personal protective equipment (PPE) such as a particle mask, eye and ear protection and rubber gloves and cleaning as appropriate.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Assess the design and organization of the workspace to prevent workplace injuries when body filling.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Research short- and long-term health concerns related to body filler particles and dust in the workplace.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Prepare cost estimates of the materials used for repairing flat surfaces that have rust damage.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Estimate areas to be cut out for flat panel repairs.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Demonstrate how to measure areas to produce replacement panels.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Construct repair patches and apply correct welding procedures (e.g., lap joint or butt joint, spot or plug weld).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Select appropriate tools and procedures to prepare work areas for filling.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Examine patches to ensure repairs are ready for refinishing and painting.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Practise proper safety procedures for welding and using cut-off wheels.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Discuss how repairing rust damage contributes to environmental sustainability.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Assess the design and organization of the workspace to prevent workplace injuries when repairing panels.

outcomes.statement: Assess damaged areas and carry out repairs to contoured surfaces.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 9: Contoured Surface Repair (Core) · Suggested Time: 4-6 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Modules 4 and 5

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Prepare cost estimates of the materials used for repairing contoured surfaces.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Estimate areas to be cut out to do contoured panel repairs.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text:
Demonstrate how to measure areas and transfer to metal panels, including:

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Examine patches to ensure repairs are ready for refinishing and painting.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Estimate how much body filler and hardener is needed to repair damaged surfaces.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Perform appropriate procedures and select appropriate tools to prepare work areas for body filling.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Practice proper safety procedures for welding and using cut-off wheels.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Assess the design and organization of the workspace to prevent workplace injuries when repairing contoured panels.

outcomes.statement: Analyze workplace skills, knowledge and attitudes that lead to successful employment.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 31: Personal Skills for Success (Optional) · Suggested Time: 1-2 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Create a resume or a skills list.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Determine and practise guidelines used to participate in interviews.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Research employability skills to be successful in the workplace.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Investigate essential skills for the workplace and identify which would be most important for a career in autobody.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Establish a relationship with others in the workplace or shop setting by clearly defining roles and using effective communication.

indicators.label: f

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Create a list of personal interests, skills and traits that could lead to a career in the autobody trade.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Investigate occupations in the autobody trade (e.g., autobody repair technician, automotive restoration technician, commercial vehicle body repairer, automotive detailer, damage repair appraiser, automotive painter and insurance estimator).

indicators.text: Research which autobody-related occupations are facing shortages and which are oversubscribed locally, regionally or provincially.

indicators.text: Examine the roles, responsibilities, educational qualifications and personal and professional qualities common to people involved in autobody-related jobs.

allEvidence.quote: All PAA curricula are designed using modules, each with a single outcome for students to achieve.
Each Practical and Applied Arts curriculum is composed of modules configured into courses, along with suggestions for modules that are suitable for middle or secondary level survey courses.

allEvidence.observation: Each entry on the course's outcomes page is one module: the entry is titled with the module name and shows a “Module Code” (the outcome code in sk.json); the module's own page prints one “Outcome” with its indicators. outcomes.statement: Demonstrate, with teacher guidance, proper instrumental tone and technique.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Employ efficient breathing and breath support.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Play with correct posture and hand and instrument position.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Produce resonant tone consistently within appropriate register (e.g., adapt oral cavity).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Utilize correct instrument-specific embouchure.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Apply accurate articulations (e.g., placement of tongue, attack and release, lengths of notes).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Investigate extended techniques (e.g., vibrato where appropriate, experiment with timbral shading, multiple tonguing).

outcomes.statement:
Demonstrate fluency and proficiency in rudiments (i.e., batter percussion) and scales (i.e., wind instruments and mallet percussion) including:
- 7 major and related minor scales
- chromatic scales.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Play 7 major and related minor scales using multiple articulation and rhythmic patterns in ranges accessible to the student’s specific instrument.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Play chromatic scales in ranges accessible to the student’s specific instrument.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text:
Play batter percussion rudiments including:
- single stroke roll
- double stroke roll
- paradiddle
- multiple bounce roll.

outcomes.statement: Describe and apply, with guidance, aural skills related to sectional, ensemble and personal playing.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Hear and match pitch.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Discern accuracy of notes.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Match musical nuances such as length of note, tone colour and articulations within instrument section and full band.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Discern pitch variances (e.g., tuning, pitch accuracy, intonation) and make appropriate adjustments.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Create and reproduce musical ideas accurately using call and response utilizing more than one note.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Notate (e.g., traditional, non-traditional, graphic) simple melodic and rhythmic dictation accurately.

outcomes.statement: Interpret and represent musical ideas in a variety of ways, including standard music notation, to expressively communicate ideas.

indicators.text: Read and interpret, with teacher guidance, standard written musical communication.

indicators.text: Use critical thinking to revise, refine and share music through notation.

indicators.text: Represent musical ideas using standard notation.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explore non-standard notation (e.g., Aleatoric).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Reflect on progress of music reading and writing ability.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify the points of tension and release.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Apply expressive indicators (e.g., dynamics).

indicators.text: Respond to conductor’s gestures.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Shape phrases musically.

indicators.text: Interpret style with expression.

indicators.text: Determine the appropriate performance practice for the style of a given piece of music.

indicators.text: Discuss with teacher the intention of the piece.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Identify composer’s, performers’ and own intent for the piece.

indicators.label: i

indicators.text: Experiment with diverse music elements, techniques, tools, language and practices.

indicators.text: Experiment with improvisation (e.g., call and response).

indicators.text: Compose a short melody or riff (e.g., written, improvised).

outcomes.statement: Discuss the historical, cultural and social contexts of repertoire.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss musical elements that indicate the music’s context (e.g., instrumentation, style, cultural background).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explore the purpose and intent of the piece and apply this learning to own interpretation.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Identify relevant world events, views and cultural contexts that enhance understanding of the repertoire.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Describe the background of the composer.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Examine issues of appropriation in music.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Explore how evolving technology and media have influenced and changed how music is created, produced, distributed and shared (e.g., instrument evolution, recording, printing press, online music sites).

outcomes.statement: Explore a variety of Canadian and international music literature.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Listen to, and perhaps perform, selected pieces from Canadian and international music literature including historically under-represented composers (e.g., inclusive of Saskatchewan, Canadian, Indigenous, minority, gender and sexually diverse composers).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Study and/or perform wind band works composed by living composers (e.g., inclusive of Saskatchewan, Canadian, Indigenous, minority, gender and sexually diverse composers).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Connect composers’ personal experiences to the literature where appropriate (e.g., What inspired this composer to write this piece?).

outcomes.statement: Identify characteristics of high quality repertoire.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss characteristics of high quality repertoire.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Examine and play a range of repertoire (e.g., traditional wind band, composers of diverse genders, Indigenous, self- published, young composers, variety of genres and styles).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Examine and play repertoire that utilizes a variety of compositional techniques and devices.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Discuss criteria used in the process of designing a well-rounded concert program, considering diversity, focus and quality of repertoire selected.

outcomes.statement: Research and discuss First Nations and Métis traditional cultural methods of teaching, learning, creating and performing instrumental music.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text:
Generate inquiry questions to examine the meaning of “ways of knowing” such as:
- What are some cultural ways of knowing?
- What are some subject area or discipline-based ways of knowing (e.g., scientific ways of knowing, artistic ways of knowing)?

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Research and engage with Elders and local musicians and composers to learn about traditional instrumental music and Indigenous ways of knowing.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Investigate protocols and traditional/natural laws related to creating and performing instrumental music (e.g., gifting of music, issues surrounding cultural appropriation).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Engage with First Nations and Métis musicians (e.g., in person or online) to investigate how instrumental music is taught, learned, created and performed.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text:
Examine connections between spirituality and music across diverse cultures and traditions, for example:
- religious patrons
- music commissions
- music in ritual and ceremony
- cultural storytelling.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Examine the role of music in expressing Indigenous cultural and individual identity, past and present (e.g., treaty education outcome SI10: Analyze the spirit and intent of treaties and investigate the extent to which they have been fulfilled).

evidence.observation: The outcomes page groups the outcomes under 9 unit headings.

courses.name: Career and Work Exploration 10, 20, A30, B30

outcomes.statement: Investigate the career/life development process.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 1: An Introduction to Career Development (Core) · Suggested Time: 1-2 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss career/life development as a non-linear and life-long process.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Differentiate between job, occupation and career.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Describe the three levels (i.e., awareness, exploration and experiential) of the career/life development process.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Reflect on the career journey to date for self and a trusted adult.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Discuss potential future experiences that will have an impact on one’s lifelong career journey.

outcomes.statement: Explore transferable skills.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 2: Transferable Skills (Core) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explain the term transferable skills and provide examples of transferable skills within the context of specific occupations or jobs.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Compare the skills described by the Employability Skills and the skills described by the Essential Skills taxonomies which were developed by the Conference Board of Canada and Human Resources and Service Development Canada respectively.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Compare transferable skills to soft skills.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Showcase one’s transferable and soft skills in a personal career portfolio.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Explore volunteer activities within the community and discuss the opportunities they provide for enhancing one’s transferable skills.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Discuss opportunities to enhance one’s transferable skills through leisure activities.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Analyze local and provincial employment advertisements found in a variety of sources (e.g., online, print and social media) for common job requirements, including skills.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Explore and discuss ways to develop and improve upon one’s skill set while still in high school.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Describe how skills developed in high school can be transferred or applied to the workplace.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Discuss how transferable skills might evolve and change throughout one’s career journey.

outcomes.statement: Construct a personal career portfolio.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 3: Career Portfolios (Core) · Suggested Time: 5-10 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 2

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Reflect upon personal accomplishments, strengths, talents, skills, traits, abilities, interests, education and training as the basis for the development and organization of one’s career artifacts.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Generate a list of the types of artifacts (e.g., certificates, examples of school work/projects, photographs, videos, blogs, vlogs, personal web sites, awards, resume, cover letter and micro-credentials) that showcase one’s accomplishments, strengths, talents, skills, traits, abilities, interests, education and training.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of organizing one’s career artifacts in a print or online/digital portfolio.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Discuss common steps (e.g., collecting, reflecting and selecting) for determining artifacts that should be included in a career portfolio.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Discuss the benefits of having separate personal and career portfolios for school, career goals, personal life and work.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Develop one’s career portfolio that includes a resume, cover letter and other relevant artifacts.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text:
Reflect on the content within one’s career portfolio to answer questions such as:
- Who am I?
- What are my strengths and weaknesses?
- How have I demonstrated my talents, skills and abilities?
- What are some of my accomplishments both in and out of school?
- What are my interests?

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Describe the process and rationale for editing or modifying career artifacts (e.g., documents such as a cover letter or resume) to suit the needs of a specific job application.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Explore how on-line platforms and social media tools can be used to develop and/or organize career artifacts.

outcomes.statement: Explore types of work.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 4: Types of Work (Core) · Suggested Time: 2-3 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 1

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Differentiate between types of work such as full-time, part-time, seasonal, contract, gig, casual, shift, self-employment, entrepreneurship and volunteer.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Discuss when and why individuals might engage in each type of work.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Generate a list of jobs in one’s community and classify them according to the types of work.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Discuss how being employed or volunteering supports positive mental health and engaged citizenship.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text:
Reflect on questions such as:
- Why do people work?
- Why do people choose a particular occupation?
- What are my career goals and how will I achieve them?
- Why do I want to or not want to pursue a particular career?

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Research the concept of non-traditional careers and provide examples relevant to one’s community, province and country.

outcomes.statement: Explore the potential impact of networking on one’s career journey.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 5: Recognizing Networks (Optional) · Suggested Time: 2-3 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 1

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Define networking.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Differentiate among personal, social and career networks.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text:
Describe one’s personal, social and career networks by answering questions such as:
- Whom do I know?
- What do I do outside of school?
- What opportunities exist or could exist because of these networks?

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Recognize how networking can impact one’s career opportunities and support one’s career journey.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Discuss how online and social media activity as well as one’s digital identity can positively and negatively impact such things as employment status, employability and career opportunities.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Identify potential allies (e.g., people, groups, businesses, post-secondary institutions and training institutions) that could be a part of one’s network to support at least one career development interest.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Describe ways (e.g., volunteering, job shadows and informational interviews) to build and expand networks.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: List the advantages and disadvantages of networking with a variety of allies.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Discuss the mutual benefits of contributing to and receiving support from a network.

outcomes.statement: Access and assess sources of career information.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 6: Sources of Career Information (Core) · Suggested Time: 1-2 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 1

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss how to determine if a source of career information is considered credible.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Research sources of career information found within one’s school.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Identify a variety of sources of career information (e.g., online job sites, social media sites, local career centres, regional colleges, post-secondary institutions, online career planning programs, government agencies, newcomer centres, print publications, peers and adults) and how they can support career development.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Compare the types of career information available through a variety of sources.

outcomes.statement: Explore industry sectors.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 7: Industry Sectors (Core) · Suggested Time: 1-2 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 1 and 2

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Research various ways of classifying and organizing occupations, including the National Occupational Classification (NOC) tool and the North American Industry Classification System (NAICS).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: List the main industry sectors at the local, provincial and national levels.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Provide examples of occupations and job opportunities within each sector at all three levels.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Discuss how political, environmental, economic, technological and other factors can impact industry sectors.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Identify transferable skills that are common to many industry sectors.

outcomes.statement: Analyze how a variety of factors influence career decisions and planning.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 9: Self-Awareness and Career Choices (Core) · Suggested Time: 4-8 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Complete personal inventories to determine one’s values, learning styles, interests, personality, emotional intelligence, strengths, multiple intelligences and/or virtues.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Reflect on how results from personal inventories connect to perceptions of self and potential career opportunities.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Investigate work placement opportunities in one’s community based on the results from personal inventories.

outcomes.statement: Analyze fair and cooperative workplace practices and procedures.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 14A: Employment Standards A (Core) · Suggested Time: 1-2 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Describe individual’s rights and responsibilities with respect to fair treatment in the workplace as outlined by the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms and the Saskatchewan Human Rights Code.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: List fair workplace practices covered by The Saskatchewan Employment Act, 2019.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text:
Brainstorm a list of questions new employees should ask employers before beginning work, and role-play appropriate ways to ask them. Questions may include:
- What is my schedule of work hours?
- What is my wage?
- How and when will I be paid?
- What deductions will be made from my pay cheque?
- Who is my supervisor?

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Discuss and suggest ways to address conflict situations that may occur in the workplace.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Propose resolutions to workplace conflict as represented in a variety of scenarios.

outcomes.statement: Analyze the importance of rights and responsibilities in relation to workplace safety.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 15A: Workplace Safety – Rights and Responsibilities (Core) · Suggested Time: 1-3 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text:
Describe and reflect on the three basic rights that all workers have under Part III – Occupational Health and Safety in The Saskatchewan Employment Act, 2019:
- the right to know - the hazards at work and how to control them;
- the right to participate - in finding and controlling workplace hazards; and,
- the right to refuse - work that you believe is unusually dangerous.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Research employer and worker responsibilities with respect to health and safety standards as required by law in Saskatchewan.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Discuss steps that can be taken to refuse potentially unsafe work.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Role-play scenarios to demonstrate how to properly refuse potentially unsafe work.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Explain the purpose of The Saskatchewan Employment Act, 2019 and associated Regulations, and how they affect safe workplace practices.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Investigate how workers can participate in and support health and safety activities in the workplace. (e.g., Occupational Health and Safety Committees, professional development, training and following safety procedures).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Discuss the importance of reporting workplace incidents, dangerous occurrences, injuries, or illnesses immediately and the proper procedure to do so.

outcomes.statement: Explore workplace hazards and injury prevention.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 16A: Workplace Safety – Hazards and Injury Prevention (Core) · Suggested Time: 2-5 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 15A

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss how a workplace injury might affect the injured worker and others such as the employer, supervisor, work colleagues, family and friends.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Differentiate between a workplace hazard and risk.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Differentiate among the four Occupational Health and Safety (OHS) hazard categories including physical (e.g., heavy lifting, repetitive motion, slipping/tripping, working at heights, working alone, cuts and burns), chemical (e.g., chemicals, fumes, vapours and gases), biological (e.g., viruses, fungi, bacteria, mold; bodily fluids; sewage; animal/pet waste; and influenza), and psychological (e.g., harassment and bullying, stress, fatigue and shift work).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Provide examples of potential workplace hazards in the five major categories.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Describe employers’ and employees’ rights and responsibilities pertaining to workplace hazards and how they can work together to prevent workplace hazards.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Discuss the importance of proper orientation, training, appropriate supervision, workplace inspections and following safe work practices, and provide examples of each for a variety of industries.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Identify potential safety hazards in a variety of environments including home, school, and workplace.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Explore safety statistics related to young workers in the workplace in Saskatchewan and Canada and compare the statistics to those of workers in other age brackets.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Describe current prevention programs or agencies (e.g., Mission Zero, Work Safe Saskatchewan and Saskatchewan Safety Council) in Saskatchewan that are designed to raise awareness of and prevent workplace incidents.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Explain health and safety regulations common to a specific occupation of interest.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Identify employer responsibilities in relation to safety hazards.

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Discuss the need for health and safety legislation and regulations.

outcomes.statement: Explore the Workplace Hazardous Materials Information System (WHMIS).
outcomes.printedWith: Module 17A: Workplace Safety – Workplace Hazardous Materials Information System (WHMIS) (Core) · Suggested Time: 2-5 hours · Level: Advanced · Prerequisite: Module 16A

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss what the Workplace Hazardous Materials Information System (WHMIS) is and its purpose and scope in the workplace.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Differentiate between general education and workplace training in regards to WHMIS 2015.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Discuss factors that determine the required level of workplace specific training in WHMIS 2015.

indicators.label: d
e
indicators.text: Define the four parts of WHMIS 2015 (i.e., hazard identification and product classification; labels with warning symbols; Safety Data Sheets (SDS); and worker education and worksite specific training) that help workers handle hazardous materials safely.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Identify the roles and responsibilities of the employer, worker, and supplier in relation to the safe handling of hazardous materials.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Describe the two main types of WHMIS 2015 labels (i.e., supplier and workplace).

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Differentiate between the supplier label and workplace label.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Identify hazard classes and categories.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Describe the purpose and contents of current hazard pictograms.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Identify the 16 sections of a Safety Data Sheet (SDS).

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Describe the usefulness of Safety Data Sheets (SDS) in helping to control hazardous materials.

indicators.label: m
indicators.text: Role-play a variety of scenarios that require one to evaluate hazardous materials and respond appropriately.

outcomes.statement: Analyze components of a pay stub.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 21: Understanding Earnings (Core) · Suggested Time: 1-2 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Differentiate among the various types of pay periods for employees such as weekly, bi-weekly, semi-monthly and monthly, and discuss their impact on personal budgeting.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Discuss methods of payment such as direct deposit, cash and cheque.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Identify the information that must be listed on a pay stub or statement of earnings as required by law (i.e., Part II Employment Standards in The Saskatchewan Employment Act, 2019).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Differentiate among deductions that are required (i.e., income tax, Canadian Pension Plan and Employment Insurance), allowable (e.g., employee contributions to pension plans; charitable donations voluntarily made by an employee; and volunteer employee purchases from the employer for goods, services or merchandise) and illegal (e.g., deductions for alleged theft, damages, breakages and poor quality work).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Calculate gross pay for various earning situations such as contract, hourly and commission.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Identify strategies for dealing with a payroll error.

outcomes.statement: Explore factors that contribute to a successful work placement experience.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 80A: Work Study Preparation A (Core) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Modules 3, 9

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explain the roles and responsibilities of each partner (e.g., student, parent or guardian, teacher or other school staff and employer) involved in the work placement.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Research the business/organization to become familiar with its operations.

indicators.label: c
d
indicators.text: Identify safety hazards that could potentially be encountered during the work placement experience.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text:
Compose a list of questions related to workplace hazards and safety to ask of the work placement employer such as:
- What physical, chemical, ergonomic or biological hazards should I be aware of in my work placement?
- When will I receive job safety training and orientation before I begin work?
- Where do I find fire extinguishers, first aid kits and emergency assistance?
- What type of safety gear or other clothing am I expected to wear? Is it provided?
- What should I do if I get injured or have an accident in the workplace?
- How can I contact my health and safety committee or representative?
- Are there any health and safety procedures I should follow?
- Who is the first aid person?
- Where are safety notices posted?
- What should I do in case of a fire or emergency?

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Identify employment standards (e.g., use of a uniform) that may pertain to one’s work placement.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Reflect on one’s right to know, right to participate and right to refuse while in the work placement.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Develop personal and learning goals for the work placement in consultation with the parent or guardian, teacher or other school staff member and employer.

outcomes.statement: Prepare for the work placement experience.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 81A: Work Study Preparation B (Core) · Suggested Time: 5-8 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 80A

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Update personal career artifacts (e.g., resume and cover letter) as required for the work placement, and provide to the work placement employer.

indicators.label: b
c
indicators.text: Compile an employer information package that includes documents (e.g., permission forms, logs and self- and employer- evaluation forms) needed for the work placement.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Describe how factors such as one’s educational and other experiences including paid, unpaid and volunteer work; self-concept; personality; needs; values; interests; knowledge; skills; attitudes; and career goals and plan might impact one’s contribution in the workplace.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text:
Brainstorm a list of questions to ask the employer before beginning the work placement; these may include:
- What is my schedule of work hours?
- Who is my supervisor?
- What should I wear?
- What personal grooming standards are expected?
- When will I be provided with safety training?

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Develop a list of questions that might be asked by the employer in the preplacement interview and prepare answers for them.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Participate in an interview with the employer prior to beginning the work placement.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Reflect on one’s performance during the interview.

outcomes.statement: Participate in a work placement experience.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 82A: Work Placement (Core) · Suggested Time: 30-50 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 81A

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Apply relevant skills and abilities during the work placement experience.

indicators.label: b
c
indicators.text: Document observations of employment standards, workplace ethics, privacy, culture, rights and responsibilities, occupational health and safety, and networking during the work placement.

outcomes.statement: Relate one’s work placement experience to personal and career goals.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 83A: Work Study Follow-up (Core) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 82A

indicators.label: a
b
c
indicators.text: Update artifacts (e.g., resume and evidences of learning) within one’s career portfolio following the work placement.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: In appreciation prepare a letter, note, card or other communication for the work placement employer.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Develop and/or revise personal and career goals based on the work placement experience.

evidence.quote: All PAA curricula are designed using modules, each with a single outcome for students to achieve.

allEvidence.quote: All PAA curricula are designed using modules, each with a single outcome for students to achieve.
Each Practical and Applied Arts curriculum is composed of modules configured into courses, along with suggestions for modules that are suitable for middle or secondary level survey courses.

allEvidence.observation: Each entry on the course's outcomes page is one module: the entry is titled with the module name and shows a “Module Code” (the outcome code in sk.json); the module's own page prints one “Outcome” with its indicators. The site lists the course levels under “Course Configurations”.

modules.name: Module 1: An Introduction to Career Development (Core)
Module 15A: Workplace Safety – Rights and Responsibilities (Core)
Module 16A: Workplace Safety – Hazards and Injury Prevention (Core)
Module 17A: Workplace Safety – Workplace Hazardous Materials Information System (WHMIS) (Core)
