outcomes.statement:
Examine the significance of God's covenantal relationship with humanity through the stories of:
- Moses
- David
- selected prophets of the Old Testament.
outcomes.printedWith: [SH, KG]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text:
Interpret lessons learned about hearing and heeding the call of God through the stories of:
- Moses (e.g., God commissions us to do His work)
- David (e.g., the smallest or seemingly least can be great with God) prophets of the Old Testament (e.g., Miriam – courageously live and celebrate your faith in God, Jonah - you cannot run from the call of God, Samuel - sometimes we need others to help us discern God is calling us).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Give examples of how individuals within the Catholic community, including oneself, respond to the revelation of God's commitment through covenant.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explain the significance of the name of God revealed to Moses (i.e., "I am"), and collaborate to examine the significance of other key faith experiences of Moses.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Identify ways the story of Moses foreshadows the story of Jesus including Passover for the Paschal mystery.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text:
Examine Catholic perspectives on the Davidic covenant such as:
- David's rise to and loss of power (e.g., trust in God)
- the role of Jerusalem in salvation history (e.g., capital city uniting the northern and southern tribes of Israel)
- the importance of the Temple in salvation history (e.g., physical reminder of the covenants with Adam, Noah, Abraham, Moses and David giving added significance to Mt. 12:6).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Identify how David fulfills the roles of priest, prophet and king, and discuss one's own call to such roles within the covenant.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Examine connections between David and the Messiah as presented through various prophets (e.g., Samuel, Isaiah, Jeremiah).

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Represent how the prophets play the role of bridge from Moses to Messiah within salvation history.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text:
Discuss various ways the prophets describe the Eucharistic covenant of the Messiah such as:
- new covenant (e.g., Jeremiah)
- everlasting covenant (e.g., Isaiah)
- covenant of peace (e.g., Ezekiel).

outcomes.statement: Examine the history of the development of the four Gospels and consider implications for faith formation.
outcomes.printedWith: [KG]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text:
Outline and explain the three stages of Gospel formation including:
- life and teaching of Jesus Christ
- oral tradition
- written Gospels.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explain why the Gospels were not written immediately following the death and resurrection of Jesus (e.g., expectation of impending Second Coming, prevalence of oral tradition, literacy rates, etc.).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Discuss the influence of oral teachings (i.e., stage two of Gospel formation) on the written Gospels (i.e., stage three of Gospel formation).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Discuss the impact on personal faith of skepticism concerning the historical accuracy of the Gospels (e.g., accuracy of oral traditions, limited historical documents on the life and teaching of Jesus).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Identify the target audiences of all four Gospels and discuss implications for the writing style, content, and sequencing of the Good News according to each of the four evangelists (i.e., Matthew, Mark, Luke and John).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text:
Discuss how understanding Gospel formation and intent influences the development of faith using examples such as:
- the development of the synoptic gospels
- the theory of a potential Q-source
- presence of unique content within John's Gospel
- conflicting interpretations of scripture (e.g., contextualists vs. Bible literalists).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Explain key uses of the Gospels after they were written (e.g., prayer, liturgy, catechesis, evangelization) and examine their influence on communal and personal faith development.

outcomes.statement: Contrast the Mosaic Law perspective on morality and sin with a contemporary Christian perspective of relationship building with God.
outcomes.printedWith: [SH, DHP, CH]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss the place of the Ten Commandments within Mosaic Law.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Discuss the shift in understanding the Ten Commandments as laws (e.g., enforced by scribes and Pharisees) to a relationship with God in the spirit of the law (e.g., Jesus as fulfillment of the law).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text:
Contrast how each of the Ten Commandments was understood from a legal perspective and a contemporary relational context through discussions such as:
- keep holy the Sabbath (e.g., adherence to Sabbath laws moving towards relationship building with God)
- honour mother and father (e.g., moving from honouring parents towards honouring parents and other elders within the community)
- do not commit adultery (e.g., rules and punishment pertaining to extra-marital sex moving towards personal responsibility for sexual morality)
- do not covet (e.g., person as possession moving towards recognition of the dignity of the person).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Distinguish the difference between merely avoiding evil and doing good using examples from Mosaic law and relational perspectives (e.g., the parable of the Good Samaritan).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text:
Discuss legalistic and relational considerations in making a moral judgement including:
- the moral object (i.e., action)
- the moral intention (i.e., motive)
- the moral circumstance (i.e., context and consequence).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Collaborate with peers to represent the Catholic teaching that a good intention can never justify an evil act.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Discuss examples of diminished responsibility for immoral acts (e.g., conditions for mortal sin).

outcomes.statement: Express Catholic perspectives on forgiveness, mercy, generosity, justice and joy within the ongoing nature of salvation history.
outcomes.printedWith: [SH, SSM]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text:
Examine Catholic connections between:
- original sin and forgiveness, mercy, generosity, justice and joy
- personal sin and forgiveness, mercy, generosity, justice and joy

indicators.label: b
indicators.text:
Respond to Christian religious artworks and writings pertaining to forgiveness, mercy, generosity, justice and joy such as:
- Rembrandt's The Prodigal Son
- Michaelangelo's The Creation of Adam
- various Byzantine icons such as Christ the Pantocrator or The Mother of Perpetual Help
- local church art such as stained glass and statues
- excerpts from Pope Francis's Joy of the Gospel
- The Jesus Prayer (i.e. Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me, a sinner)
- Gospel parables such as The Prodigal Son, The Good Samaritan, The Workers in the Vineyard
- various poems in honour of Saint Mother Teresa

indicators.label: c
indicators.text:
Create a representation (e.g., visual, written, digital) incorporating distinguishing features of forgiveness from a Catholic perspective such as:
- forgiveness does not excuse an act
- forgiveness does not remove responsibility of the offender to repair damage done by an act
- forgiveness desires positive change, not revenge
- forgiveness does not have limitations.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text:
Investigate why and how one should forgive or seek forgiveness when forgiveness is difficult in situations such as:
- genocide and terrorism (e.g., Holocaust, Holodomor, Rwanda, recent terrorist acts such as 9/11)
- racial segregation including First Nations residential school experiences and others (e.g., Apartheid and slavery)
- abuse and violence (e.g., sexual, emotional, domestic)
- bullying (e.g., cyber, physical, emotional, mental, spiritual)
- betrayal by a friend or family member.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Recognize conversion as a process involving contrition, confession and correction.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Discuss ways that sacramental reconciliation involves forgiveness, mercy, generosity, justice and joy.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text:
Express how humility can lead to:
- joy
- generosity
- a Magnificat moment (i.e., modest recognition of one's talents as gifts from the Creator)
- social justice.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text:
Examine how individuals, although flawed, can exemplify characteristics of:
- forgiveness lived (e.g., Immaculée Ilibagiza, Rev. Dale Lang)
- mercy lived (e.g., Sister Helen Prejean, Oskar Schindler)
- generosity lived (e.g., St. Vincent de Paul, St. Marguerite d'Youville)
- justice lived (e.g., Malala Yousafzai, Ovide William Mercredi of the Cree Nation, Aung San Suu Kyi, Gabriel Dumont of the Métis Nation)
- joy lived (e.g., St. André Bessette, St. Thérèse of Lisieux , St. Philip Neri).

outcomes.statement:
Investigate the existence, source, and purpose of miracles through examples from:
- the Old Testament
- the New Testament
- the historical era of the past 200 years.
outcomes.printedWith: [SH, CH]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Recognize the value of wonder and awe in relation to the beauty of miracles of life, Creation, and all works of an omnipotent God.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Compare secular and religious perspectives on miracles including the Catholic emphasis on a miracle's source and purpose (e.g., message or resulting teaching).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text:
Explain the Catholic understanding of the source, purpose and validity of various miracles such as those involving:
- Moses (e.g., burning bush, plagues, parting of the Red Sea)
- Jesus (e.g., water to wine, healing, commanding weather, casting out demons, raising the dead)
- Pentecost (e.g., the miracle of the tongues)
- Church authenticated miracles in modern history (e.g., Fatima, Lourdes, St. Padre Pio, Our Lady of Guadalupe and the tilma of St. Juan Diego).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text:
Investigate the Church's approach to claims of miracles including:
- canonization of saints (e.g., venerable to blessed to saint)
- validation processes (e.g., use of research and science)
- examination for purpose (e.g., a discernable message from God)
- authentication of a miracle, deeming it worthy of belief but not a requisite of faith.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Discuss various motives of fraudulent claims of miracles (e.g., power, money, fame, religious zealotry/fanaticism).

outcomes.statement: Evaluate the essential Christian conviction of Jesus as the Messiah.
outcomes.printedWith: [SH, KG, CH]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss the concept of Messiah as developed within Jewish history and prophesized within the Old Testament.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Examine the implications of naming John the Baptist as the last prophet and the prophet of the Most High.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Provide examples of how God spoke to people prior to and following the Word becoming flesh and living among humanity in Jesus.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text:
Analyze how events from Scripture support the conviction of Jesus as Messiah such as:
- the Incarnation (e.g., the Word became flesh, Jn. 1: 1-14)
- infancy narratives of Jesus including the role of Mary
- baptism of Jesus
- temptation of Jesus
- statements made by Jesus indicating his messianic nature such as Mt. 12: 6 and Luke 4: 16-21
- Transfiguration of Jesus
- Institution of the Eucharist at the Last Supper
- Agony in the Garden
- death and Resurrection.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text:
Analyze how the miracles of Jesus in Scripture support a claim of Jesus as Messiah including miracles such as:
- curing the sick
- casting out demons
- controlling nature
- raising the dead.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Outline beliefs and discuss motives of those who do not view Jesus as Messiah including followers of the new atheism, Jews and Muslims.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text:
Assess arguments naming Jesus as the Messiah from Catholic teaching authorities such as:
- the magisterium (e.g., John Paul II's Redemptoris Missio #5 and Dives In Misericordia #3)
- saints (e.g., St. Augustine, St. Teresa of Avila)
- theologians (e.g., Joseph Ratzinger/Pope Benedict XVI, Dr. Josephine Lombardi)
- apologists (e.g., C.S. Lewis, Peter Kreeft).

outcomes.statement: Investigate Catholic evangelization as a call from God.
outcomes.printedWith: [SH, KG, CH]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explain how the call to evangelize is both individual and communal in nature.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Distinguish between examples of evangelization (e.g., involving zeal, respect for freedom) and proselytization (e.g., involving coercive indoctrination, unjust use of force and power).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text:
Examine how effective evangelization incorporates the Canadian Conference of Catholic Bishops' five important actions of the Catholic Church in pursuit of her mission:
- Proclaim Jesus Christ
- Worship Christ through the sacraments
- Form a communion of people
- Give witness, and
- Serve.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Investigate how individual Catholics, although flawed, have led others into a relationship with God through their example (e.g., Catholics in the community and well known individuals such as Pope John Paul II, Saint Mother Teresa, Jean Vanier, Saint Kateri Tekakwitha, Chiara Lubich, Catherine Doherty, Father Athol Murray).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Investigate how proselytization may lead to societal challenges such as assimilation practices or religious extremism.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Role play the evangelization of those who oppose Christianity (e.g., atheistic scientist, agnostic, secular humanist or moral relativist).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text:
Demonstrate connections among:
- the call to evangelization in contemporary society
- the Scriptural question: 'Am I my brother's keeper?'
- Pope Francis' concepts of a "culture of encounter" (e.g., Evangelii Gaudium 3) and "missionary disciples" (e.g., Evangelii Gaudium 120).

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Analyze what is meant by the 'new evangelization' of the Catholic Church and propose methods to achieve it.

outcomes.statement: Examine the benefits, challenges and responsibilities of being both a member of a church and an engaged citizen.
outcomes.printedWith: [KG, DHP, CH]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explain Jesus' statement to "Give back to Caesar what is Caesar's and to God what is God's" (Mk. 12:17).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Contrast Peter's words: "we must obey God rather than any human authority" (Acts 5:29) with Paul's writings on submitting to governing authority (e.g., Romans 13: 1-7).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Debate issues of the primacy of conscience versus the authority of church and government (e.g., misuse of power, civil disobedience, conscientious objection, other issues addressed in the Pastoral Letter on Freedom of Conscience and Religion, April, 2012 - CCCB).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Examine Christian perspectives on political themes such as globalization, economic inequality and self-interest.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text:
Discuss benefits and challenges of the ten responsibilities of a good government identified by the Canadian Conference of Catholic Bishops, 2001 including:
- respect the dignity of the person
- accept the rule of law
- promote the common good and good order
- protect the family
- safeguard the right to life of every person
- be responsible for the economy and well-being of citizens
- give access to work and just wages
- ensure religious freedom
- look after the health of citizens
- defend the country.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text:
Discuss benefits and challenges of the six responsibilities of citizens to the country identified by the Canadian Conference of Catholic Bishops, 2001 including:
- obey civil authority
- vote
- participate in public life
- pay taxes
- welcome immigrants and refugees
- defend the country.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Examine the obligation of a Catholic to assist those who are politically marginalized by governmental policies including First Nations and Métis peoples and others (e.g., veterans, refugees).

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Construct meaning for the expression 'politically active', and inquire into how living according to the Gospel is a political act (e.g., called to transform culture).

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Examine how a Christian life may lead to supporting the work of Canadian social movements and organizations (e.g., Chalice, Christian Near East Welfare Association, Development and Peace, World Wildlife Fund Canada, Métis Nation - Saskatchewan).

outcomes.statement:
Examine Catholic social teachings and actions involving:
- reverence for life
- treatment of the marginalized
- social sin.
outcomes.printedWith: [DHP, CH]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text:
Discuss effects, culpability and individual responsibility resulting from:
- original sin (i.e., Adam and Eve)
- personal sin (i.e., actual sin)
- social sin (i.e., structures of sin).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Contrast Catholic teachings on reverence for life, treatment of the marginalized and social sin with moral relativist examples.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Use scripture to support understanding and application of Catholic social teachings on reverence for life, treatment of the marginalized and social sin.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text:
Use the experiences of Mary to deepen understanding of Catholic social teachings regarding issues such as:
- reverence for life (e.g., "yes" to the angel Gabriel, mourning of Jesus)
- treatment of the marginalized (e.g., Mary as widow, as refugee, as homeless, as poor)
- social sin (e.g., Mary living in a male-dominated society).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text:
Explain how Scripture and Church teachings influence personal views on:
- life issues (e.g., abortion, euthanasia, palliative care, Dr. assisted-suicide, suicide, capital punishment)
- the treatment of the marginalized (e.g., the poor, elderly, disabled, those suffering from discrimination, human trafficking)
- social sin within contemporary society (e.g., pornography, prostitution, gambling).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Examine the cause and effects of various poverties (e.g., economic, relational, spiritual) in the world and how the Catholic community seeks to address them.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text:
Analyze and discuss how a person's views might be challenged when presented with Church teaching regarding the 'Preferential Option for the Poor' supported in Scripture and Tradition such as:
- Ex. 22:20-26, Is. 58: 5-7, Mt. 25:34-40, Lk. 4:16-21
- Pope Paul VI's encyclical Populorum Progressio #23, Pope John Paul II's encyclical Centesimus Annus #58.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text:
Discuss the marginalization of First Nations, Métis and Inuit peoples of Canada through topics such as:
- the Truth and Reconciliation process and Calls to Action
- Jordan's Principle (e.g., First Nations and Métis children disadvantaged due to conflicts involving federal and provincial bureaucracy)
- treaties that remain unfulfilled.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text:
Apply to societal issues such as sanctity of life, marginalization and social sin the five steps of effective social action identified by the Canadian Conference of Catholic Bishops:
- Be present to the poor.
- Develop understanding of the causes of suffering.
- Judge the situation in light of Gospel values and Church teaching.
- Think and act creatively, guided by the vision of the kingdom of God.
- Act together (in solidarity) to transform unjust situations.

outcomes.statement: Analyze Catholic prayer teachings and reflect on their influence on one's prayer life.
outcomes.printedWith: [KG, CH, SSM]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text:
Analyze and discuss how one's prayer life may be influenced by Catholic teachings regarding:
- why pray
- how to pray
- what to pray for
- when to pray
- to whom a person should direct prayer (e.g., God the Father, God the Son, God the Holy Spirit)
- through and with whom a person may be encouraged to pray (e.g., Mary, saints, the angelic host).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text:
Discuss relationships among and benefits of:
- personal prayer (i.e., prayers dealing with personal issues)
- private prayer (i.e., prayers made by oneself)
- communal prayer (i.e., praying with others).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text:
Create an arts expression in response to the five types of prayer listed within the Catechism of the Catholic Church including:
- petition (e.g., asking for what one wants)
- intercession (e.g., prayer for others)
- thanksgiving (e.g., gratitude for gifts of life and love, moving away from selfishness, enjoying what life brings)
- praise and worship (e.g., respect for God, celebrates everything coming from and belonging to God, results in bringing God's love to others)
- blessing and adoration (e.g., recognition of the nature of God, leads to being 'poor in spirit', recognizes everything comes from and belongs to God and therefore everything can be used for the glory of God).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Investigate similarities and differences in prayer among Christian, Jewish, First Nations and Métis traditions (e.g., mealtime prayers, prayers of thanksgiving, praise and worship, petition and intercession).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Examine the infusion of cultural traditions within Catholic ecclesial prayer rituals including First Nations traditions (e.g., smudging ceremonies within the Catholic church, Way of The Cross events incorporating cultural art works, Theophany Water Blessing, diverse Holy Week cultural traditions such as Catholic Filipino and Ukrainian Catholic).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Explain the Catholic view that prayer should be affective in nature (e.g., causing personal change or growth) and thereby leads to acts of goodness (e.g., being an instrument of God's will, deepening one's connection to God).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Construct a plan for personal prayer and action using Jesus as a model (e.g., prayed in solitude, led others in prayer, fasted).

outcomes.statement: Express personal beliefs about life after death and spiritual beings considering Catholic perspectives and other views.
outcomes.printedWith: [KG, CH, SSM]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss the relationship between scientific inquiry and spiritual and religious beliefs (e.g., physical evidence for spiritual claims).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text:
Pose questions for inquiry regarding the spiritual nature of one's existence through the use of examples such as:
- creation stories and myths
- beliefs about the Creator
- the eternal nature of spirit or soul
- Elders' knowledge of vision quests and spiritual ways of knowing
- spiritual beings such as angels, demons, animal spirits, ghosts
- spiritual apparitions and supernatural experiences.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text:
Investigate concepts of life after death from various spiritual and religious viewpoints considering perspectives such as:
- Christian views about heaven, hell and purgatory
- Byzantine and Orthodox understandings of the journey of theosis
- First Nations, Métis and Inuit traditions
- Judaism, Islam, Hinduism, Buddhism traditions
- Atheism.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Examine the role of saints in Catholic tradition and contrast this to other approaches to prayer related to the deceased including traditional First Nations' ceremonies and others (e.g., Catholic prayer with and through the saints, Catholic prayer for and through the dearly departed, Eastern Christian concept of eternal memory, the Hindu cycle of rebirth).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text:
Assess how one's exposure to varying spiritual and religious viewpoints influence personal beliefs about life, death and spiritual beings considering concepts such as:
- personal ethics and morality
- sin and forgiveness
- obedience and freedom
- hope.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Contrast Catholic teachings (CCC 1673, 1237, 2116, 2117) about exorcism and acts of divination (e.g., séance, Ouija boards, astrology, palm reading) with pop culture views (e.g., dismissive harmless games, portrayals in horror films).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text:
Examine perspectives on life after death and spiritual beings by responding to arts expressions such as:
- Traditional Powwow dances
- On Eagle's Wings by Michael Joncas (Psalm 91 and Isaiah 40:31)
- The First Nation Art Garden (Toronto Zoo's Turtle Island Conservation Program)
- the murals of Berthold Imhoff in St. Peter's Cathedral at Muenster, Saskatchewan.
- The Ecstasy of St. Teresa of Avila sculpture by Bernini
- The Fall of the Rebel Angels painting by Pieter Bruegel
- The Ladder of Divine Ascent, St. John Climacus
- excerpts from Dante's Inferno or John Milton's Paradise Lost
- other contemporary works (e.g., music, literature, cartoons, visual art, film).

outcomes.statement: Examine principles, benefits and challenges of interfaith dialogue.
outcomes.printedWith: [SH, KG, DHP, CH, SSM]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text:
Examine key principles of interfaith dialogue such as commitment to:
- accept others as equal partners
- learn and share rather than teach
- respect diversity within and among religions
- include all religious and spiritual communities who wish to be engaged in dialogue
- seek to understand what is true and holy in other religions (e.g., Nostra Aetate)
- challenge the misuse of religion for political gain or to justify violence or coercion
- critique one's own tradition and seek to understand criticisms of that tradition
- critically appraise online materials and conversations about diverse religious and spiritual traditions
- collaborate on common goals (e.g., peace, environment, poverty, human dignity).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Discuss Jewish, Christian and Muslim views on the role of key religious historical figures such as Abraham, Isaac, Ishmael, Noah, Moses, Mary, Jesus and Mohammed.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Compare rituals of worship, forms of prayer, development of moral codes, and religious artistic expression of Jews, Christians and Muslims.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Describe the effects of persecution on interfaith dialogue throughout history faced by Jews (e.g., anti-Semitism), Christians (e.g., martyrdom) and Muslims (e.g., Islamophobia).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text:
Investigate how interfaith dialogue is supported by understanding historic events and movements such as:
- genocidal acts (e.g., the Holocaust, Holodomor, the Kurdish Genocide: Al-Anfal Campaign)
- the Crusades
- religious extremism within Judaism (e.g., the Kingdom of Israel/Tzrifin Underground)
- religious extremism within Christianity (e.g., Ku Klux Klan)
- religious extremism within Islam (e.g., Al-Qaeda).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Research case studies where interfaith dialogue results in positive change among Jews, Christians and/or Muslims (e.g., Albania's Muslim and Christian populations, Pope Paul VI's Nostra Aetate, the work of Saskatchewan born Sister Rosaleen Zdunich B.Ed. M.Sc. ).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text:
Describe the relationships between interfaith dialogue and Pope Francis' concepts of:
- building a 'culture of encounter' (e.g., Evangelii Gaudium - The Joy of the Gospel)
- 'care of our common home' (e.g., Laudato Si' – Praise be to You).

outcomes.statement: Describe how one's experience in a Christian Action Project, rally and/or retreat affects one's life and understanding of the call to evangelize.
outcomes.printedWith: [DHP, SSM]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Create, in collaboration with one's peers and teacher, a plan for participation in a Christian Action Project, rally and/or retreat.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explain how the planned Christian Action Project, rally and/or retreat might affect one's life, faith development and call to evangelize.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Examine the impact of faith-motivated service and communal endeavors on individuals and communities.

evidence.observation: The “Outcomes and Indicators” table lists the Catholic Studies 10 outcomes as one numbered sequence under a single heading, with no unit, strand, theme or module headings.

allEvidence.observation: The “Outcomes and Indicators” table lists the Catholic Studies 10 outcomes as one numbered sequence under a single heading, with no unit, strand, theme or module headings.

outcomes.statement: Demonstrate basic fundamentals of vocal technique.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Sing with breath support (e.g., practise appropriate breathing technique and recognize how it helps support sound production and vocal health).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Describe and demonstrate quality singing in response to given criteria and considering cultural context.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Hear and match pitch and discern accuracy of notes.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Discuss the importance of vocal warm ups and regular practise.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Examine different ranges (i.e., alto, bass, baritone, tenor, soprano) on a choral score.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Identify own range, with teacher guidance, and recognize that voice range may change over time.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Recognize, experiment with, and demonstrate different vocal registration (e.g., head voice, chest voice, falsetto, speaking voice).

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Demonstrate understanding of fundamentals of tone production (e.g., breath management, supported projection, characteristic tone quality across the ranges, vowel sounds).

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Discuss basic principles of vocal anatomy (e.g., vocal bands/folds, how to produce a sound, sound source, articulators and resonators).

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Discuss and demonstrate the difference between pronunciation (e.g., the act of speaking words correctly), enunciation (e.g., the art of speaking words clearly and concisely) and diction (e.g., the "choice of words" used in writing, speaking or singing).

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Demonstrate and articulate the importance of proper posture and body alignment for singing.

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Demonstrate choral blend through vowel unity and understand the role it plays in intonation.

indicators.label: m
indicators.text: Identify factors and apply techniques for maintaining vocal health.

outcomes.statement: Demonstrate skills (e.g., intonation, pitch breathing, alignment) and practices necessary for ensemble singing.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text:
Demonstrate ensemble skills such as:
- adjusting dynamics
- blending vowels
- placing consonants
- adjusting vibrato
- maintaining own part.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text:
Demonstrate personal and interpersonal skills necessary for ensemble music making including:
- etiquette
- rehearsal protocols
- leadership.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Recognize opportunities for applying interpretation abilities (e.g., inflection, tone, emulating instrumental sounds).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Maintain accurate pitch when singing harmony.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Demonstrate fluency and growth in vocal techniques and musicality when singing advanced vocal ensemble repertoire.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Apply processes (e.g., focusing on a specific part, experimenting with phrasing, running through from start to finish, working on sections, isolating variables, making group choices), with teacher guidance, for collective practice, rehearsal and performance.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Examine various musical functions in a song (e.g., melody, harmony, bass line).

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Incorporate movement in ensemble work (e.g., use movement to experience music concepts) recognizing how singing involves the whole body.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Demonstrate ability to respond to the conductor.

outcomes.statement: Demonstrate ability to interpret music using various visual (e.g., standard and/or non-standard notation, written musical scores, graphic score) and aural music systems.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Demonstrate ability to respond to notation systems such as letter names, solfege, scale degrees and aural cues when singing in the context of the repertoire studied.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Demonstrate ability to read, notate, understand and interpret written musical scores and various notation systems.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Sight sing a short passage (e.g., at a lower difficulty level than the repertoire studied).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Demonstrate ability to learn music through aural transmission.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Interpret expressive terms and music symbols within the context of the repertoire (e.g., tempo, dynamics, form, style, articulation, graphic symbols).

outcomes.statement: Experiment with processes for improvising, arranging and composing.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Investigate ways that music elements (e.g., tempo, rhythm) can be used to express musical ideas.

indicators.label: b

indicators.text: Reflect on individual and group compositions and arrangements, identifying strengths and challenges encountered.

outcomes.statement: Identify and experiment with stylistic practices of various vocal and choral music traditions.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Sing (e.g., warm up, excerpt, repertoire, short folk song) in a minimum of two languages.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Incorporate stylistic features reflective of the socio-cultural contexts of the choral repertoire being studied.

outcomes.statement: Investigate the role of choral music in the context of various cultures, places and eras.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Discuss the contribution of choral music in building Saskatchewan communities, past and present.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Observe and listen to performative practices of various choirs (e.g., cultural performance practices, influence of composer’s place and time on the work).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Interview a conductor to discuss the conductor’s work and roles (e.g., factors influencing repertoire selection, stylistic features, language considerations).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Respond to examples of choirs performing related repertoire.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Research the meaning of cultural appropriation and its relevance to vocal and choral music.

outcomes.statement: Examine the role of choral music and Indigenous vocal music in maintaining traditions, reflecting cultural identities and conveying oral histories.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss various purposes of choral and vocal music (e.g., ceremonial, social, commercial, artistic expression, storytelling).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Engage with First Nations and Métis singers to identify regional and individual singing styles.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Research the role vocal music plays in Indigenous cultures in Saskatchewan, past and present (e.g., treaty education outcome SI10: Analyze the spirit and intent of treaties and investigate the extent to which they have been fulfilled).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Examine sources of inspiration for the songs of First Nations and Métis musicians and composers.

outcomes.statement: Examine the impact and role of choral music in own life.

indicators.text: Examine and describe the various roles that singing and choral music play in students’ lives.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Examine how choral music is used in media and infused in daily life (e.g., to influence consumers via advertising, shopping environments).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Investigate relationships between choral and vocal music and personal wellness including mental health, and identify and discuss associated research.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Discuss how one becomes a discerning consumer and/or producer of choral music (e.g., criteria for judgement of quality, purchase of recordings or tickets to performances).

indicators.label: e

outcomes.statement: Identify and describe legal and ethical considerations concerning music copyright and performance rights.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Investigate and report on current issues and resources connected to copyright law such as “intellectual property”, “open source” and “creative commons”.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Identify and discuss some issues regarding posting of music online including possible consequences and permanence of web postings.

outcomes.statement: Describe own process for improvement as individual singers and as an ensemble.

indicators.text: Examine individual roles within the ensemble (e.g., personal responsibility, collective, role of conductor).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Reflect on what went well in rehearsal and performance.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Identify areas for improvement.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Co-construct goals or criteria for rehearsals and performances.

indicators.label: e

indicators.label: f

outcomes.statement: Describe, through critical listening, various genres and styles of choral music.

indicators.text: Discuss the sounds, harmonies, rhythmic patterns and text in diverse choral traditions.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Use music terminology to describe what is heard.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Consider and explain how music selections are reflections of their place and time.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Examine different genres and styles of choral performances.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Describe and justify one’s preferences for various examples of choral styles.

indicators.text: Respond to various types of choral music genres performed by Saskatchewan-based ensembles, considering inclusion and diversity of genres, cultures, genders, eras and styles.

outcomes.statement: Explore basic sewing techniques and construction details.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss and practise types of seams and seam finishes.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Practise sewing basic seams (e.g., plain seam, basted seam).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Practise sewing basic seam finishes, (e.g., zigzagged, serged, pinked).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Demonstrate techniques (e.g., clipping, trimming) used to remove bulk to enhance the appearance of seams.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Demonstrate a variety of beginner sewing techniques such as top stitching, applique and casings in the creation of a sewing project.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Apply a variety of beginner construction details (e.g., seam finishing, sewing on fasteners, sewing on trims, simple top stitching) in the creation of a sewing project.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Practise pressing during sewing (e.g., seams, casings, hems).

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify tools used in hand sewing (e.g., measuring tape, needle, thread, scissors, fabric).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Discuss safety procedures as they apply to hand sewing (e.g., focus eyes on the needle, use scissors with caution).

indicators.label: c
d
indicators.text: Practise a variety of simple hand stitches (e.g., running stitch, over cast stitch, back stitch, basting).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Create an item using simple hand sewing techniques (e.g., coasters, bookmark, sunglasses case, sock puppet, simple stuffed animal).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Examine the traditional ways First Nations and Métis people use hand sewing techniques for the creation of such items as clothing, shelter and equipment.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify parts of a sewing machine (e.g., needle, bobbin case, spool pin, presser foot).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Discuss safety procedures as they apply to machine sewing (e.g., keep finger away from moving parts, focus eyes on the needle, use scissors with caution, turn off machine when not in use).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Apply ergonomic recommendations when sewing (e.g., feet flat, back straight, shoulders and neck relaxed).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Practise sewing machine basics (e.g., zigzag and straight stiches, reverse stiches).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Demonstrate the ability to set up a sewing machine for operation, (e.g., winding a bobbin and threading a machine and a bobbin, adjusting sewing tension).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Create a project using a sewing machine (e.g., simple stuffed animal, pillow case, place mats, napkins).

outcomes.statement: Examine historical influences on the modern food service industry.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 1: The Food Service Industry (Core) (Core) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss the circumstances that led to the creation of the food service industry at the time of the French Revolution.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Discuss historical (e.g., King Henry IV, Antonin Carême and Auguste Escoffier) and contemporary (e.g., food network, convenience food, food blogs and fast food) influences on the food service industry.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Examine how current food service industry terminology is based on terminology (e.g., sous chef) and practices (e.g., brigade system) used at the time of the French Revolution.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Differentiate between a classic kitchen brigade system (e.g., chef de cuisine, chef de partie, saucier, garde-manger and pâtissier) and a modern (e.g., executive chef, sous-chef, line cook and pastry chef) kitchen brigade.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Identify the duties of common back-of-the-house (e.g., executive chef, sous chef, station chef and line cook) and front-of-the-house (e.g., maitre d’, server and food runner) roles in food service operations.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Research the effects of technological developments (e.g., tools, electricity, electronics and computers) on the food service industry.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Examine how innovative technologies (e.g., food preservation and storage techniques), consumer concerns (e.g., food safety and nutrition) and new foods (e.g., convenience foods) influence the modern food service industry.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Identify the types of establishments (e.g., institutional kitchens, work camps, hotels, hospitals, bakeries, home-based and mobile food vendors) related to employment opportunities in the food service industry.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Discuss the role of the food service industry in the community.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Examine cultural, economic, technological, social and environmental factors that influence the food service industry in Saskatchewan.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Describe how current food trends impact the food service industry.

outcomes.statement: Examine the importance of professionalism in the food service industry.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 2: Professionalism in the Food Service Industry (Core) · Suggested Time: 2-4 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
b
indicators.text: Research expectations for employee and employer professionalism in the food service industry.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Discuss working conditions and employment standards common to the food service industry.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Identify common worker injuries reported within the food service industry.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Identify types of workplace harassment and related resolution procedures (e.g., provincial labour mediation and conciliation services).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Describe the rights and responsibilities of employees and employers, including the right to refuse process.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Recognize and apply safe and fair work practices including freedom from violence, harassment and bullying.

outcomes.statement: Apply kitchen safety and sanitation practices.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 3A: Kitchen Safety and Sanitation (Core) · Suggested Time: 8-12 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss the importance of safety in a commercial kitchen.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explain the purpose of food safety standards and regulations, including the role of public health inspectors.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Identify potential worker safety hazards in a commercial kitchen.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Research injuries (e.g., strained muscles, cuts and lacerations, slips, falls and pepper burns) common among workers in commercial kitchens.

indicators.label: e
f
indicators.text: Identify industry standard personal protective equipment (PPE) such as safety goggles, gloves, footwear, masks, headwear and protective clothing.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Describe ways to reduce and prevent injury to self and others from unsafe work acts or environments.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Demonstrate personal hygiene (e.g., hand washing and hair restraint) and safe dress (e.g., closed-toe shoes, apron and gloves) when working in a commercial kitchen.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Explain the importance of sanitation in a commercial kitchen.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Discuss practices to maintain a safe and sanitary kitchen, including prevention of pest infestation.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Maintain a clean and sanitary work area, including surfaces (e.g., floors, walls and tables) tools and equipment.

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Practise safe and hygienic washing of dishes, tools and cookware, either manually or using a dishwasher.

indicators.label: m
indicators.text: Discuss the importance of reporting workplace incidents or injuries immediately and the proper procedure to do so.

indicators.label: n
indicators.text: Identify common causes of commercial kitchen fires.

indicators.label: o
indicators.text: Examine procedures for preventing and dealing with commercial kitchen fires.

indicators.label: p
indicators.text: Review the fire evacuation plan for the work area and building.

indicators.label: q
indicators.text: Research Workplace Hazardous Materials Information System (WHMIS) standards that apply to a commercial kitchen.

outcomes.statement: Examine appropriate procedures to ensure food safety in the kitchen.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify the causes of food contamination (e.g., biological, chemical and physical) that can occur in a commercial kitchen.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: List examples of biological (e.g., bacteria and viruses), chemical (e.g., cleaners and disinfectants) and physical (e.g., glass or metal fragments) contaminants.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Identify causes of food-borne illnesses (e.g., food poisoning and food allergies).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Differentiate between direct contamination and cross-contamination.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Discuss common food safety steps (e.g., clean, separate, cook and chill) to reduce food contamination.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Differentiate date labelling (e.g., best-before, packaged on and expiration) on pre-packaged foods.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Explain the importance of kitchen sanitation and personal hygiene in the prevention of food contamination and food-borne illnesses.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Examine safe and sanitary practices to dispose of kitchen waste.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Discuss the role of municipal, provincial and national food safety legislation and regulations.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Demonstrate appropriate food safety standards when receiving, selecting, handling, preparing, serving and storing food.

outcomes.statement: Create quick breads using muffin, biscuit and creaming methods.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 29: Quick Breads (Core) · Suggested Time: 5-10 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Modules 4A, 5B, 5C

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Define quick breads.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Discuss leavening agents (e.g., baking soda, baking powder and steam).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explain how gluten is developed in quick breads.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Discuss the importance of properly mixing batter (e.g., tunneling).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Differentiate the two types of batters (i.e., soft doughs and pour batters).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Describe the three methods (i.e., muffin, biscuit and creaming) of creating quick breads.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text:
Create quick breads, using each of the three methods:
- muffin (e.g., banana bread, cornbread, popovers, dumplings, muffins and pancakes);
- biscuit (e.g., buttermilk, cheddar, herb, bannock and scones); and,
- creaming (e.g., biscuits, banana bread and loaves).

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Compare muffins made using the biscuit method and muffins made using the muffin method.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Develop criteria to assess created quick breads.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Demonstrate safe and proper use of bakeshop tools and equipment.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Demonstrate food safety standards when preparing, serving and storing quick breads.

outcomes.statement: Produce yeast breads using lean and rich doughs.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 30A: Yeast Breads (Core) · Suggested Time: 6-10 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 29

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify the three types (i.e., lean, rich and rolled-in) of yeast doughs.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Research and discuss the effects of leavening agents, including yeast, on dough.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Examine the stages in yeast bread production including scaling ingredients, mixing, kneading, fermenting, punching, scaling dough, rounding, shaping, panning, proofing, baking, cooling and storing.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Identify the three mixing methods (i.e., straight dough, modified straight dough and sponge) for yeast doughs.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Identify the appropriate mixing method for the three types of yeast dough.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Produce lean doughs such as hard rolls, baguettes, pizza dough and rye breads.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Produce rich doughs such as cinnamon rolls, doughnuts and brioche.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Compare the characteristics (e.g., fat, sugars and texture) of lean and rich doughs.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Demonstrate safe and proper use of bakeshop tools and equipment.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Demonstrate food safety standards when preparing, baking, serving and storing yeast breads.

outcomes.statement: Create high-fat cakes and cupcakes.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 31A: Cakes (Core) · Suggested Time: 3-6 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Modules 5B, 5C

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Define high-fat cake and provide examples (e.g., butter cake and pound cake).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Differentiate between high-fat and low-fat cakes.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text:
Identify and practise the three main goals of cake batter mixing:
- creating uniform batter;
- forming and incorporating air cells in the batter; and
- developing the proper texture in the finished product.

indicators.label: d
e
indicators.text: Bake a cake or cupcake using various mixing methods such as creaming method, one-stage method, two-stage method and flour-batter method.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Differentiate between boxed cake mixes and two-stage method, considering cost, taste, texture and volume.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Demonstrate safe and proper use of bakeshop tools and equipment.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Demonstrate food safety standards when preparing, baking, serving and storing cakes and cupcakes.

outcomes.statement: Prepare simple icings for cakes or cookies.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 32A: Icing and Cake Decorating A (Optional) · Suggested Time: 5-8 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Modules 5B, 5C

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explain the function of icings (e.g., adds flavour, creates eye appeal and provides a protective coating to seal in moisture).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify basic varieties of icings including fondant, buttercream, foam-type, fudge-type icing, flat-type icing, royal and whipped cream.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Discuss ingredients, kitchen tools and techniques required to prepare icings.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Practise the correct procedures (e.g., cooling, trimming, brushing crumbs and filling) for icing cupcakes, cookies and sheet cakes.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Use the three main icing methods for cupcakes (i.e., dip, spread and piping).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Discuss, with peers, qualities that determine the visual appeal of a cake (e.g., colour combination, texture and type of icing).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Decorate cupcakes, sheet cakes or cookies with a simple buttercream, royal icing or whipped cream.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Demonstrate safe and proper use of bakeshop tools and equipment.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Demonstrate food safety standards when preparing, serving and storing icings.

outcomes.statement: Prepare starch-thickened puddings, custards and whipped cream.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 33A: Custards, Creams and Puddings A (Optional) · Suggested Time: 5-10 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Modules 5B, 5C

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Examine key concepts in the formation of custards and puddings including gelatinization and coagulation.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Discuss why starch-thickened puddings need to be boiled in order to thicken.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Differentiate between cornstarch pudding, blanc mange and cream puddings.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Prepare a starch-thickened pudding such as chocolate, tapioca, bread or rice pudding.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Prepare a custard using convenience base or from scratch.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Compare homemade pudding to convenience products in regard to cost, labour, texture and taste.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Identify and follow the procedure for whipping cream (e.g., use a cold bowl and cream, add the sugar gradually once the cream has started to thicken and do not over beat).

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Practise stabilizing whipped cream with gelatin or cream of tartar.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Prepare whipped cream and use as a dessert topping or filling.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Develop criteria to assess the finished products.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Demonstrate safe and proper use of bakeshop tools and equipment.

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Demonstrate food safety standards when handling, preparing, cooking, serving and storing puddings, custards and whipped cream.

outcomes.statement: Investigate career opportunities in the food service industry.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 41: Career Opportunities in the Food Service Industry (Core) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify career opportunities in the food service industry in one’s community.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Research which occupations in the food service industry are facing shortages and which are oversubscribed locally, regionally or provincially.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Examine the roles, responsibilities, educational qualifications and personal and professional qualities common to people working in the food service industry.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Create a list of personal interests, skills and traits that may lead to a career in the food service industry.

indicators.label: e
f
indicators.text: Discuss apprenticeship, including its advantages and disadvantages, as a pathway to a career in the food service industry.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Communicate research findings related to occupations in the food service industry through a display, brochure, video, presentation software, website or an oral presentation.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Discuss a plan for obtaining one’s dream job in the food service industry.

outcomes.statement: Identify various roles and influences of communication media in school and society.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 1: Communication Through Media (Core) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss and clarify the purposes for communication media including established examples such as video, audio, and interactive media and emerging examples such as blogs, wikis, social networking, and multiple platforms.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify and explain a communications model which includes aspects such as the message, the sender, the mode of transmission, the receiver, and any interactivity.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Describe specific examples where there is emphasis on communication in society (e.g., school, community, home).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Provide some judgement of and justification for effective communications processes and practices (e.g., ads, business, embedded media).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Reflect and articulate personal learning goals for using communication media.

outcomes.statement: Investigate and articulate legal issues related to media such as copyright, privacy, and consent.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 2A: Legal and Ethical Issues (Core) · Suggested Time: 2-3 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Define the term “copyright” in relation to Canadian law and assess its impact on a Communication Media class.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Describe the three factors that place some works in the public domain and cite some examples of these works along with reasons for their inclusion.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Investigate and report on current issues and resources connected to copyright law such as “open source”, “creative commons”, and stock resources.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Investigate and report on the need for consent in various circumstances such as location, appearance, material, and music.

outcomes.statement: Investigate and articulate the tasks and skills, including project management, required by various media during the stages of preproduction, production, and postproduction.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 3: Production Stages (Core) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 1

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Create broad definitions of preproduction, production, and postproduction as they pertain to communication media.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Compare two different media in terms of the work done during preproduction, production, and postproduction.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Identify the key roles in various types of media productions and generate a list of their functions during preproduction.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explain project management concepts including timelines, breakdown into smaller tasks, budget, roles, responsibilities, and delivery.

outcomes.statement: Assess the career opportunities in existing and emerging communication media in Saskatchewan, Canada, and globally including post-secondary education and training programs.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 4: Career Opportunities (Core) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify specific examples of skills required in Communication Media courses that fall into the categories identified by Human Resources and Skills Development Canada (HRSDC) as Essential Skills and by the Conference Board of Canada (CBofC) as Employability Skills.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify the Essential Skills from HRSDC and Employability Skills from the CBofC and correlate them to the skills needed to build a successful career in communication media.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Investigate programming offered by the universities inside and outside of Saskatchewan as well as SIAST and other technical institutes to examine the breadth of post-secondary education programs available in communication media studies including industry association programming such as the Saskatchewan Motion Picture Industry Association and the Saskatchewan Music Association.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Contribute to the collective knowledge of the class through research and sharing on the general activities and opportunities for careers in media production including entrepreneurial aspects.

outcomes.statement: Clearly articulate and demonstrate an understanding of the preproduction process.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 5: Preproduction Processes (Core) · Suggested Time: 2-3 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 3

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify and explain effective strategies to create the production elements during preproduction such as creating the production, determining the intention, identifying the content, predicting the audience effect, creating a treatment, writing a script, and making a storyboard.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify types of hardware and software used in media communications and explain how they are used effectively to produce communications.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Apply critical thinking and decision making regarding the relationship among the production intention, the target audience, and the technology format.

outcomes.statement: Develop and demonstrate increasing skill through the practice and use of equipment (e.g., camera, lights) and processes (e.g., camera work, set lighting) during the typical steps of the production stage of shooting video and beginning postproduction.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 6A: Video Production (Core) · Suggested Time: 10-20 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 5

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify the key components of a video camera and explain the function of each as well as the benefits of turning off the automatic settings for the camera.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify various video formats and explain their current general usage.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Identify and demonstrate industry standard practices of video camera use for positioning (e.g., eye level, high and low angles, point of view), framing (e.g., wide shot, close-up, two shot), movement (e.g., tilt, pan, zoom), and depth of field.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Discuss the purposes of lighting in a video and reasons why different lighting would be used (e.g., mood, clarity of images).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Demonstrate an understanding of motivated lighting effects such as ambient, manipulated, one, two, and three-point lighting.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Understand and explain the challenges for the recording of audio in a single system video production.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Demonstrate postproduction techniques by editing video shot to complete a simple cut such as an entrance or exit cut.

outcomes.statement: Produce audio through interpretation and application of accepted practices in audio concepts, processes, and equipment selection.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 7A: Audio Production (Core) · Suggested Time: 5-10 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 5

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Critique the importance of quality sound in a variety of audio applications.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Assess audio equipment needs in a variety of situations and choose the best microphone application to meet those needs.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Effectively employ audio production equipment to produce a variety of audio formats such as MP3, AIFF, and WAV.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Practise using audio equipment to produce recordings of increasing quality and complexity.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Identify and discuss the analog and digital elements of audio collection and manipulation.

outcomes.statement: Develop and demonstrate skill to create and produce interactive media.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 8A: Interactive Media (Core) · Suggested Time: 10-20 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 5

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Use a variety of planning techniques (e.g., research, design briefs, task lists, mock-ups, storyboards, site maps) to design an interactive media project such as web pages, social media, or a blog.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Use application software and equipment to perform a variety of production tasks (e.g., inputting, manipulating, and outputting audio; embedding and linking graphics; posting media on the Internet).

outcomes.statement: Create an effective production project based on a personal or group vision for communicating with the larger society beyond your classroom.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 9A: Project (Core) · Suggested Time: 20-30 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 3

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Determine class production ideas and participate in preproduction planning as part of a production team with defined roles.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Create a project description which includes goals, intended audience, equipment requirements, software requirements, treatment, storyboard, detailed timeline, and assessment criteria.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Demonstrate skill with the use of video, audio, and/or interactive media.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Assess personal and group goals through a process of reflection and self-assessment.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Engage classmates and/or others in an exhibition of the project.

outcomes.statement: Generate an increased level of engagement of an audience through imaginative use of visual effects.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 12: Visual Effects (Optional) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 3

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify an example of visual effects and justify why the production is or is not effective in terms of communication to the audience.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Research types of visual effects used such as optical, chemical, and mechanical effects to share with the class.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explore and review effects from a variety of sources.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Incorporate visual effects into personal or group projects, as appropriate, to increase audience engagement.

outcomes.statement: Effectively use audio to increase the engagement of an audience.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 13: Audio Effects and Music (Optional) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 3

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify an example of audio effects and/or use of music and provide an opinion of why the example is more effective in engaging the audience.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Research sources and production techniques for audio effects.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explore and review audio effects from a variety of sources.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Incorporate effects and/or music into personal or group projects, as appropriate, to increase audience engagement.

outcomes.statement: Apply safety standards to prevent injuries in the construction and carpentry workspace.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 1A: Safety (Core) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss worker and employee rights and responsibilities as they relate to workplace safety and how they can prevent injuries.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify common safety hazard categories and hierarchy of control common to the construction industry.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Assess and mitigate the risks (e.g., slips, trips, falls) and potential safety hazards in the jobsite and shop workspace.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Research the benefits of completing the different certifications and programs offered by Work Safe Sask, Sask Safety Council, Sask Prevention and the Ministry of Labour Relations and Workplace Safety.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Explore basic safety procedures (e.g., storage and maintenance of tools, clean workspace and caution when working at high heights and power tools) as they apply to the jobsite and shop workspace.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Develop a list of rules for workplace safety including proper personal protective equipment (PPE), sanitation, neat and tidy work area and reporting workplace accidents and safety incidents.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Act consistently to focus on personal tasks while maintaining consciousness of others working in proximity.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Demonstrate the utilization and maintenance of protective devices on equipment.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Perform proper lockout and de-energizing of equipment before beginning inspections or repairs.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Identify the advantages and disadvantages of using each category of industry standard personal protective equipment (PPE) for respiratory, hearing, sight and body protection such as masks, ear plugs, safety goggles and shields.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Demonstrate PPE cleaning procedures.

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Demonstrate the correct use of safety equipment (e.g., eye wash station, shower, first aid station, shop ventilation, fire extinguishers and caging devices) in the workplace.

indicators.label: m
indicators.text: Post and maintain emergency phone numbers in a visible location.

indicators.label: n
indicators.text: Discuss appropriate actions in the event of an injury in the workplace, including whom to contact, how to report and first-aid procedures.

outcomes.statement: Explore tree growth and lumber production.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 2: Wood (Core) · Suggested Time: 2-3 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Investigate the structure and growth of common lumber trees including concepts such as pith, heartwood and annual rings.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Classify common woods as softwoods or hardwoods and open- or closed-grained.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explore the creation process of dimensional lumber from falling a tree to retail sales in a lumber yard.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Describe common wood defects such as warp, check, cup and bow.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Discuss the effects of moisture on dimensional lumber.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Assess current logging practices in Saskatchewan and Canada and express an opinion about the sustainability of the wood product industry.

notes: The Ministry CSV words it: “Demonstrate an understanding of tree growth and lumber production.”.

outcomes.statement: Describe how a variety of wood products are manufactured.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 3: Manufactured Building Products (Core) · Suggested Time: 2-3 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 2

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Compare the manufacturing processes and categories for various engineered structural wood panels (i.e. plywood, oriented strand board, and composite panels).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Classify the common uses of non-structural panels such as hardwood, plywood, medium density fibreboard (MDF), hardboard and particleboard.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Summarize the advantages of glued-laminated timber (glulam) over conventional timber beams.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Justify the use of wood I-joists and floor trusses over traditional joists in residential construction.

notes: The Ministry CSV words it: “Demonstrate an understanding of how a variety of wood products are manufactured.”.

outcomes.statement: Determine the cost of material for a small project.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 4A: Project Estimating A (Core) · Suggested Time: 1-2 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 2

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Describe the difference between the nominal size and the actual size of lumber.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Utilize the appropriate formula to calculate the number of board feet in a small project.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Calculate the cost of a small project given a material list and the cost of the lumber and hardware.

outcomes.statement: Investigate the advantages and disadvantages of various alternative building materials and processes over wood and wood products.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 5A: Alternative Building Materials and Processes A (Core) · Suggested Time: 2-3 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 3

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Investigate recent innovations in residential building (e.g., low-E argon windows, insulated concrete forms, recycled plastic decking), and compare them to traditional products and methods.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Research energy and resource efficient alternatives in residential construction.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Compare the efficiency advantage (e.g., lifespan, reduction of waste, recycling of materials) of manufacturing building materials to traditional materials.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Analyze the benefits and drawbacks of metal framing versus traditional wood framing.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Investigate the growing trends of residential construction in Saskatchewan such as using straw bales.

outcomes.statement: Show proficiency and accuracy when measuring materials.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 6A: Measuring and Layout A (Core) · Suggested Time: 4-8 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 1

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Illustrate accurate measurements to 1/16” or 1-2 millimetres with a pocket tape measure.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Operate a combination square to draw a line parallel to a board’s side.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Calculate area, perimeter, and volume using simple formulas and a tape measure.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Illustrate how to draw a line at 90 and 45 degrees using a framing square.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Practice how to check for level and plumb using a carpenter’s level.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Investigate several other measurement devices (e.g., plumb bob, sliding T-bevel, tramel points, dividers).

outcomes.statement: Demonstrate proficiency with a variety of hand tools to accomplish cutting, shaping, smoothing and boring wood.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 7A: Hand Tools A (Core) · Suggested Time: 4-8 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 6A

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify the hand tools in the shop and describe their function.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Utilize hand tools best suited to accomplish a task.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Perform the correct technique in using a hand tool.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Describe safety precautions for each hand tool used in the class including correct PPE.

outcomes.statement: Develop proficiency using a variety of hand tools for a construction project.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 7C: Hand Tools C (Core) · Suggested Time: 4-8 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 7B

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify basic tools used to construct a building (e.g., hammer, speed square, tape measure, cats paw and level)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Use hand tools required to construct a building.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explain when a hand tool is more appropriate to use instead of a portable power tool when constructing a building.

outcomes.statement: Develop proficiency using a variety of portable power tools.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 8A: Portable Power Tools A (Core) · Suggested Time: 5-8 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 7A

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Demonstrate the correct use of a jigsaw including cutting curves and replacing the blade.

indicators.text: Recognize the cultural-linguistic world views of Dakota speakers, such as how not having a word for “goodbye” reflects Dakota beliefs and values.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Discuss how language is integral to understanding and participating in ceremonies. *Note that sacred aspects of ceremonies are not appropriate for classroom discussion and not everyone can participate in certain ceremonies.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text:
Practise protocols associated with the Dakota culture, such as:
- boys remove their hats when praying; and,
- offer gifts when asking for knowledge or gathering offerings from the land.

outcomes.statement: Explore personal identity as a Dakota language learner.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Reflect on personal experience with language (e.g., languages spoken, language learning history, family, heritage languages and traditional languages).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Describe benefits of being bilingual or plurilingual.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explain how identity and kinship are referred to differently depending on the gender of the speaker as well as their relationship with, and the gender of, the person to whom they are referring.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Identify terminology that is used to describe maternal or paternal relationships.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Celebrate accomplishments by using Dakota language to congratulate and encourage.
