outcomes.statement: Demonstrate dance technique and apply terminology related to a range of dance types and styles.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Experience various dance types and styles (e.g., ballroom as a type of dance including waltz, foxtrot or tango styles; ballet as a type of dance including classical or contemporary styles; modern as a type of dance including Graham or contact improvisation styles; hip hop as a type of dance including B-boying, funk, or up rock styles).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Define and use dance terminology and technique associated with selected dance types and styles.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Practise technique and strategies for safe execution of dance movements.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Participate in warm-up and cool-down activities appropriate to the type and style of dance.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Describe understanding of the elements of dance (i.e., body, action, space, time, energy).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Recognize and practise body alignment specific to the dance type and style (e.g., powwow as a type of dance including hoop or fancy styles; jazz as a type of dance including swing or jitterbug styles).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Learn the foundational techniques associated with different dance types and styles.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Investigate and pose questions about the protocols and expectations associated with a particular dance type and style.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Recall and dance a sequence using the style, technique and protocols observed.

outcomes.statement: Create solo, duo or group dances to reflect aspects of daily life.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Create dance from everyday movements using the elements of dance and the principles of composition.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Use an everyday item or daily routine as inspiration for dance making.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Experiment with dance elements and choreographic form in dance-making process.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explore various dance-making methods and practices.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Incorporate movements and aspects of daily life into a dance composition.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Use popular dance from various eras (e.g., Charleston, twist, jitterbug) as inspiration for own work.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Adapt choreography for a range of abilities.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Practise collaboration, problem solving and clear communication during the dance-making process.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Collaborate with peers and teacher during dance-making process.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Record (e.g., video, invented notation, journal notes) dance-making ideas for future use.

outcomes.statement: Perform solo, duo or group dances to reflect aspects of daily life.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Perform movement or dance composition to convey aspects of daily life.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Perform movement or dance compositions of various dance types and styles.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Perform popular dances from various eras.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Collaborate, problem solve and communicate clearly during rehearsal and dance performance (e.g., making adjustments in the moment, dealing with unforeseen technical difficulties).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Rehearse and refine composition to convey the dance maker’s vision.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Perform a choreographed dance composition.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Demonstrate one’s optimal level of ability when dancing.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Co-construct, with guidance, criteria for evaluating performance.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Apply peer and teacher feedback during rehearsal process to improve performance.

outcomes.statement: Examine self (e.g., one’s mental, spiritual, physical, emotional growth) in relation to dance as a discipline.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Create a dance journal and identify areas of growth including strengths and challenges.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Practise mindful and/or contemplative exercises (e.g., written reflection, video, blog) as a daily dance practice.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Reflect on personal beliefs while addressing common misconceptions about dance.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Demonstrate personal expression through dance.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Identify and collaborate, where possible, with local role models, mentors, Elders, Knowledge Keepers and artists.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Demonstrate safe movement practices (e.g., anatomical alignment and joint mechanics) important for injury prevention.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Recognize how dance promotes compassion and empathy for the human experience.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Participate, digitally or in-person, in collaborative dance work with community.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Reflect on how dance has created a sense of community in the classroom.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Examine how own dance can address larger questions of personal worldview (e.g., identity-related inquiry questions such as Where do I belong?).

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Take personal risks in developing and sharing dance work.

outcomes.statement: Respond critically and constructively to dance compositions using established criteria.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss potential criteria and terminology used to analyze dance compositions.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify and articulate goals and intentions for dance, based on relevant criteria (e.g., time: duration, rhythm, tempo).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Identify strengths and areas for improvement in own work.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Reflect on own, peers’ and others’ dance compositions, through various means (e.g., written, blog, discussion, interdisciplinary response).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Examine and discuss how dance compositions convey ideas, vision and/or messages.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Assess dance compositions according to established criteria including use of dance elements, choreographic form (e.g., canon, ABA, rondo) and devices (e.g., repetition, contrast, tension).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Respond to dance compositions on an emotional, associative and formal intellectual level using frameworks and/or processes (see online curriculum resources).

outcomes.statement: Analyze how dance reflects the social events and trends of a time and place.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Investigate the origins and evolution of various types of dance and examine styles within each type (e.g., jazz as a type of dance including styles such as swing or Charleston, Ukrainian traditional folk dances versus contemporary innovations).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Describe how dance makers respond to social events and trends of their time and place.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Research ways that dancers and dance makers express ideas through movement and incorporate similar ideas in own dance.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Transfer understanding of other choreographer’s work into own dance compositions (e.g., Linda Rainer’s use of pedestrian movement).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: View, reflect upon and respond to dances that draw on the social events and trends of a time and place.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Take part in, reflect upon and respond to dances that draw on the social events and trends of a time and place.

outcomes.statement: Examine methods used for accessing and interpreting material in dance.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Research and discuss creation and production methods used in Western dance (e.g., written text, music, images, choreography) including ownership and copyright.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Research and discuss First Nations and Métis dance practices associated with specific cultural contexts (e.g., gifting dances to others, protocols related to powwow and regalia, Métis sash symbolism).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Practise ethical use of source material in own work.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Investigate the relationship between copyright and social media practices.

outcomes.statement: Investigate Saskatchewan First Nations and Métis dances.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Engage, digitally or in-person, with First Nations Elders, Knowledge Keepers, community leaders and/or dancers to identify characteristics of contemporary powwow dances (e.g., men’s and women’s Fancy Dance, men’s and women’s Traditional, women’s Jingle dress, men’s Chicken, men’s Grass).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify characteristics of round dances, and the types of round dance associated with different places (e.g., round dance as a social dance and round dance as a ceremonial dance).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Identify characteristics of First Nations social dances (e.g., partner dances) such as the Owl Dance and/or society dances such Buffalo and Hoop.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Engage, digitally or in-person, with Métis Elders, community leaders and/or dancers to differentiate characteristics of traditional Métis dances (e.g., Rabbit Dance, Duck Dance, Red River Jig).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Examine characteristics of traditional and contemporary First Nations dances, drawing where possible and appropriate on the experience of students and expertise of community members.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Discuss characteristics of traditional and contemporary Métis dances, drawing where possible and appropriate on the experience of students and expertise of community members, and discuss the historical and social contexts involved in Métis dance and music.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Analyze connections between First Nations dances, the land and communities (treaty education outcome SI10 - analyze the spirit and intent of Treaties and investigate the extentto which they have been fulfilled).

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Examine the role of Métis dances as a form of artistic expression and social connection in communities.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Examine the evolution of powwow dancing (e.g., prohibitive legislation, period of revival, modern powwows).

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Recognize different purposes for ceremonial dance versus social dance (e.g., Sun Dance versus powwow social dance).

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Describe various powwow protocols and their purposes.

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Examine and describe the different roles of men and women in traditional dance, local and beyond.

indicators.label: m
indicators.text: Conduct research (e.g., interview, articles) on a local First Nation or Métis dancer and report on findings such as philosophy or focus, subject or themes expressed, discipline specific or interdisciplinary work, and potential influence of traditional practices (e.g., ask questions such as, Do traditional practices and/or Elders influence the work you create? Does your culture influence the subject matter or themes of your work?).

outcomes.statement: Develop a personal dance expression in response to a cultural and/or historical event.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Examine different types and styles of dance and identify key characteristics of each (e.g., ballroom as a type of dance including waltz, foxtrot or tango styles; ballet as a type of dance including classical or contemporary styles; modern as a type of dance including Graham or contact improvisation styles; hip hop as a type of dance including B-boying, funk, or up rock styles).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Observe and explore dance and dance practices in a range of media and/or cultural contexts(e.g., movies, technologies, manias).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Research and create a timeline (e.g., photograph, tableau, video, drawing) of historical milestones in dance.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Research a cultural and/or historical event represented by a dance artist.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Critique a variety of dance types and styles in their given time period and describe similarities and differences among them.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: View and critique dance performances (e.g., live, video, film).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Create a response (e.g., written, oral, interdisciplinary creation) to a dance performance.

outcomes.statement: Identify and examine a dance expression and dance artist(s) inspired by a historical and/or cultural event.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify and explore historical and/or cultural events expressed through dance types andstyles.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Research the origins and development of particular dance artists.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Identify exemplary artists representing particular dance types and styles(e.g., Afro – Caribbean as a type of dance including calypso, merengue or mambo styles; ballet as a type of dance including classical or contemporary styles; powwow as a type of dance including grass or fancy styles; modern as a type of dance including Graham or contact improvisation styles; hip hop as a type of dance including B-boying, funk, or up rock styles).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Research interdisciplinary collaborators with prominent dance artists.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Investigate historical contexts in the making of dances (e.g., raked stages, technology, film).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Explore cultural and historical contexts and their influence in the making of dances (e.g., depression era, women’s movement, industrial revolution).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Interpret cultural and/or historical events and how they impacted dance types and styles.

outcomes.statement: Investigate career paths related to various aspects of dance.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Research careers in dance (e.g., physiotherapist, adjudicator, examiner, teacher, performer, costume designer).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Complete a survey to identify careers that would suit one’s strengths, beliefs and interests.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Identify current aspirations in relation to dance.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Create a biography and a dance resume, including information about dance experience and accomplishments.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Create a job description for a dancer, choreographer or dance maker.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Identify how personal identity and/or cultural ancestry influences one’s career in dance.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Research a dancer, choreographer, or dance maker including analysis of their personal style, unique strengths, approaches and philosophies towards dance.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Explore post-secondary options and requirements related to careers in dance.

indicators.text: interacts with classmates in pairs or small groups to plan and complete class projects using the Dene language;

indicators.text: discusses and promotes positive interactions and relationships in the school by inviting (Elders into the classroom to share with students);

indicators.text: analyzes an unfamiliar word through its word parts and the context to comprehend;

outcomes.statement: perform language functions that allow learners to inquire.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: discusses and plans ways to obtain information or assistance from peers, helpers, leaders in the community for a variety of purposes (ask for assistance or guidance from others);

indicators.text: describes events and experiences in logical progression, such as how birch syrup is gathered in spring, or how to set a fish net, or how different groups of people interacted with one another on the plains and in the north; and,

indicators.text: reflects on identity through the Dene world-view and language by asking questions; "How does my use of Dene shape the way I understand nature? Or how does my use of Dene shape the way I understand the Dene culture?";

indicators.label: b

indicators.label: d

indicators.label: e

outcomes.statement: Explore design studies and the stages of a design process.

indicators.label: a
b
c
indicators.text:
Examine how the design process is non-linear and recursive, and includes:
- communication of the problem or need by the end user to the designer; and,
- clarification of perception of end user expectation by the designer; or need held by the designer; provided (i.e., test, refine and improve, test again).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Create a visual representation (e.g., flow chart, concept map, story board) of the stages of a design process.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Apply the steps of the design process to a simple design challenge.

b
c

outcomes.statement: Investigate the role of modelling and prototyping in the design process.

indicators.label: a
b
indicators.text: Define the term model and explain the purpose for modelling in the design process.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Identify critical attributes that differentiate a prototype from a model.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Describe situations in which either a model or a prototype is an important aspect of the design process.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Differentiate between a physical and an analytical prototype.

indicators.label: f
g
indicators.text: Speculate on reasons for creating either a comprehensive prototype (e.g., similar in appearance and including most components and attributes of a final product), or a focused prototype (e.g., implementing and testing one or two components and attributes of a final product).

indicators.label: h
indicators.text:
Create a prototype from a given scenario to illustrate a design process, including:
- an annotated sketch of a solution to a design problem;
- two-dimensional and three-dimensional models of the solution to the design problem using digital tools; and,

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Critically evaluate the efficacy of design decisions made within the prototype.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Adapt and refine the design to reflect data gleaned from the testing of prototypes.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Elicit feedback for a prototype using the terminology of the design process.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text:
Differentiate among processes for designing:
- a product for personal use (e.g., snowboard, hair dryer, backpack);
- a system (e.g., computer or transportation network, supply chain); and,
- an industrial process (e.g., power generating station, water treatment plant).

indicators.label: b
c
indicators.text: Differentiate between types of engineering challenges to be solved, including structural, mechanical, electrical and systems engineering.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Apply the design process to an engineering challenge scenario, such as building a tower with limited materials or building a bridge to hold maximum weight with minimum material.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Elicit feedback using the appropriate terminology from the design process.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Create a visual representation and narrative description of the engineering design process.

indicators.text: Differentiate between art and design.

indicators.label: f

indicators.label: g

outcomes.statement: Assess the importance and value of universal design in designing products and spaces.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 8: Universal Design (Core) · Suggested Time: 7-10 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 2

indicators.label: a
b
indicators.text: Differentiate between user-centred design and universal design.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Research ways in which design has resulted in exclusion of individuals from accessing objects or spaces.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Identify individuals, groups and organizations that have advocated for change in design thinking and individual and systemic dispositions toward design.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Examine ethical and economic reasons for inclusion of universal design in all design processes.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Explain how universal design facilitates empowerment and self sufficiency among individuals and organizations encountering designed spaces, objects or events.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Describe ways in which universal design is beneficial to all individuals regardless of life stage or physical abilities.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Create an inventory of universal design features in school and community spaces.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Explore the benefits of universal design applications such as levered doorknobs, taps in sinks and tubs, strategically placed assisted lifts and grab bars, governors on water heaters, adjustable height cupboards and tables, no barrier entries to buildings in single family dwellings and multi-unit residential dwellings.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Propose universal design improvements that would enhance user experiences with a variety of private and public spaces and products.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Suggest considerations required in the design process to develop products and places that are accessible to people with a wide range of abilities, to the greatest extent possible.

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Explain why universal design is important to include in all spaces, not just industrial, commercial or publicly accessed buildings and spaces.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Examine existing products (e.g., a pencil, a pen, a backpack) or procedures (e.g., the process of moving from classroom to classroom for various classes, the process for borrowing library books) and critically evaluate their form, function(s) and limitations, including universal design considerations.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Hypothesize why decisions regarding form and function were made in the original design process.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Determine what problems or opportunities for modification exist to improve or broaden the application of products or procedures to achieve a desired outcome.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Identify modifications to improve a current design.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Summarize how each step of the design process is engaged in the improvement of a product or procedure.

indicators.label: g

outcomes.printedWith: Module 11: Aesthetics and Function in Design (Core) · Suggested Time: 10-12 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 2

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Define aesthetics (i.e., that which is considered beautiful or tasteful), form (i.e., an object’s shape, size and material from which it is made), and function (i.e., the purpose of an object or what it helps people do) as they relate to design.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify the relationship between function and aesthetics, and function and form.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Assess the aesthetic choices used to convey the intended functionality of a variety of products.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explore the impacts of aesthetics and function on the human psyche.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Explore alternative materials and processes that might be used in creating a product.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Identify a variety of products that share a function but use a variety of aesthetic choices, such as colour, shape, size and surface texture.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Describe how the aesthetic choices of form can detract from or enhance the functionality of a variety of products (e.g., a convertible rooftop on a car may look attractive but is not functional to heat the interior of the car in cold temperatures).

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Explore how form impacts the way we interact with a product, leading to preference of one product over another (e.g., clothing, washroom fixtures).

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Speculate how differing cultural contexts can change the way that certain aesthetic features are perceived (e.g., clothing, universal design norms).

indicators.label: a

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify potential sources of critique for improvement, emphasizing the importance of communication with the end user or client as essential to the work of professional designers.

indicators.text:
Critique design solutions using a process that includes the following stages:
- Describe: What do you see (e.g., colour, shape, form)?
- Analyze: What did the producer intend?
- Interpret: Is the product successful in conveying the message or achieving its purpose? Is the product successful using elements and principles of visual design? and,
- Evaluate: What changes would I suggest? What factors need to be considered in assessing the feasibility of the potential changes?

outcomes.statement: Investigate inspiration and departure points for dramatic work.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Use personal narratives to explore concepts of memory, history and experiences relating to identity (e.g., cultural, gender expression, urban or rural perspectives, pop culture influences, sexual orientation, social status, youth or elder, immigrant).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Generate ideas for exploration through improvisation and devised scene-work.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explore connections and ways to expand upon inspirations and departure points.

outcomes.statement: Explore a variety of genres, styles and performance practices.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Examine a range of genres, styles and performance practices (e.g., Métis and First Nations stories and culturally-based performance traditions, comedy, tragedy, mime, naturalism, Francophone and Fransaskois performance and theatre history, expressionism, modernism) and, respecting cultural protocols that may exist for specific communities, use selected ideas as inspiration for own dramatic work.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Discuss and reflect on ways that selected genres, styles and performance practices can be adapted and incorporated in own work (e.g., using masks and story to examine a contemporary social issue, using mime and expressionist conventions to represent the protagonist’s internal state).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Assess the strengths of the drama work and/or performance and reflect on the collaborative approaches, challenges, and individual contributions encountered in the creative process.

outcomes.statement: Demonstrate the purposeful use of artistic voice to communicate perspective.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Use interviews as a source to create a scene that uses artistic voice to represent a perspective (e.g., authority figure, newcomer, family member, Métis activist, community leader, friend).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Demonstrate perspective and voice through the performance of an original or published monologue

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Create a scene that demonstrates at least two opposing voices.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Adapt a scene from the perspective of a supporting character or a character not present.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Discuss how empathy is fostered through experimentation with voice and perspective.

outcomes.statement: Investigate a creative process for building a play or scene from devised material.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explore the ways that identity, personal experiences and worldview shape creative work.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Create a devised play and/or scene through collective processes that may include: brainstorming, idea generating, researching, exploring, improvising, writing, journaling, storyboarding, editing, refining, framing the story with theatre devices, rehearsing and presenting.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Discuss interpersonal processes (e.g., negotiation, shared power, shared responsibility, collaboration, consensus, group skills, community making, ensemble building) required to create devised drama or theatre pieces, and reflect on the successes and challenges encountered in own work.

outcomes.statement: Present and sustain a performance for an audience (e.g., peers, invited guests, public).

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Use the language of theatre effectively in performance (e.g., stage directions, lighting cues, blocking).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Sustain role during various situations that may occur while performing (e.g., unexpected laughter, stage mishap, technical trouble) and discuss solutions for future occurrences.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Identify individual theatrical roles (e.g., actor, theatre technician, writer, dramaturge, director, designers, critic, stage manager, administrator, choreographer, musical director) and discuss how they work together effectively for performance.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Consider how various spaces impact performance potential and audience response or interaction (e.g., theatre in the round, site-specific theatre, auditorium, outdoors, classroom).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Consider and apply safe and proper use of tools, technologies and materials (e.g., lights, sound systems, makeup and skin care, set and/or prop construction).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Assess the strengths of the performance and reflect on the collaborative approaches, challenges, and individual contributions encountered in the creative process.

outcomes.statement: Respond critically, using appropriate theatrical language, to student and/or professional work and genres.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: View a live or recorded performance and discuss the role of the audience in various types of performances (e.g., conventional Western theatre, children’s theatre, forum theatre, site-specific theatre).

indicators.label: b
c
indicators.text: Describe, analyze and interpret, using the language of theatre, a selected piece of dramatic work, withholding judgement while formulating an informed opinion.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Analyze directorial decisions made in a contemporary production including the casting, staging and design choices.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Compare the social and political climate of the time in which a play was created and first produced with later productions, and evaluate the play using the language of theatre.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Identify the purpose of various conventions (e.g., dimming of lights, actor’s entrance, blackouts, curtain calls) and how they impact the audience experience.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Identify various stage and audience seating arrangements (e.g., thrust, proscenium, in the round, pen-air, promenade, site-specific) and consider how each affects both the actors’ performances and the audience’s response.

outcomes.statement: Investigate educational opportunities for theatre artists in Saskatchewan, and examine possible careers and training paths.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify theatre artists, groups and performance venues in Saskatchewan, and examine various paths available to work in these careers

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explore the training options available through mentorship, university, college, workshops and specific courses.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Examine how artists represent their training/experiences in an artist biography.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Reflect on own skills and experiences and represent them (e.g., written or videotaped artist bio, headshot, cover letter).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Volunteer or job shadow, where possible, in a professional or community theatre or theatre school.

outcomes.statement: Examine dramatic performance and theatre history from a variety of traditions.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss connections between Indigenous artistic traditions (e.g., song, dance, stories) and the land, identities and worldviews (e.g., treaty education outcome SI10 - examine the spirit and intent of Treaties and investigate [through drama work] the extent to which they have been fulfilled).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Recognize that artistic practices are sometimes specific to a treaty territory, cultural and/or language group in Saskatchewan and Canada.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Create a timeline of theatre traditions around the world.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Reflect on how drama and theatre performances relate to a specific time, place and culture (e.g., examine dramatic arts and theatre traditions and practices from the homelands of newcomer students).

outcomes.statement: Examine how drama represents human experience and impacts individuals.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Respond to dramatic works, student created or other, and reflect on the impact on self and audience.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Gather an audience’s reaction to a dramatic work through discussion or written means.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Reflect on the ways that viewing or reading dramatic work has challenged own views or beliefs (e.g., climate change, gender and sexual diversity, unfulfilled treaty promises, interpersonal relationships).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Reflect on own interactions with forms of dramatic work most enjoyed, and describe ways these choices are connected to personal perspectives and/or experiences.

outcomes.statement: Research the role of storytelling and oral history in an Indigenous culture, past or present, and, respecting protocols, use this learning to inspire own stories and dramatic work.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Tell own story (e.g., drawing on memories, cultural background, personal experiences, family history).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Discuss the significance of oral transmission of Métis, First Nations, and/or Inuit history and family stories.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Examine how stories may be used for different purposes (e.g., to explain how the world works, how to behave, oral and/or written histories).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Engage, where possible, with an Elder, Knowledge Keeper or First Nations storyteller to hear stories and learn about protocols concerning the telling and gifting of traditional stories.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Investigate how Indigenous traditional knowledge is transmitted (e.g., oral, digital, multimedia) and/or influential in drama and theatre work.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Listen to a traditional or contemporary Métis story (e.g., invited guests, online) and respond through one or more art forms.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Discuss the role and importance of language and sharing of stories in the preservation and evolution of cultural identity (e.g., treaty education outcome SI10, indicator -- imagine what society would look like today if all treaty obligations had been completely fulfilled and what it could look like into the future).

outcomes.statement: Apply principles and techniques for injury prevention to ensure safety in the work area.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 1A: General Safety (Core) · Suggested Time: 2-5 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Recognize and apply safe and fair work practices including freedom from violence, harassment and bullying.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify industry standard personal protective equipment (PPE) such as safety goggles, footwear, hearing protection, headwear and protective clothing.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Review the fire evacuation plan for the work area including the location of fire alarms, fire extinguishers and exits.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Describe ways to reduce personal injury or material and equipment damage as a result of unsafe work acts or environments.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Discuss appropriate actions in case of an injury or accident, such as whom to contact and first-aid procedures.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Explain the purpose of ventilation in a confined environment.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Identify hazardous materials and relevant WHMIS procedures.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Describe the importance of a clean work area and methods used to maintain a clean work area.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Identify risks and potential safety hazards (e.g., tools on floor, exposed live wires and extension cords).

outcomes.statement: Demonstrate safe practices when working with electricity and equipment.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 2A: Electrical Safety (Core) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 1A

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss risks and potential safety hazards common to the electrical industry.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify legislation and industry standards related to working with electricity and equipment.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Identify the presence of live voltage using tools such as a multimeter or non-contact voltage tester.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Demonstrate proper lockout and tagout procedures.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Explain the purpose of ventilation in a confined environment when working with electrical devices such as a soldering iron.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Demonstrate safe practices (e.g., check equipment for damaged wires and proper grounding and ensure work area is clean and dry) when working with electrical equipment.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Understand the need for circuit protection in electrical circuits.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Inspect electrical equipment for hazards before use.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Understand fall protection equipment (FPE) requirements and usage.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Discuss the uses of aerial work platforms (e.g., scissor lift) and fall protection.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Demonstrate safe practices when using elevation equipment (e.g., ladder, scissor lift and scaffolding).

outcomes.statement: Identify and use hand and power tools safely and appropriately.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 3A: Hand and Power Tool Safety (Core) · Suggested Time: 2-5 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify and follow safe work practices associated with hand and power tools.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Describe safety precautions including the use of personal protective equipment (PPE) required for each tool used.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Select and use appropriate hand and power tools.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Classify tools according to their capabilities (e.g., cutting, striking and holding) and method of power (e.g., hand, power and electric).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Maintain and store tools appropriately.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Inspect tools before use, and in consultation with the instructor, tag out for repair as required.

outcomes.statement: Explain the basics of electron theory.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 5A: Electrical Principles - Electron Theory (Core) · Suggested Time: 2-3 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explain the structure of an atom, using Bohr’s atomic model, with respect to electrons, protons and neutrons.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Discuss the role of electrons as carriers of electric charge.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Demonstrate that like charges repel and unlike charges attract (i.e., Law of Electrostatics).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Differentiate between static and current electricity.

outcomes.statement: Determine current, voltage and resistance in simple circuits.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 5B: Electrical Principles - Current, Voltage and Resistance (Core) · Suggested Time: 3-6 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 5A

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Define common electrical terms including current, voltage, resistance, units of measurement (e.g., volts, amperes and ohms), insulators, semiconductors and conductors.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explain the relationship between current, voltage and resistance using Ohm’s Law (Voltage [V] = Current [I] x Resistance [R]).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Calculate current, voltage and resistance values for different simple circuits.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Verify the current, voltage and resistance readings in simple circuits.

outcomes.statement: Differentiate between alternating current (AC) and direct current (DC).
outcomes.printedWith: Module 5C: Electrical Principles - Alternating Current and Direct Current (Core) · Suggested Time: 2-3 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 5B

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explain the operating principles of AC and DC.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Research the history of the competition between supporters of AC and DC.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Identify common applications of AC (e.g., house wiring and distribution of power) and DC (e.g., cell phones, flashlights and hybrid cars).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explain why either AC or DC may be preferable for specific applications.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Draw common AC and DC waveforms.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Observe a sine wave and label the characteristic parts including cycle, wavelength, wave height, period and frequency.

outcomes.statement: Explain how power is typically generated and distributed in Canada.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 6A: Power Production and Distribution (Core) · Suggested Time: 4-6 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Compare different types (e.g., coal, natural gas, hydro, solar, wind, nuclear, geothermal and biomass) of power generation.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Research how power is distributed (e.g., different voltage power lines, transformers, distribution substations and transformers) to residences, businesses and industry throughout Saskatchewan.

indicators.label: c

outcomes.statement: Examine the diversity and impact of Saskatchewan’s energy and mining sectors.

indicators.label: a

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explore the principles of energy release, conversion and utilization.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explain the fundamental differences between matter and energy.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Identify the renewable and non-renewable energy and mineral resources found in Saskatchewan and the local area.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Describe the main stages of the exploration, mining and drilling processes.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Research the role of government ministries and Indigenous peoples in the energy and mining sectors.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Investigate some of the commercial enterprises that engage in mining, drilling and support activities in Saskatchewan.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Explore the impact of the energy and mining on society (e.g., communication technology, manufacturing, agriculture and consumer products and services).

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Investigate the history of the hiring practices in the energy and mining sectors to include diverse groups (e.g., women, Indigenous peoples and immigrants).

indicators.label: j

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Identify local energy and mineral companies.

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Discuss local, national and global current events in the energy and mining sectors.

outcomes.statement: Explore the safety standards of the energy and mining industries.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Analyze the historical safety statistics on injuries in the energy and mining industries.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify strategies to mitigate risks and potential safety hazards in energy, petroleum and mining operations.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explore the use of zero energy state and lockout tagout features of equipment.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explain how the Globally Harmonized System (GHS) is used.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Examine the reliance on basic safety policies when using advanced technology.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Describe ways to reduce personal injury because of unsafe work activities (e.g., lifting heavy objects, travelling underground and blasting) or environments (e.g., working around large and noisy equipment, radiation exposure and working underground).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Investigate ways to mitigate damage to equipment because of unsafe work activities or environments.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Explore the safety regulations, procedures, equipment and personnel at local or regional mining, drilling and power generation sites.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Describe the use of personal protective equipment (PPE) (e.g., masks, ear plugs, safety goggles and footwear) for respiratory, hearing, sight and body protection.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Discuss the hierarchy of controls including elimination, substitution, engineering, administrative controls and PPE.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Identify potential fire hazards and prevention procedures in underground mines, well sites and processing plants.

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Explain the importance of emergency response teams, drills and procedures at a mine site.

indicators.label: m
indicators.text: Assess the consequences of failure of one or more worker safety programs or controls, whether through accident or not following established procedures.

indicators.label: n
indicators.text: Explore the chief hazards and risks (e.g., high voltage power lines, turbines and ground falls) faced by workers in energy and mining industries.

outcomes.statement: Explore Saskatchewan's landforms and natural environments and their relationship to the location of renewable and non-renewable resources.

indicators.text: Define physical geography.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explain how the geological processes of weathering, evaporation and erosion transform the Earth's land surface over time.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Provide specific examples from Saskatchewan’s landscape that illustrate the numerous branches of physical geography (e.g., geomorphology, hydrology, glaciology, biogeography, climatology and geomatics).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Examine the impact of continental glaciation in shaping Saskatchewan’s key topographic features (e.g., Qu’Appelle valley).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Discuss the variance of current vegetation zones of Saskatchewan and why some areas are devoid of resource production (e.g., forestry in central Saskatchewan and environmentally protected areas).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Explain the difference between and provide local examples of renewable and non-renewable resource.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Describe how the physical geography and climate of Saskatchewan are unique to the rest of Canada and other parts of the world.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Identify where the most prominent natural resources are geographically located (e.g., clay and potash in southern regions and uranium in northern Saskatchewan).

outcomes.statement: Investigate the scientific theories and principles that explain the formation of landforms on Earth and their relationship to the location of renewable and non-renewable resources.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Examine the significance of the fundamental scientific principles of geology (e.g., principle of uniformitarianism, principle of superposition, principle of faunal succession and theory of plate tectonics) in understanding the present nature of Earth's surface, crust and sedimentary strata.

indicators.text: Describe the formation of sedimentary strata in terms of origin of sedimentary material, transportation, deposition and lithification.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Explain the role of sedimentary strata in the preservation of fossil materials, including fossil fuels (e.g., folding and hydrocarbon traps).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Discuss the purpose of a stratigraphic chart and its importance to the energy and mining industries.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Explore the Phanerozoic eon including its age, eras and formations and its relevance to modern day Saskatchewan geology.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Describe the types of resources and commodities that are utilized from different formations (e.g., Bakken formation produces light oil).

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Identify mine locations, types of deposits and estimated reserves of natural resources (e.g., uranium, other metals, helium, diamonds, coal, oil, natural gas and potash) in Saskatchewan.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Explain why geology and geological history are important in the energy and mining industries.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Define groundwater.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Describe the importance of groundwater based on its uses and availability locally and worldwide.

indicators.text: Explain the hydrologic cycle with a focus on groundwater components.

indicators.label: d

indicators.text: Explore how groundwater is extracted and the purpose of different types of wells (e.g., drilled vs. bored, withdrawal vs. monitoring and domestic vs. industrial).

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Investigate the extraction of groundwater and the advantages and disadvantages on the environment and community at large (e.g., animals, vegetation, land subsidence and sinkhole formation, and the people of our province including surrounding Indigenous communities).

indicators.text: Explore the impact The Saskatchewan Treaty Land Entitlement Framework Agreement on the energy and mining industries.

indicators.label: j

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Investigate the factors (e.g., land, forests and waterways) considered when conducting an environmental impact study.

indicators.text: Compare the environmental scores of the resource industry in Saskatchewan to the rest of the world.

outcomes.statement:
Comprehend and respond to a variety of visual, oral, print, and multimedia texts that address:
- identity (e.g., Foundational Stories);
- social responsibility (e.g., Destiny and Challenges of Life); and
- social action (agency) (e.g., Human Existence).

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: View, listen to, read, and respond to First Nations and Métis resources and other texts that reflect diverse personal identities, worldviews, and backgrounds (e.g., appearance, culture, socio-economic status, ability, age, gender, language, social structures, and decision making).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify connections between self, texts, and culture.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Develop understanding and interpretations of a variety of texts by drawing upon personal experiences and prior knowledge of texts and language.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Comprehend key ideas and supporting details (both explicit and implicit), and determine their literal and implied meaning.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Identify and evaluate effectiveness of text organization and elements.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Respond thoughtfully and critically to text providing support from text to justify response.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Generate significant and thought-provoking questions about what is viewed, listened to, and read.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Respond personally and critically to individuals, events, and ideas presented in a variety of First Nations, Métis, and other Canadian and international texts.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Generate relevant questions about texts on issues related to identity, social responsibility, and social action (agency).

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Discuss ways in which texts convey, challenge, or support and affirm individual and community values and behaviours.

outcomes.statement: View, interpret, summarize, and draw conclusions about the ideas and information presented in a variety of illustrations, charts, graphs, and television, film, and video presentations including a documentary or current affairs program.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: View, interpret, and summarize grade-appropriate literary and informational texts created by First Nations, Métis, Saskatchewan, Canadian, and international authors from various cultural communities.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Select, use, and evaluate purposefully a variety of before (page 24), during (page 25), and after (page 26) strategies to construct meaning when viewing.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text:
Understand and apply language cues and conventions to construct and confirm meaning when viewing including:
- Pragmatic cues: recognizing and understanding formal English and how stylistic choices affect the meaning and impact of the message; recognizing different English dialects and problems inherent in "standard" English supremacy.
- Textual cues: recognizing and understanding the distinctive formats of a range of visual and multimedia texts and their textual and organizational features.
- Syntactic cues: recognizing and comprehending basic English sentence structures including common kernel structures and how they have been expanded with qualifiers and how they have been compounded and transformed (as questions, exclamations, inversions, negatives).
- Semantic/Lexical/Morphological cues: recognizing and comprehending when and how words are used in a concrete or abstract and a denotative or connotative way.
- Graphophonic cues: recognizing and comprehending the structure and patterns of high-frequency, topic-specific, and new words encountered in viewing.
- Other cues: recognizing and comprehending textual features such as graphic aids (e.g., diagrams, graphs, timelines, table of contents and index) and illustrations (e.g., photographs, images, drawings, sketches); recognizing intonation, nonverbal cues and body language; recognizing gestures, facial expression, sound, visual, and multimedia aids that were used to enhance presentation.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text:
Demonstrate active viewing behaviours including:
- determine what the text is representing
- identify and analyze how the text was constructed
- identify the intended audiences and points of view in the text
- infer the assumptions, interests, beliefs, and values embedded in the text and the credibility and purpose of the author
- recognize language and media techniques and conventions in television, film, and video presentations
- analyze how the text uses argument, images, placement, editing, and music to create emotion and impact
- evaluate and critique the persuasive techniques.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Analyze contrasting texts, evaluating the ways verbal and non-verbal (visual and multimedia) features are organized and combined for different meanings, effects, purposes, and audiences in different social contexts.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Investigate the source of media presentation or production including who made it, why, and for whom it was made.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Evaluate how genders and various cultures and socio-economic groups are portrayed in mass media.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Prepare and present a critical response to what was viewed.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: View and discuss the meaning and characterization implicit in the action of a scene from a play, film, television production (e.g., dialogue, movement, physical position of characters), noting visual features (e.g., set, costumes, and character appearance).

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Discuss the characterization, mood, and historical setting achieved by an actor and director in a live performance or film version of a play.

- Graphophonic cues: recognizing and comprehending the structure and patterns of high-frequency, topic-specific, and new words encountered in listening; identifying and explaining word structure and patterns that help support understanding.

indicators.text:
Create spoken, written, and other representations that include:
- a clear thesis and logical points to support messages and arguments
- appropriate details to support thesis
- a style and voice appropriate to audience and purpose
- coherence, logical progression, and support for ideas
- clear patterns of organization
- convincing conclusion.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text:
Develop and present a project-based inquiry related to a theme or topic of the course:
- collaborate to determine group knowledge base and to define inquiry or research purpose and parameters
- formulate questions to focus and guide inquiry or research
- develop and use an inquiry or research plan to identify and access relevant ideas and information from a variety of sources
- determine the credibility, accuracy, completeness, and usefulness of a variety of information sources for a particular inquiry or research plan
- access information using a variety of tools (e.g., electronic networks, libraries, taped oral histories)
- organize information using appropriate forms (e.g., charts, diagrams, outlines, electronic databases)
- analyze and understand implications and consequences of plagiarism (i.e., ethical, legal, professional)
- draw logical conclusion from information and consider how to best present to identified audience
- document sources accurately using standard format (such as Modern Language Association [MLA], and American Psychological Association [APA])
- cite reference for all sources of information including summarized and paraphrased ideas from other authors.

- exhibit logical structures appropriate to audience, purpose, and context
- have a central foci and strong messages
- organize ideas in logical and appropriate sequences
- include smooth transitions
- use a variety of forms and technologies such as sound, photographs, and models
- provide logical and convincing conclusions.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Select, use, and evaluate purposefully a variety of before (page 28), during (page 29), and after (page 30) strategies to construct and communicate meaning when using other forms of representing.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text:
Understand and apply the language cues and conventions to construct and communicate meaning when using various forms of representing.
- Pragmatic cues and conventions: selecting and using language register appropriate for the subject, context, audience, and purpose; using conventional "standard" English when required.
- Textual cues and conventions: selecting and using text form appropriate for subject, purpose, and audience.
- Syntactic cues and conventions: selecting and using formal spoken and written sentences that are meaningful, clear, correctly punctuated, and devoid of ambiguous expressions; demonstrating control over such elements as subject-verb agreement, pronoun-antecedent agreement, verb forms, and parallelism.
- Semantic/Lexical/Morphological cues and conventions: using words precisely, accurately, and for effect (e.g., to create imagery, to communicate figuratively, to communicate symbolically, as an allusion).
- Graphophonic cues and conventions: using the sounds of letters and syllables and the placement of accents to determine the pronunciation and spelling of words.
- Other cues and conventions: using communication elements such as handwriting, consistent font, neatness, underlining, indentations, spacing, and margins to enhance the clarity and the legibility of communication; using appropriate visual and multimedia aids to enhance presentation; choosing appropriate font size and style when word processing.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text:
Prepare, rehearse, and confidently deliver a visual or multimedia presentation, explaining key ideas and events (actual or based on text studied) using appropriate combination of charts, diagrams, pictures, sounds, models, drama, and print with:
- An effective introduction that sets the direction for presentation by getting attention of audience, introducing the topic, presenting the central idea or purpose, identifying the main point, and making audience eager to see and hear the rest of the presentation.
- A body that organizes information logically so audience can follow.
- A conclusion that helps audience understand what is important in the presentation.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Present information using print and non-print aids to engage and inform a familiar audience.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Use props, visual aids, graphics, and electronic media to enhance the appeal and accuracy of presentations.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Use a variety of technological functions (including computer software) to publish original work.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Use and adapt production techniques and technologies to communicate information, ideas, narrative, or other messages, integrating verbal, visual, and dramatic features to achieve a range of effects.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Analyze, organize, and convert information into different forms (e.g., charts, graphs, drawings).

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Experiment with a variety of text forms (e.g., advertisement, tableau, drama) and techniques (e.g., graphics).

outcomes.statement: Use oral language to express a range of information and ideas in formal (including a prepared talk on a familiar topic, an oral presentation of a passage of prose or poetry, and a retelling of a narrative or a recounting of an experience or event) and informal (discussion and group work) situations.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text:
Participate in small- and large-group discussions, observing the courtesies of group discussion, and demonstrate effective group interaction skills and strategies:
- understand the purpose and direction of the group
- adjust to roles in group
- develop harmony, listen, observe, and respond to and clarify one another's ideas
- be respectful but also critical
- build upon and extend the thoughts of others
- work co-operatively and collaboratively with others in small groups on structured tasks
- question others, exploring the potential of their contributions, and offer clarification and elaboration upon own ideas when necessary
- assume some of the work necessary to maintain discussion and advance it (e.g., by summarizing, raising questions, extracting significant points, making connections, setting agenda)
- assume the responsibility for independent and individual summary and closure.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Select, use, and evaluate purposefully a variety of before (page 28), during (page 29), and after (page 30) strategies to construct and communicate meaning when speaking.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text:
Understand and apply the language cues and conventions to construct and communicate meaning when speaking including:
- Pragmatic cues and conventions: selecting and using language register appropriate for the subject, context, audience, and purpose; using conventional "standard" English when required.
- Textual cues and conventions: selecting and using mode of discourse (e.g., descriptive, narrative, expository, or persuasive) and text form appropriate for subject, purpose, and audience.
- Syntactic cues and conventions: selecting and using formal spoken sentences that are meaningful and devoid of ambiguous expressions; demonstrating control over such elements as subject-verb agreement, pronoun-antecedent agreement, verb forms, and parallelism (average spoken sentence length – 10.9 words).
- Semantic/Lexical/Morphological cues and conventions: using words precisely, accurately, and for effect (e.g., to create imagery, to communicate figuratively, to communicate symbolically).
- Graphophonic cues and conventions: using the sounds of letters and syllables to correctly pronounce words.
- Other cues and conventions: using appropriate volume and intonation; using appropriate non-verbal cues and body language; using appropriate gestures, facial expression, sound, visual, and multimedia aids to enhance presentation.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text:
Prepare, rehearse, and deliver a talk on a familiar topic that includes:
- An effective introduction that sets the direction for speech by getting attention of audience, introducing the topic, stating the central idea or purpose, identifying the main point, and making audience eager to hear what else you have to say.
- An attention getter (e.g., an amazing fact or startling statement; an attention-grabbing illustration; a short demonstration or colourful visual aid; a series of questions or a short history of the topic; a strong statement of why the topic is important to you and audience).
- A body logically and coherently organized so audience can follow.
- A conclusion that helps audience understand what they listened to and why it was important.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text:
Prepare, rehearse, and deliver an oral reading/interpretation of prose, poetry, or other texts including:
- arranging materials effectively
- using techniques of speech and delivery to interpret possible meanings
- thinking about how the ideas and characters in the text could be communicated with voice
- using voice (e.g., expression, pacing, tone, dialect) for characterization and effect.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Support the ongoing discourse of the classroom by contributing to the talk; listening attentively to the offerings of others; refraining from sarcasm or insult that silences others; and helping, when necessary, to draw others into the discussion.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Plan a class meeting on a real topic of concern with the aim of reaching a consensus about the action that might be taken.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Speak confidently, clearly, and persuasively to communicate and explore information, ideas, and opinions.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Develop, explain, and justify opinions.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Recognize and adjust oral presentation elements effectively (i.e., articulation, pronunciation, volume, tempo, pitch, stress, gestures, eye contact, facial expression, and poise) in keeping with purpose, audience needs, and individual cultural and linguistic background.

outcomes.statement: Compose and create a variety of written literary (including a historical persona essay and a review) and informational (including an observation (eye-witness) report and researched or technical report) texts attending to various elements of discourse (e.g., purpose, speaker, audience, form).

indicators.label: a
indicators.text:
Write essays that:
- have a central foci and strong messages
- structure material in appropriate styles for different audiences
- define the main idea by selecting relevant, logical details to achieve the purpose and to meet the reader's perceived needs
- organize ideas in a logical and appropriate sequence
- include smooth transitions
- provide logical and convincing conclusions.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Select, use, and evaluate purposefully a variety of before (page 28), during (page 29), and after (page 30) strategies to construct and communicate meaning when writing.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text:
Understand and apply the language cues and conventions to construct and communicate meaning when writing including:
- Pragmatic cues and conventions: selecting and using language register appropriate for the subject, context, audience, and purpose; using conventional "standard" English when required.
- Textual cues and conventions: selecting and using mode of discourse (e.g., descriptive, narrative, expository, or persuasive) and text form appropriate for subject, purpose, and audience.
- Syntactic cues and conventions: selecting and using formal written sentences that are meaningful, clear, correctly punctuated, and devoid of ambiguous expressions; demonstrating control over such elements as subject-verb agreement, pronoun-antecedent agreement, verb forms, and parallelism (average written sentence length – 11.7 words).
- Semantic/Lexical/Morphological cues and conventions: using words precisely, accurately, and for effect (e.g., to create imagery, to communicate figuratively, to communicate symbolically, as an allusion).
- Graphophonic cues and conventions: using the sounds of letters and syllables and the placement of accents to determine the pronunciation and spelling of words.
- Other cues and conventions: using communication elements such as handwriting, consistent font, neatness, underlining, indentations, spacing, and margins to enhance the clarity and the legibility of communication; writing legibly with appropriate speed and control; choosing appropriate font size and style when word processing.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text:
Retell a narrative or recount an experience or event (e.g., a memory, an essay of experience) that:
- introduces the action and draws in the reader
- identifies the story's main character and establishes the setting
- uses dialogue to establish characters and create the drama
- provides an effective ending that logically "winds up" the events.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text:
Write an observation report/eyewitness account (e.g., an incident report, an event report) that:
- tells when and where the event happened
- accounts the details of an event in a logical order
- uses descriptive details (including sights, sounds, tastes, textures, and smells) that show the reader what happened, as if he or she were seeing it firsthand
- uses order of location (top to bottom, front to back, left to right, head to toe) or time order (first, next, then, and so on) to organize details
- uses specific verbs
- establishes the time and the place
- answers 5W and H (who, what, when, where, why, and how) questions for facts about what happened
- includes thoughts and comments that bring experience to life
- uses an engaging voice that sounds interested and knowledgeable.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text:
Write an inquiry report (e.g., research report, an I-Search, a technical report) that:
- addresses what makes the subject worth investigating
- puts central ideas into a focus or thesis statement
- includes information related to focus or thesis, is current, and drawn from reliable, relevant sources that are cited
- presents an introduction (revealing story or quotation; important background information; interesting or surprise facts; reason for choosing subject)
- includes a body that develops logically the details of the subject
- provides a conclusion that leaves reader with a clear understanding of the importance of research and draws a conclusion with a final statement.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text:
Write a historical persona essay (e.g., biographical narrative, response to a historical photo) that:
- includes a historic person
- defines important moments in the historic person's life so essay is well-focused and organized
- shows understanding of the person, the events, and gathered details about the place and time
- includes reflections and observations about person's life and experiences
- includes the people the person might have met and creates accurate depictions of those individuals
- uses the "I" voice (imagined self to be the person and to be part of these events) in order to get a feel for the experience.
- includes thoughts and feelings
- uses dialogue to bring characters to life
- employs an easy-to-follow organization.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text:
Write a review (e.g., evaluating a literary work) that:
- includes thoughtful explanations and specific references to the text itself
- expresses opinion about the value or worth of the subject in order to help audience decide
- explores strengths and weaknesses of work and includes passages from text as examples
- justifies opinion
- addresses what makes the text interesting, exciting, engaging, believable, unforgettable, and significant
- does not retell plot but recognizes theme (general observation about life or human nature) of the text and the relevance of literary techniques (e.g., setting, characters, point of view, basic conflicts, plot development, and use of literary elements such as figurative language and sound).

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Experiment with and explore a variety of written text forms (such as poems, memorandums, legends) and techniques (such as foreshadowing, flashback, imagery, allegory, figurative language, symbolism, point of view, parallelism, hyperbole) and explain their appeal.

outcomes.statement: Establish and apply criteria to evaluate own and others' work.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Use feedback to evaluate own effectiveness and set goals in language learning and use.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Evaluate own and others' contributions to group process and provide support where needed.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Contribute to the creation of rubrics and other assessment and evaluation tools used to assess visual, oral, written, multimedia, and other products submitted.

indicators.text: Consider alternative ways of reaching goals.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Celebrate special accomplishments by using language to congratulate and encourage, to publicly recognize, and to properly recount the achievement.

outcomes.statement: Set personal language learning goals and select strategies to enhance growth in language learning.

indicators.text: Use feedback to evaluate own effectiveness and set goals in language learning and use.
