indicators.text: View, listen to, read, comprehend, and respond to a variety of contemporary and traditional texts including First Nations and Métis resources that present different viewpoints and perspectives on issues and reflect diverse personal identities, worldviews, and backgrounds (e.g., appearance, culture, socio-economic status, ability, age, gender, language).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Apply personal experiences and prior knowledge of texts and language to develop understanding and interpretations of variety of texts.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Respond personally and critically to individuals, events, and ideas presented in a variety of First Nations, Métis, Canadian, and international texts.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Discuss ways in which texts convey and challenge individual and community values and behaviours.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Identify how human experiences and values are reflected in texts.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Test ideas and values against ideas and values in texts.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: View, listen to, read, and respond to historically or culturally significant works (texts) that reflect and enhance studies in history and social science.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Identify recurrent patterns and themes in texts.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Analyze how a text is related to the themes and issues of a particular period in time.

outcomes.statement: View, interpret, and report on ideas and information from more than one source to develop and support positions on various topics related to the course including identity, social responsibility, and personal agency.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: View, comprehend, interpret, and summarize grade-appropriate visual and multimedia texts created by First Nations, Métis, Saskatchewan, Canadian, and international developers and artists from various cultural communities that address identity, social responsibility, and personal agency.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Select, use, and evaluate purposefully a variety of before (page 24), during (page 25), and after (page 26) strategies to construct meaning when viewing.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text:
Understand and apply language communication cues and conventions to construct and confirm meaning when viewing including:
- Pragmatic cues: recognizing and comprehending language registers that are varied and used for effect.
- Textual cues: recognizing and comprehending the organization of thoughts and ideas of a range of visual and multimedia texts and their organizational features.
- Syntactic cues: recognizing and comprehending a variety of sentence patterns for communicating and clarifying meaning.
- Semantic/Lexical/Morphological cues: using a dictionary or other source to determine a word's meaning(s).
- Graphophonic cues: recognizing the correct form and usage of a word.
- Other cues: recognizing and comprehending how features including graphic aids (e.g., diagrams, graphs, timelines) support and enhance the message.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: View, interpret, and draw conclusions about the ideas and information presented in a variety of illustrations, maps, charts, graphs, and other visual texts.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Evaluate how genders and various cultures and socio-economic groups are portrayed in representations by the mass media.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Recognize persuasive techniques (including propaganda) being used in visual and multimedia texts, and analyze and assess the impact of specific media, techniques, and designs.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Prepare and present critical response to what was viewed.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Identify and evaluate the verbal and visual features including images, colour, layout, graphics, and messages in consumer products (e.g., clothing, electronic products, food, entertainment services).

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Respond to and discuss various meanings, ideas, and effects describing how verbal and static and moving visual features are combined for different purposes and audiences in CD covers, posters, and videos of popular songs and singers.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Attend a performance of a play and discuss the specific scenes, main character, and technical production aspects of the presentation.

outcomes.statement: Listen to, comprehend, interpret, and summarize information and ideas presented in a variety of literary and informational texts including group discussion, oral readings, interviews, prepared talks, and a talk-back show about a topic or issue being studied.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Listen to, interpret, and summarize grade-appropriate literary and informational texts created by First Nations, Métis, Saskatchewan, Canadian, and international authors from various cultural communities that address identity, social responsibility, and personal agency.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Select, use, and evaluate purposefully a variety of before (page 24), during (page 25), and after (page 26) strategies to construct meaning when listening.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text:
Understand and apply language cues and conventions to construct and confirm meaning when listening including:
- Pragmatic cues: recognizing and comprehending language registers that are varied and used for effect (e.g., characterization, dialect) and that have been influenced by the context (e.g., community in which it was learned).
- Textual cues: recognizing and comprehending the organization of thoughts and ideas of a range of oral texts and their organizational features.
- Syntactic cues: recognizing and comprehending how word order and sentence patterns communicate meaning in English and also when they do not communicate clearly.
- Semantic/Lexical/Morphological cues: using a dictionary or other source to determine a word's meaning(s) and etymology.
- Graphophonic cues: recognizing the correct form and usage of a word.
- Other cues: recognizing and comprehending how features including voice production factors (e.g., articulation, tone, tempo, pronunciation, volume, emphasis, pitch, pause) and non-verbal cues (e.g., gestures, stance, eye contact) clarify intent of message.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text:
Demonstrate active listening behaviour including:
- concentrate, focus, attend, and filter distractions
- analyze explicit and implicit messages, viewpoints, and concepts
- recognize overall plan or organization including transitional expressions
- paraphrase what was listened to and heard
- distinguish fact from opinion
- identify and analyze persuasive techniques
- evaluate perspective, credibility, and logic
- use effective notemaking strategies and a variety of written or graphic forms to organize, summarize, and share ideas acquired from listening
- prepare and ask relevant questions and respond appropriately
- analyze the overall effectiveness of the message.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Understand the factors that interfere with good listening (e.g., environment, speaker, listener) and filter out distractions.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Prepare and present critical response to what was listened to and heard supporting conclusions with reference to what was presented.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Apply appropriate listening strategies when interviewing (including preparing and asking relevant questions, making notes, responding correctly and effectively, compiling and reporting responses).

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Formulate and support judgements (using convincing evidence) about the ideas under discussion.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Listen to and evaluate several excerpts from a range of phone-in talk-back shows about a particular issue.

outcomes.statement: Read, interpret, and summarize a wide variety of classical and contemporary literary (including drama, biography, autobiography, poetry, short stories, novels) and informational (including letters, diaries, memoranda, electronic communications) texts.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Read, interpret, and summarize grade-appropriate literary and informational texts created by First Nations, Métis, Saskatchewan, Canadian, and international authors from various cultural communities that address identity, social responsibility, and personal agency.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Select, use, and evaluate purposefully a variety of before (page 24), during (page 25), and after (page 26) strategies to construct meaning when reading.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text:
Understand and apply language cues and conventions to construct and confirm meaning when reading including:
- Pragmatic cues: recognizing and comprehending language registers that are varied and used for effect (e.g., characterization, dialect) and that have been influenced by the context (e.g., community in which it was learned).
- Textual cues: recognizing and comprehending the organization of thoughts and ideas in a variety of written and other texts including distinctive features of genres (e.g., prose, poetry) and organizational patterns within each genre (e.g., chronological, spatial, enumerative, problem and solution, cause and effect, comparison and contrast).
- Syntactic cues: recognizing and comprehending how word order and sentence patterns communicate meaning in English and also when they do not communicate clearly.
- Semantic/Lexical/Morphological cues: using a dictionary or other source to determine a word's meaning(s), usage, pronunciation, and etymology.
- Graphophonic cues: recognizing and using the correct form and usage of a word to determine the pronunciation (e.g., "project" as a noun versus as a verb).
- Other cues: recognizing and comprehending how features such as layout and accompanying graphics clarify intent of message.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text:
Demonstrate active reading behaviours including:
- establish a purpose for reading such as to learn, interpret, and enjoy
- skim, scan, and read closely
- identify and analyze explicit and implicit messages, viewpoints, concepts, persuasive techniques, and propaganda techniques (e.g., testimonial, band wagon, stereotyping)
- recognize and analyze text structures and elements
- relate understanding of a range of texts to personal experience, purposes, audience, and other texts
- evaluate perspective, credibility, and logic
- differentiate fact from opinion
- differentiate between literal and figurative statements
- test own ideas and values against those in text
- recognize, comprehend, and discuss the significance of allusions and symbols in context
- construct images based on text descriptions
- discuss and analyze meanings, ideas, language, and literary quality in a range of contemporary and historical texts, taking account of purpose, audience, and time
- use notemaking, marginal notes, and outlining to better understand texts.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Read fluently and independently a wide range of contemporary and historical texts, adapting reading processes and strategies for different purposes (including for information and enjoyment).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Recognize stylistic devices and techniques such as characterization, flashback, foreshadowing, and hyperbole.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Describe, discuss, and analyze the distinctive conventions, structures, and language features of a range of texts and explain how they suit the topic and purpose.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Read about a particular event or issue, using texts from a range of sources, including magazines, newspapers, cartoons, and letters to the editor to identify different points of view or angles.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Compare the characteristics of different texts and consider the reason for these differences, in terms of topic, purpose, and point of view.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Read and interpret critically the main ideas, events, and themes of a variety of literary texts including stories, novels, scripts, poetry, and non-fiction works, and prepare and present critical responses to what was read.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Read and make generalizations, supported by specific details and examples, about key concepts, characters, themes, and techniques in literary texts.

outcomes.statement:
Compose and create a range of visual, multimedia, oral, and written texts to explore:
- identity (e.g., Diversity of Being);
- social responsibility (e.g., Degrees of Responsibility); and
- social action (agency) (e.g., Justice and Fairness).

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Develop and articulate defensible points of view on individual, community, national, and world issues.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text:
Create spoken, written, and other representations that include:
- a clear thesis and logical points to support thesis
- appropriate details to support thesis
- a style and voice appropriate to audience and purpose
- coherence, logical progression, and support for ideas
- clear patterns of organization
- a justifiable conclusion.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text:
Develop a project-focused inquiry related to a theme or issue of the course:
- generate relevant questions that can be researched
- refine topics and clarify ideas
- compile information from primary and secondary sources in systematic ways
- synthesize the content from several sources or works by various authors dealing with a single issue
- interpret and report on ideas and information from more than one source to develop and support positions on various topics
- extend ideas presented in primary or secondary sources through original analysis, evaluation, and elaboration
- compile ideas and information into reports, summaries, and other formats and draw conclusions.

outcomes.statement: Create and present a visual or multimedia presentation supporting a prepared talk on a researched issue, using either digital or other presentation tools.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text:
Prepare and present visual and multimedia presentations and a research talk/report that:
- use logical structures appropriate to audience, purpose, and context
- have a central foci and strong messages
- organize ideas in a logical and appropriate sequence
- include smooth transitions and ensure smooth flow from visual to visual
- exhibit a variety of forms and technologies such as sound, photographs, and models, and understand how ideas are communicated through elements of design such as colour, shape, line, and texture
- use props, visual aids, graphics, music, sound effects, photos ("clip-art"), and electronic media to enhance the appeal and accuracy of presentations, and ensure words on visuals are easy to read
- ensure each visual fits audience and purpose
- provide logical and convincing conclusions.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Select, use, and evaluate purposefully a variety of before (page 28), during (page 29), and after (page 30) strategies to construct and communicate meaning when using other forms of representing.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text:
Understand and apply language cues and conventions to construct and communicate meaning when using various forms of representing including:
- Pragmatic cues and conventions: selecting and using language that includes people across cultures, races, genders, ages, and abilities and avoids common usage problems including imprecision and the use of jargon, slang, euphemism, clichés, gobbledygook, and "abusages" (such as "Me and John...", "I can't get no...,""Like,...").
- Textual cues and conventions: creating visual and multimedia texts that are unified (i.e., all elements combined to form a single whole or "oneness") and coherent (i.e., consistent, logically arranged, and connected).
- Syntactic cues and conventions: using sentences that are varied in form (e.g., parallelism, inversion, subordination); are free of misplaced qualifiers and dangling qualifiers; show agreement of subject and verb, consistency in verb tense, pronoun agreement, and clear pronoun reference; and use correctly that/which, who/whom, and punctuation.
- Semantic/lexical/morphological cues and conventions: using words correctly including prepositions (e.g., suited to, suited for), homonyms (e.g., to, too, two), plurals and possessives (e.g., the cat's paws, students' projects, people's pets), and meaning (e.g., then/than; few, fewer/less, lesser).
- Graphophonic cues and conventions: recognizing and using Canadian spelling conventions and clear pronunciation to aid spelling (e.g., accept, except).
- Other cues and conventions: using appropriate visual elements (e.g., colour, layout, graphics, illustrations) and media technologies to clarify and enhance message.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Select, interpret, and synthesize information from visual texts and present it effectively, using a range of visual and layout features and appropriate technologies for variety of purposes.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Select a section of narrative text and use it as a basis for a dramatization using narrator where appropriate, dialogue, action, backgrounds, costumes, props, music, sound effects, and language that retain the intent and tone of the original text.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Prepare and present a real-life action or role play an event such as buying or selling something and present the role play to class.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Select a character from a novel and plan a seminar that gives an analysis of the character and includes the use of digital or other presentation tools to show the relationships between the character and other characters in the novel (e.g., a family tree), video or still photography to demonstrate ideas for a film setting, and a sound recording to record dialogue from the text or an interview with the character with appropriate musical accompaniment.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Develop imaginative or creative representations to share interpretations and ideas.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Use persuasive techniques (e.g., rhetorical question, repetition, parallelism, analogy, appeal to authority) in visual and multimedia texts.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Experiment with a variety of text forms (e.g., advertisements, posters, videos) and techniques (e.g., colour, typeface, graphics).

outcomes.statement: Use oral language to express a range of information and ideas in formal (including a prepared talk on a researched issue, an interview, an oral reading of prose or poetry, and an explanation and defence of a personal point of view) and informal (including discussion and group work) situations.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text:
Participate in small- and large-group discussion, observing the courtesies of group discussion, and demonstrate effective group interaction skills and strategies including:
- assume some of the work necessary to maintain discussion and advance it (e.g., by summarizing, raising questions, seeking clarification, extracting significant points, making connections, setting agenda).
- maintain and demonstrate respectful behaviours
- stick to topic and keep goals in mind
- listen carefully
- co-operate by staying positive, waiting turn, and avoiding put-downs
- disagree respectfully
- encourage others by trying to understand their ideas and asking for opinions
- clarify and restate speaker's ideas to confirm meaning.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Select, use, and evaluate purposefully a variety of before (page 28), during (page 29), and after (page 30) strategies to construct and communicate meaning when speaking.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text:
Understand and apply language cues and conventions to construct and communicate meaning when speaking including:
- Pragmatic cues and conventions: selecting and using language that includes people across cultures, races, genders, ages, and abilities and avoids common usage problems including imprecision and the use of jargon, slang, euphemism, clichés, gobbledygook, and "abusages" (such as "Me and John...", "I can't get no...,""Like,...").
- Textual cues and conventions: creating oral texts that are unified (i.e., all elements combined to form a single whole or "oneness") and coherent (i.e., consistent, logically arranged, and connected).
- Syntactic cues and conventions: using sentences that are varied in form (e.g., parallelism, inversion, subordination); are free of misplaced qualifiers and dangling qualifiers; show agreement of subject and verb, consistency in verb tense, pronoun agreement, and clear pronoun reference; and use correctly that/which, who/whom, and punctuation.
- Semantic/lexical/morphological cues and conventions: using words correctly including prepositions (e.g., suited to, suited for), homonyms (e.g., to, too, two), plurals and possessives (e.g., the cat's paws, students' projects, people's pets), and meaning (e.g., then/than; few, fewer/less, lesser).
- Graphophonic cues and conventions: recognizing and using Canadian spelling conventions and clear pronunciation to aid spelling (e.g., accept, except).
- Other cues and conventions: using appropriate oral elements (e.g., volume, intonation); using appropriate non-verbal cues and body language; using appropriate gestures, facial expressions, sound, and visual and multimedia aids to enhance message.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Use oral language to interact purposefully, confidently, and appropriately in a variety of situations including participating in one-to-one, small-group, and large-group discussions (demonstrating an awareness of the relationship of language to group and community membership, acknowledging and paraphrasing views that differ from own, reassessing own viewpoints, prompting and supporting others, solving problems, resolving conflicts, building consensus, articulating and explaining personal viewpoint, discussing preferences, speaking to extend current understanding, and celebrating special events and accomplishments).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Work in pairs to develop and script an interview on an issue of interest or on an incident in a literary text, for a particular audience and purpose.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: In role, rehearse and record interview or present interview to the group.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Work in pairs to prepare and present closing argument for and against a selected fictional character on a charge which could have been levelled at a character.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Select three poems related to theme and present them to a group of peers using voice to clarify meaning by emphasizing rhythm, highlighting particular words or phrases, and signalling the role and effects of line endings, stanza breaks, and other elements of structure.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Recognize and use elements of classical speech forms (including introduction, body with transitions, conclusion) in formulating rational arguments and apply the art of persuasion.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Recognize and adjust oral presentation elements (i.e., articulation, pronunciation, volume, tempo, pitch, stress, gestures, eye contact, facial expression, and poise) in keeping with purpose, audience needs, and situation.

outcomes.statement: Create a variety of written informational (including a business letter, biographical profile, problem-solution essay) and literary (including fictionalized journal entries and a short script) communications.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text:
Write informational and literary texts that:
- use various elements of discourse (e.g., purpose, speaker, audience, form) in narrative, expository, persuasive, informational, and/or descriptive texts
- exhibit logical structures appropriate to audience, purpose, and context
- have a central foci and strong messages
- structure material in appropriate styles for audience
- define the main idea by selecting relevant, logical details that meet the reader's perceived needs
- organize ideas in a logical and appropriate sequence
- include smooth transitions
- provide logical and convincing conclusions.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Select, use, and evaluate purposefully a variety of before (page 28), during (page 29), and after (page 30) strategies to construct and communicate meaning when writing.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text:
Understand and apply language cues and conventions to construct and communicate meaning when writing including:
- Pragmatic cues and conventions: selecting and using language that includes people across cultures, races, genders, ages, and abilities, and avoids common usage problems including imprecision and the use of jargon, slang, euphemism, clichés, gobbledygook, and "abusages" (such as "Me and John...", "I can't get no...,""Like,...").
- Textual cues and conventions: creating written texts that are unified (i.e., all elements combined to form a single whole or "oneness") and coherent (i.e., consistent, logically arranged, and connected).
- Syntactic cues and conventions: using sentences that are varied in form (e.g., parallelism, inversion, subordination); are free of misplaced qualifiers and dangling qualifiers; show agreement of subject and verb, consistency in verb tense, pronoun agreement, and clear pronoun reference; and use correctly that/which, who/whom, and punctuation.
- Semantic/lexical/morphological cues and conventions: using words correctly including prepositions (e.g., suited to, suited for), homonyms (e.g., to, too, two), plurals and possessives (e.g., the cat's paws, students' projects, people's pets), and meaning (e.g., then/than; few, fewer/less, lesser).
- Graphophonic cues and conventions: recognizing and using Canadian spelling conventions and clear pronunciation to aid spelling (e.g., accept, except).
- Other cues and conventions: using appropriate written elements (e.g., font size, type face, formatting); writing legibly with appropriate speed and control; using communication elements such as neatness, underlining, indentations, spacing, and margins to enhance clarity and legibility of communication.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text:
Write an explanation and defence of personal point of view that:
- explains writer's beliefs about an important subject
- identifies focus of essay in opening paragraph
- organizes ideas in a logical and appropriate sequence
- includes smooth transitions
- provides logical and convincing conclusions.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text:
Write a biographical profile that:
- includes key ideas learned about the person
- begins by sharing some important background information
- describes the subject and explains what he or she accomplished
- ends by leaving the readers with something to think about and consider

indicators.label: f
indicators.text:
Write a problem-solution essay (e.g., an essay in which you analyze a problem and present one or more solutions) that :
- focuses on a problem that is important to self
- identities the problem in a clear statement
- analyzes the problem thoroughly, explaining its parts, history, and causes
- weighs possible solutions, what is being done to address the problems, and suggestions or solutions
- determines what readers need to know
- explains why situation exists and how it can be fixed
- includes all the important facts and reasons
- ends effectively explaining what the writer would like to see done.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text:
Write a business letter (e.g., letter of complaint, e-mail request) that:
- uses a consistent style (semi-block or full block)
- presents information completely and in the correct order
- includes all the parts of a business letter – heading, inside address, salutation, body, complimentary closing, and signature
- states purpose clearly and immediately
- gives complete and accurate details
- states clearly what the writer wants the reader to do
- avoids expressions that are wordy, clichéd, vague, or discriminatory
- begins, continues, and ends with courteous tone
- determines what the recipient needs to know.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text:
Write fictionalized journal entries (e.g., of a literary character or a historical figure) that:
- focus on a made-up character or someone read about or observed
- focus on an ongoing event or experience
- contain impressions, reflections, and observations about life, people, and experiences
- give insight into the personality and values of the character.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text:
Write a short script (e.g., a short play or a script for an advertisement) that:
- includes stage directions that indicate the time and place of the action, entrances and exits, and what characters are doing on stage
- gives details of setting that lead into the beginning of the script
- employs dialogue (characters' words) that moves the action along
- builds around a believable conflict or problem that makes sense in the lives of the main characters
- includes (if multimedia) graphics, music, Blend In, Cut To, Fade In, Fade Out, Insert, and other elements.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Experiment with and explore a variety of written text forms (such as letter of complaint, obituary, brochure) and techniques (such as figurative language, literary devices, anecdotes).

outcomes.statement: Establish and apply criteria to evaluate own and others' work.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Use feedback to evaluate own effectiveness as a communicator.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Evaluate own and others' contributions to group process and provide support where needed.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Set goals in language learning and use; identify strategies to achieve those goals.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Consider alternative ways of reaching goals.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Celebrate special accomplishments by using language to describe and discuss achievements.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Analyze how characters, conflict (e.g., character vs. self, character vs. character, character vs. society, character vs. nature), setting and point of view in fiction and non-fiction texts reflect worldviews, values or social issues.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Interpret fiction and non-fiction texts by offering plausible meanings or perspectives, using specific textual evidence for support.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Examine how fiction and non-fiction texts use structure, evidence, tone and rhetorical devices (e.g., appeals, repetition, direct address) to inform, provoke thought or persuade.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explore how an author’s/creator’s stance, bias or context influence interpretation of fiction and non-fiction texts.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Explore connections among ideas, observations, opinions, themes and emotions across a variety of texts from diverse voices.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Compare how different text forms (e.g., poem, infographic, speech) explore similar social issues or themes and assess how the form impacts interpretation.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Identify how the mode of communication influences the message and impacts the audience’s understanding, perception, emotional response and engagement (see Appendix A).

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Apply comprehension and metacognitive strategies (e.g., previewing, questioning, visualizing) to support the construction of meaning across modalities and text types (see Appendix B and Appendix C).

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Reflect on how texts raise questions or offer insights about identity, social responsibility or social agency (action).

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Develop original descriptive, narrative, poetic, expository and persuasive compositions that demonstrate understanding of genre-specific purposes, structures and language features (see Appendices D-H).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Experiment with various modalities (e.g., written, oral, visual, multimodal) to determine which one(s) best support(s) the purpose, audience and message of the composition.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Compose both fiction and non-fiction texts, thoughtfully considering the elements of each form, such as fact-based development in non-fiction and imaginative techniques in fiction.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Integrate multimodal elements (e.g., sound, image, movement, visual design) thoughtfully when composing in hybrid formats to enhance the delivery of the intended message.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Develop compositions that explore personal and collective identities, promote social responsibility and inspire social agency (action).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Revise compositions for clarity, coherence and impact, considering how effectively genre and form are aligned to audience and purpose.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Develop composition stamina by creating a longer-form text that sustains ideas, organization, purpose and audience engagement across the whole composition.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Experiment with genre-specific features (e.g., character development in narrative, rhetorical appeals in persuasion, vivid imagery in description) to shape the composition’s tone, structure and impact (see Appendices D-H).

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Explain how form, genre, audience and purpose shape the creative choices made throughout the composition process.

outcomes.statement: Reflect on the role of stories, narratives and oral traditions in expressing diverse values and worldviews, including First Nations, Métis and Inuit perspectives.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify how stories, narratives and oral traditions convey knowledge, values and teachings within specific cultures or communities.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Examine how the structure (e.g., cyclical, linear) and delivery (e.g., relational, community, or cultural context) of stories, narratives and oral traditions are connected to the worldview they express.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explore how First Nations, Métis and Inuit stories, narratives and oral traditions express relationships to land, community and identity.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explore how stories, narratives and oral traditions serve as acts of resistance to erasure within First Nations, Métis and Inuit peoples' communities.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Compare the purposes and functions of stories across cultures (e.g., to teach, to entertain, to remember, to resist, to connect).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Identify how engaging with stories, narratives and oral traditions encourages careful listening and respect for experiences different from one’s own.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Consider how stories, narratives and oral traditions can be used to reclaim peoples’ voices and worldviews (e.g., Indigenous resurgence, preservation of cultural memory, intergenerational storytelling, maintaining connection to language).

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Reflect on how a story, narrative or oral tradition can influence one’s thinking or values.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Explore how stories, narratives and oral traditions can help people understand experiences of migration, displacement, adaptation and belonging across different communities and cultural contexts.

outcomes.statement: Reflect on how personal experiences, social contexts and cultural backgrounds influence both the interpretation of texts and creation of compositions.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Reflect on how one’s lived experiences, values or worldview influence decisions about form, tone, genre and audience in original compositions.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explore how cultural background or social context can influence an author’s/creator’s choices in themes, perspectives or representations within texts.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Examine how texts by authors/creators with diverse backgrounds or lived experiences can expand or shift personal or collective viewpoints on social issues, cultural practices or historical events.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Reflect on the responsibility authors/creators hold when representing identities, cultures and experiences that differ from their own.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Consider how the meaning or impact of a text can shift over time based on personal growth and changes in context (e.g., cultural, social, historical, political).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Explore how understanding an author’s/creator’s personal, social or cultural context deepens comprehension of and engagement with the text.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Consider personal, cultural or social context as a source of insight, voice or meaningful engagement with the audience when developing original compositions.

outcomes.statement: Examine how authors/creators strategically integrate elements in multimodal texts to communicate ideas and engage the audience.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explain how various modes (e.g., text, visuals, audio, movement) contribute individually and collectively to a text’s overall meaning (see Appendix K).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explore how multimodal elements can emphasize or highlight perspectives, biases or calls to action.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Analyze how creators intentionally combine modes (e.g., visual imagery, sound effects, text, movement, narration) to serve distinct purposes, such as clarifying process, evoking emotion or emphasizing key ideas (see Appendix K).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Identify ethical considerations in multimodal compositions (e.g., crediting authors/creators, respectful representations, considering privacy and consent), including how images, sound, movement, text or design choices may influence audience emotions, understanding or trust.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Evaluate how the interaction of elements (e.g., how audio complements visuals, how text layout affects pacing) either strengthens or detracts from the overall message (see Appendix K).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Compare the impact of multimodal communication versus single-mode communication (e.g., purely text-based or purely visual) in terms of accessibility, emotional resonance or clarity of message.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Analyze how mentor multimodal compositions integrate elements effectively (e.g., alignment between message and media, pacing of visuals and audio, and transitions between modes and organization).

outcomes.statement: Combine multimodal elements strategically to convey messages with clarity, emotion and intention.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Plan multimodal compositions by selecting and intentionally combining elements (e.g., text, visuals, sound, movement) in ways that support purpose, audience, message and tone across modes (see Appendix K).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Combine modes thoughtfully (e.g., visual imagery, sound effects, text, movement, narration) to guide the audience’s attention and deepen understanding (see Appendix K).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Combine design features (e.g., colour palettes, font size and style, white space, transitions, image placement) to create emphasis, rhythm or emotion (see Appendix K).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Reflect on how changes in one element (e.g., altering tone of voice, background visuals) influence the interpretation of other elements and the overall cohesion of the composition.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Revise compositions to improve the relationship between elements, ensuring that each serves a clear purpose within the whole.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Apply accessibility strategies when combining modes (e.g., using captions with video, high contrast visuals with clear text, alt-text for images) to ensure clarity, usability and inclusion for all audiences (see Appendix K).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Consider cultural diversity, emotional safety and audience perspectives when making design choices, reflecting on how language, imagery and form may include, exclude or impact audiences.

outcomes.statement: Examine how form, style, tone, structure, purpose and language features of different genres can shape meaning and enhance audience impact.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Examine the purposes and functions of descriptive, narrative, poetic, expository and persuasive genres (see Appendices D-H).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify how structural choices (e.g., spatial order in descriptive, cause-effect in expository) shape the clarity and emotional impact of each genre (see Appendices D-H).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Examine how language features such as imagery, rhetorical appeals, figurative language, sentence variety and diction serve different purposes within and across genres.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Examine how perceived neutrality in genres, such as expository or informational writing, may still reflect an author’s/creator’s bias, framing choices or selective evidence that influence audience interpretation.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Explain genre-specific strategies in mentor texts and how they connect to the message, theme or argument.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Examine how genre language features engage audiences differently through mood, tone, voice and stylistic conventions (see Appendices D-H).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Investigate how genre language features adapt to different formats (e.g., oral retellings, multimodal representations, digital compositions) while maintaining core genre characteristics.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Compare how similar thematic topics (e.g., love, resistance, belonging) are explored through different genres and how genre-specific choices affect audience interpretation.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Explore how genre expectations can be deliberately followed or blended to enhance meaning or impact.

outcomes.statement: Experiment with form, style, tone, structure and language features in original descriptive, narrative, poetic, expository and persuasive compositions to suit different purposes and audiences.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Experiment with different perspectives (e.g., shifting between first-person, second-person, or third-person point of view; retelling an event from another character’s perspective; using limited, omniscient or unreliable narration) to explore how voice shapes audience engagement and interpretation.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Disrupt conventional structures (e.g., using nonlinear timelines, in medias res openings, cliffhangers, fragmented or reverse order) to test how sequencing affects tension, pacing and clarity.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Transform an existing text or idea into a new form (e.g., found poem from a news article; personal story retold in dramatic monologue; visual collage from an essay) to explore meaningmaking across genre and modes.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Experiment with multimodal or non-verbal storytelling techniques to express ideas when language is limited, absent or intentionally minimized.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Transform language creatively (e.g., vernacular, repetition, dialect, sensory imagery, unexpected word pairings) to evoke tone, mood, or emotion appropriate to genre and audience.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Incorporate elements like dialogue, inner monologue, or contrasting character voices to build tension, reveal motivation or develop complex conflict.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Explore form and style with low-stakes composition tasks (e.g., timed creative writes, collaborative genre mashups, character improvisations) without the pressure of perfection.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Reflect on how experimentation helped clarify intention, shift audience impact or open new possibilities for voice and genre.

outcomes.statement: Examine how craft techniques enhance the meaning and impact of texts.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explore specific author/creator moves (e.g., diction, metaphor, repetition, imagery, fragmented sentences, shifts in tone, strategic dialogue) that shape tone and mood.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Examine how craft techniques in descriptive texts (e.g., sensory detail, figurative language, spatial or chronological structure, selective focus) evoke emotion, create atmosphere or highlight significance (see Appendix D).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Examine how craft techniques in narrative texts (e.g., character and plot development, point of view, dialogue, flashbacks, setting, pacing) immerse the reader and build engagement (see Appendix E).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Examine how craft techniques in poetic texts (e.g., line breaks, stanza structure, repetition, rhythm, figurative language, imagery, sound devices) create emotion and emphasis (see Appendix F).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Examine how craft techniques in expository texts (e.g., organizational structure, text features, rhetorical questions, anecdotal examples, tone) clarify ideas and guide understanding (see Appendix G).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Examine how craft techniques in persuasive texts (e.g., counterarguments, rhetorical devices), including rhetorical appeals (i.e., ethos, pathos, logos, kairos, telos) influence beliefs, emotions or actions (see Appendix H).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Discuss how strategies in oral texts (e.g., inflection, pacing, volume, pausing, emphasis) affect audience engagement and interpretation.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Analyze how non-verbal craft techniques (e.g., facial expressions, gestures, posture, eye contact) contribute to meaning, tone, and audience impact in live or recorded performances, speeches and oral storytelling.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Analyze how creators use intentional design choices (e.g., sequencing, layout, white space, sound, visual composition) to enhance clarity, atmosphere or argument strength.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Examine how sentence- and word-level craft techniques (e.g., parallelism, rule of three, sentence length and variety, repetition, parts of speech) impact emphasis, rhythm, and meaning in texts.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Compare how different authors/creators approach similar themes, issues or ideas through distinct stylistic and structural decisions (e.g., extended metaphors, different points of view).

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Consider how diverse languages (e.g., signed, spoken, and multilingual language use) and modes of communication (e.g., captions, visual supports) convey meaning and emotion in compositions.

outcomes.statement: Use craft techniques to enhance the quality, style and impact of original compositions.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Apply specific craft techniques from mentor texts to suit audience, genre and purpose (see Appendices D-H).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Apply descriptive techniques (e.g., sensory detail, figurative language, spatial or chronological structure, selective focus) to evoke emotion, create atmosphere or highlight significance (see Appendix D).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Apply narrative techniques (e.g., character and plot development, point of view, dialogue, flashbacks, setting, pacing) to immerse the audience and build narrative tension (see Appendix E).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Apply poetic techniques (e.g., line breaks, stanza structure, repetition, rhythm, figurative language, imagery, sound devices) to create tone, emotion and emphasis (see Appendix F).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Apply expository techniques (e.g., organizational structure, text features, rhetorical questions, anecdotal examples, tone) to clarify complex ideas and guide reader understanding (see Appendix G).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Apply persuasive techniques (e.g., rhetorical appeals, direct address, rhetorical devices, tone, purposeful sentence structure) to influence thinking and action (see Appendix H).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Apply oral delivery strategies (e.g., inflection, pacing, volume, pausing, emphasis) to enhance clarity, rhythm and emotional impact in original compositions.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Apply non-verbal strategies (e.g., facial expressions, gestures, posture, eye contact) to reinforce tone, clarify meaning and strengthen audience engagement in original compositions.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Justify which craft techniques were most effective in achieving the intended impact of original compositions.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Apply sentence- and word-level craft techniques (e.g., parallelism, rule of three, sentence length and variety, repetition, strategic word choice, syntactic variation) to strengthen emphasis, rhythm, clarity, tone and meaning in original compositions.

outcomes.statement: Apply comprehension and metacognitive strategies that deepen understanding and analysis when reading, listening and viewing.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Apply global, problem-solving and support strategies to monitor learning and deepen comprehension when reading, listening and viewing (see Appendix B and Appendix C).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Make and refine predictions before and during reading, listening, or viewing by drawing on titles, genre features, prior knowledge and contextual clues.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Establish a specific purpose before reading, listening, and viewing (e.g., understanding argument, identifying genre features, evaluating author's stance) and adjust strategies (e.g., shifting from skimming to close reading when a key argument or tone shift appears) as new information is encountered.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Identify when understanding breaks down and use strategies (e.g., re-reading, summarizing, slowing down pace, asking questions for clarification) to improve comprehension.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Apply morphology strategies by analyzing word parts (i.e., roots, prefixes, suffixes) to decode unfamiliar vocabulary and enhance comprehension.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Engage with texts multiple times for distinct purposes (e.g., first encounter for basic comprehension, second for analyzing structure or language features, third for interpreting author’s/creator’s craft, tone or deeper meanings).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Explain how recognizing genre-specific craft techniques during reading, listening or viewing (e.g., narrative suspense, persuasive appeals, poetic repetition) enhances comprehension, supports interpretation and deepens awareness of purpose and audience impact.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Use support strategies during and after reading, listening or viewing (e.g., annotating texts, posing questions, taking structured notes, using graphic organizers) to map key ideas and analyze texts.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Visualize complex descriptions or abstract ideas that enhance understanding of challenging sections.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Reflect on the effectiveness of personal comprehension strategies post-task by identifying what worked, what was challenging and setting specific future goals.

outcomes.statement: Use a variety of writing and design processes to thoughtfully plan, develop, revise and refine original compositions.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explore multiple ideas, forms and craft techniques through a variety of low-stakes composition processes (e.g., quick writes, spoken brainstorms, imitation writing).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Plan original written, oral, visual and multimodal compositions using strategies (e.g., brainstorming, mind-mapping, sketching, discussion or inquiry questions) to generate ideas, clarify purpose and consider audience.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Organize ideas intentionally during planning by selecting appropriate structures, modalities, and design elements suited to the intended genre (e.g., sensory details, narrative pacing, logical organization, figurative language), purpose (e.g., to entertain, to persuade) and audience.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Experiment with early drafts by using a variety of design processes (e.g., storyboard, speech annotations, Venn diagram) to test ideas, structures and genre techniques.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Revise original compositions meaningfully by reworking content, structure, form, style or mode based on self-assessment, peer feedback and evolving clarity of purpose.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Refine original compositions by polishing language, improving coherence, fine-tuning transitions, clarifying key ideas, and aligning form and tone precisely to purpose and audience.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Revise titles in original compositions to align with purpose and genre and enhance the audience's engagement or interpretation.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Finalize original compositions for the intended audience, considering how final design, medium, and presentation choices impact meaning, accessibility and emotional resonance.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Reflect on feedback and creative intentions to determine which suggestions enhance clarity, strengthen purpose, or improve audience impact, and make intentional decisions about what to revise, retain, or reject based on creative vision.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Revise recursively by revisiting ideas, structure and techniques at multiple stages to refine meaning and expression over time.

outcomes.statement: Apply appropriate spelling, grammar, punctuation and language conventions according to genre, purpose and audience.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Apply grammar, syntax, punctuation and spelling conventions to enhance clarity and coherence in original compositions.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Adjust use of language conventions based on purpose, audience and genre (e.g., formal conventions for academic essays; strategic flexibility for creative, spoken word, or informal compositions).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Use morphological strategies (i.e., analyzing roots, prefixes and suffixes) to spell complex words accurately and to expand academic vocabulary.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Edit drafts purposefully to correct errors in spelling, punctuation and grammar, focusing on patterns of strength and recurring areas for improvement.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Utilize punctuation and syntax intentionally to control pacing, emphasis and tone in compositions (e.g., varied sentence lengths, line breaks, strategic use of commas, dashes, pauses).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Organize ideas into cohesive sections (e.g., paragraphs, scenes, stanzas, frames, slides) that reflect purposeful shifts in focus, topic, speaker, time, or tone to support clarity, coherence and audience understanding in original compositions.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Reflect on how choices in tone, formality and language precision affect audience perception and comprehension.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Recognize and discuss the evolving nature of language conventions across different cultural, social and digital contexts (e.g., how African American Vernacular English has grammatical rules distinct from Standard American English; how professional vs. peer dialogue changes in tone, formality and structure; how emojis, hashtags, or acronyms can shift meaning and tone).

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Use appropriate citation styles in formal writing (e.g., MLA for literary and artistic analysis; APA for research, informational, or social science-related texts), selecting format based on context, discipline and audience.

outcomes.statement: Analyze the credibility and effectiveness of information presented in a range of texts, including media and digital texts.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Analyze factors that contribute to credibility (e.g., author expertise, institutional affiliation, purpose, transparency of sourcing) in written, oral, visual and multimodal texts.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Analyze factors that contribute to a lack of credibility (e.g., unclear authorship, lack of expertise, missing source information, obvious bias, lack of transparency, misleading intent).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Examine how organizational structures (e.g., chronological, cause-effect) and text features (e.g., headlines, diagrams) enhance or hinder clarity and relevance.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Evaluate how effectively a text’s tone, word choice or visual elements contribute to audience understanding and message impact.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Assess whether evidence used in a text is sufficient and directly supports the argument or purpose.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Identify how a text includes, excludes or frames information to influence interpretation or understanding.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Explore how personal interest, prior knowledge or bias may shape one's perception of what is relevant or effective in a text.

outcomes.statement: Incorporate relevant, credible evidence into original compositions.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Incorporate evidence (e.g., quotations, statistics, images, examples, expert opinions) that directly supports the main idea or claim, ensuring a clear and logical connection between the evidence and the argument.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text:
Introduce evidence with framing language that clarifies its relevance:
- “According to…”
- “As shared in the interview with…”
- “The author suggests...”
- “The situation shows...”
- “The actions of the character demonstrate...”.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explain the function of each piece of evidence by explaining how it strengthens reasoning, anticipates counterarguments or deepens the central message, theme or argument.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Balance the use of direct and indirect (e.g., paraphrasing) evidence to preserve originality and avoid over-reliance on source material.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text:
Apply different strategies for tracking and attributing sources (e.g., primary, secondary, print, scholarly, AI) depending on context:
- In academic or research-based compositions, use appropriate citation styles (e.g., MLA for literary analysis, APA for informational texts).
- In informal, creative or oral compositions, attribute ideas through oral acknowledgments, captions, credits or notes in accompanying materials.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Revise compositions by improving the selection, integration and explanation of evidence to ensure stronger alignment between claims and supporting materials.

outcomes.statement: Develop a central message, theme or argument in original compositions.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Create a fully developed theme (e.g., love becomes destructive when rooted in fear) beyond a thematic topic (e.g., love).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explore a topic or question through brainstorming, freewriting or discussion to uncover meaningful insights that shape a central message, theme, or argument in original compositions.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Align structure (e.g., sequencing, paragraph focus, multimodal transitions), tone and genre-specific conventions to build coherence and strengthen the delivery of the central message, theme or argument.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Use genre-appropriate techniques (e.g., extended metaphor in poetry, symbolism in narrative, integration of charts in expository) to deepen meaning and reinforce the message, theme or argument.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Reinforce the central message, theme or argument by ensuring it is reflected not only in content, but in aesthetic or craft techniques (e.g., repetition in spoken word poetry, visual symbolism in film, motif in prose).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Ensure each section, paragraph or design element contributes meaningfully to the overall message.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Revisit central ideas across stages of composition (e.g., planning, drafting, revising) to assess how effectively they are developed.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Explore how personal lenses can shape how audiences interpret the central message, theme or argument.

outcomes.statement: Engage with others in respectful, focused dialogue to foster critical thinking and deepen comprehension.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Pose purposeful questions that invite clarification, deeper analysis or new perspectives on a composition, idea or theme (see Appendix I).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explain interpretations using evidence from texts and personal experience while remaining open to feedback and alternative viewpoints.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Engage in a variety of collaborative discussion formats (e.g., talking circles, debates, fishbowl discussion, peer conferencing, online forums) to engage in focused dialogue and deepen understanding.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Engage in conversations to analyze an author’s/creator’s message and craft techniques and how they impact the audience.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Explain ideas, interpretations or creative choices based on insights gained through discussion or conferencing.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Demonstrate respect for diverse perspectives by acknowledging differing opinions and lived experiences, using inclusive language and maintaining a constructive tone during disagreement.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Reflect on how collaborative dialogue shapes, expands or challenges personal thinking or comprehension.

outcomes.statement: Collaborate with others to generate ideas, organize and revise original compositions, contributing ideas and feedback to improve clarity, effectiveness and impact.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Generate and build ideas with various brainstorming strategies (e.g., mentor-text inspired exercises, low-stakes compositions tasks, sketching) identifying possibilities for genre, voice, or structure.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Provide thoughtful, question-driven feedback that highlights strengths, identifies gaps and invites deeper thinking about clarity, nuance or artistic intention.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Engage in conferences to discuss creative choices, offering specific suggestions about structure, language, tone, multimodal integration or genre alignment to strengthen the logical flow and impact of original compositions.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Experiment with peer-suggested feedback (e.g., altering genre, reworking perspective, shifting modality), documenting changes and analyzing how revisions improve meaning and overall effectiveness of compositions.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Experiment with new techniques or structures suggested through dialogue (e.g., trying a different opening move, adjusting pacing, reordering sections) to strengthen personal compositions.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Reflect on how giving and receiving feedback shapes understanding and informs decisions or goals for future compositions.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Collaborate with others to generate and refine ideas for individual compositions (written, oral, visual, multimodal), expanding possibilities for audience engagement, genre exploration and clarity of purpose (see Appendix J).

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Revise compositions collaboratively by incorporating techniques from mentor texts (e.g., leads, transitions, repetition), reflecting on how these choices enhance clarity or audience engagement.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Provide focused, constructive feedback (e.g., noting confusions, emotions and curiosities) to others on ways to enhance clarity, effectiveness, emotional impact or coherence in their original compositions.

evidence.quote: The suggested units and inquiry questions on page 7 offer students meaningful and authentic contexts for learning.

evidence.quote: Rather than organizing outcomes linearly or assigning them to one goal exclusively, this curriculum reflects the interconnected and recursive nature of these goals in practice.

allEvidence.quote: Rather than organizing outcomes linearly or assigning them to one goal exclusively, this curriculum reflects the interconnected and recursive nature of these goals in practice.

Rather than prescribing a fixed sequence, this curriculum supports local professional judgment in determining which outcomes to cluster, how to differentiate for student needs and how to build units or inquiries that reflect the course thematic topics and inquiry questions.

outcomes.statement: Explore how value systems, social factors, personal experiences and cultural backgrounds can influence financial decision-making.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explore the impact value systems developed in childhood can have on attitudes towards finances.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Investigate how culture, religion and family belief systems can influence trust in, and value of, financial institutions.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explore how social influences and personal experiences shape one’s attitudes toward financial decision-making.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Examine various cultural perspectives on income, budgeting, saving, sharing and accessing credit.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Research various approaches to financial decision-making based on different perspectives or traditions (e.g., halal banking, Indigenous beliefs on sharing).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Discuss how community and societal norms (e.g., expectations regarding gender roles) influence the financial well-being of self, family and community.

outcomes.statement: Examine the influence that finances have on well-being.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explore ways to gather, interpret and utilize information to make responsible financial decisions.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explore how financial security can have a positive influence on personal mental health and well-being.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explore how accessing high-risk financial loans (e.g., payday loans, cash advances) can impact mental health.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Describe the financial pressures that may be created by accessing credit cards, credit lines and loans.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Explore the potentially addictive nature of spending and its connection to financial and mental wellness.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Investigate resources, services and programs (e.g., debt consolidation, financial advice, credit counselling, addictions counselling) to support and address financial challenges.

outcomes.statement: Compare products and services provided by various financial institutions.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Compare various types of financial institutions (e.g., virtual banks, traditional banks, credit unions, alternative lenders).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify Indigenous financial institutions and others responsive to various cultures in Canada.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Compare youth, student and adult bank accounts.

indicators.label: d
e
f
indicators.text: Describe the process and requirements, including personal identification required (e.g., birth certificate, Social Insurance Number [SIN]) for applying for an account at a financial institution.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Explain how to obtain direct deposit information from your financial institution.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Explore how financial advice is provided, including the perspective of the advisor and the intent behind the advice.

indicators.label: i

outcomes.statement: Explore various ways of earning an income.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explain the importance of a Social Insurance Number (SIN) and how it is obtained.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Research payment methods for employees (e.g., wages, salary, commission, tips) and frequency of pay (e.g., biweekly, monthly, bonuses).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explore how entrepreneurs earn an income from various methods of self-employment, such as a traditional store, an online store, and services.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Investigate the risks associated with creating a personal income with lotteries, gambling (e.g., online sports betting, Video Lottery Terminals [VLT]) or fraudulent activity (e.g., theft, scams, fake reviews).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Analyze the advantages and disadvantages of different employment situations (e.g., employee, self-employment, contract, passive income, side hustle).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Examine the information provided on sample pay stubs including gross income, net income and mandatory and optional deductions.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Explain the impact of overtime on gross and net income.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Investigate income associated with treaties (e.g., treaty education outcome TR10 - Examine contemporary economic implications of Treaties for all the people of Saskatchewan and other Canadian jurisdictions).

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Discuss how to manage a substantial financial gain (e.g., generational income, gift, prize, bursary, settlement).

outcomes.statement: Investigate the role of taxes and their effect on finances.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify services funded by tax revenue (e.g., healthcare, education, infrastructure).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Differentiate between types of taxes (e.g., income tax, sales tax, property tax).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Examine how sales taxes (e.g., Provincial Sales Tax [PST], Goods and Services Tax [GST]) are applied to new and used purchases.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explore how taxation applies to Indigenous Peoples in Saskatchewan, including the eligibility criteria for exemptions related to income tax and sales tax.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Discuss the importance of accurate tax reporting and the consequences of tax fraud or evasion.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Explore the process of filing a tax return and the role of tax software, Canadian Revenue Agency [CRA] services and deadlines.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Identify the documents and information required to calculate taxes on income (e.g., TD1, TD1SK, T4, T2202, Notice of Assessment [NOA], Social Insurance Number [SIN], receipts).

indicators.label: h
i
indicators.text: Critique the statement “Working overtime or receiving a raise could actually result in earning less money overall.”

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Create a basic personal income tax return using a simple sample T4 employment form.

outcomes.statement: Examine how personal budgets contribute to effective financial planning.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Define budgeting and describe the intent of a personal budget.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explore the concepts of needs and wants and how they impact financial decisions.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Identify and justify information that may be in a personal budget, including income, savings, and expenses.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explain key considerations when developing a budget, including regular (e.g., biweekly, monthly), irregular, and unexpected income and expenses.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Discuss how personal goals (e.g., buying a car, saving for a major purchase, moving away for education) impact a budget.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Develop a plan to make a major expense (e.g., trip, musical instrument, vehicle).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Discuss how budgeting decisions vary at different stages of life to reflect shifting personal goals.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Create and justify a personal budget that includes income and expenses based on a real or hypothetical situation.

outcomes.statement: Explain the principles of saving money and the importance of a savings mindset.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss reasons for short and long-term saving of money.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explain the relationship between saving and investing (e.g., interest rate, risk).

indicators.label: c
d
e
indicators.text: Examine advantages and disadvantages associated with various saving strategies.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Explore types of high-interest and tax-saving accounts (e.g., high-interest savings account [HISA], Tax Free Savings Account [TFSA]).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Discuss the importance of including an emergency savings fund as part of a financial plan.

outcomes.statement: Explore various investment options.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Investigate the purpose of investing.

indicators.label: b
c
indicators.text: Explore types of tax-saving investment accounts (e.g., Tax Free Savings Account [TFSA], Registered Education Savings Plan [RESP], Registered Retirement Savings Plan [RRSP]).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explore the advantages of investing at an early age and the impact of growth over time.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Explain the reasons for diversification of investments.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Explain the concept of risk tolerance including risk versus reward.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Compare the advantages, disadvantages and ethical implications of various types of investment options.

outcomes.statement: Investigate credit options and the importance of responsible borrowing.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify ways for a person to access credit for the first time and build a credit score.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Discuss credit scores and how they can impact future financial activities.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explain the difference between good debt and bad debt and why individuals need to respect debt.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Differentiate between credit and debt.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Compare various options for purchasing items with payment plans (e.g., Buy Now Pay Later [BNPL], rent to own) and without payment plans (i.e., cash price).

indicators.label: f
g
indicators.text: Discuss the concept of net worth and its importance when borrowing.

outcomes.statement: Explain the importance of, and methods for, protecting personal information and financial assets.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Describe ways to secure personal and financial information, including processes for online account verification (e.g., passwords, encryption, Personal Identification Number [PIN], authenticator applications, biometrics).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Determine when personal information (e.g., Social Insurance Number [SIN], account information, passport information, personal address/location, credit card information) can be shared safely.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Identify various documents such as receipts, bank statements, job applications, resumes and passports which contain sensitive information that others could use fraudulently.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Identify how documents containing sensitive information may be protected using various tools, such as a fireproof safe, document shredder and a secure electronic folder.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Describe the levels of security associated with common payment methods such as cash, debit card, cheque, electronic transfer (i.e., e-Transfer), credit card, bank draft, wire transfer and prepaid credit card.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Discuss risks associated with online payments and contactless payment systems.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Investigate different methods people use to illegally collect personal information for profit through fraud (e.g., calls, texts, service provider emails, subscription renewals).

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Explore types of insurance (e.g., cell phone insurance, vehicle registration, tenant’s insurance, life insurance), how insurance can protect assets (e.g., total replacement, prorated coverage) and the related costs (e.g., premium, deductible, monthly payments).

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Research processes to address and rectify issues with compromised personal information and fraud.

outcomes.statement: Plan for future lifestyle, including education, career, finances and aspirations.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Define the term ‘lifestyle’.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Reflect on future lifestyle, including personal needs, wants, and financial priorities.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explore several career options of personal interest and their earning potential.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explore educational pathways and associated costs related to career choices.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Evaluate achievable lifestyle expectations based on projected income.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Discuss ways to align the earning potential of one’s chosen career with the costs associated with a desired future lifestyle (e.g., increase income, reduce expenses, adjust goals).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Design and present a personal financial plan that connects education, career, income, expenses, savings, and long-term goals.

indicators.text: Discuss the importance of focusing on personal tasks while maintaining an awareness of others working in proximity.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Demonstrate safety procedures (e.g., knife safety, proper use of equipment) as they apply to food preparation.

indicators.label: c
d

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Demonstrate safe and hygienic food and cooking preparation techniques using current and advanced technologies to produce a quality product.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Apply relevant food safety standards when preparing, cooking and serving food.

outcomes.statement: Explore the importance of safe food handling, preparation and storage.
