outcomes.statement: Investigate techniques (i.e., instrumental, vocal or creative technologies) and the elements of music for solo and/or ensemble performances.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Demonstrate instrumental or vocal technique and knowledge of the elements of music.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Develop vocabulary appropriate to genre or musical context.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: With guidance, generate technique-related inquiry questions and set short term goals for personal improvement based on the inquiry findings.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Develop the skills and techniques required for successful ensemble performances.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Demonstrate knowledge of one’s own role within an ensemble.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Track development of instrumental or vocal techniques and develop strategies to improve.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Develop the ability to communicate and interact with ensemble members and/or audience.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Demonstrate musicality (e.g., emotional expressiveness) in solo and/or ensemble performance.

outcomes.statement: Experiment with various types of notation to communicate musical ideas (e.g., graphic/invented, tablature, standard and culture-specific forms).

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Read and interpret written musical communication.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Investigate legal and ethical practices in music composition, performance and recording.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Represent musical ideas using standard notation (i.e., Western music notation, tablature).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Represent musical ideas using non-standard notation (e.g., abstract symbols and text, time-based pictographs, rap and hip hop flow diagrams with lyrics under beat numbers, braille, colour coded) and/or culture specific forms and models (e.g., unwritten, memorized with fixed and/or variable elements).

outcomes.statement: Compose to express musical ideas experimenting with the elements of music and principles of composition, respecting cultural contexts.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Express musical ideas, through composition individually and/or in ensemble settings, that can be recreated by others.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Understand and experiment with the elements of music (i.e., melody, harmony, rhythm, dynamics, form, tone, texture) and principles of composition (e.g., repetition and variation, tension and resolution, balance and unity).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Demonstrate, through rehearsal, an ability to reflect on, refine and revise solo and ensemble compositions.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Apply aural skills to making musical decisions for sound compositions.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Discuss the difference between ‘drawing inspiration from music’ versus ‘engaging in cultural appropriation or copyright infringement’ when composing.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Examine music composition processes within diverse genres and cultural contexts (e.g., partner with local musicians from various genres and cultures through artists in schools projects).

outcomes.statement: Improvise on an instrument or with voice or other creative technology, exploring and experimenting with music theory, cultural or performance practice.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Improvise around a given structure and in free form.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explore how improvisation is used within a variety of genres.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Examine the work of musicians engaged in improvisation.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Demonstrate growth in the presentation and construction of improvisation

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Demonstrate knowledge of selected musical concepts (e.g., elements of music, composition principles) through improvisation.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Demonstrate aural skills.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Imitate or transcribe musical ideas (e.g., listen and play).

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Develop language appropriate to the musical genre and style to talk about improvisation.

outcomes.statement: Investigate and respond to powwow and other social music of Saskatchewan First Nations peoples.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Engage with First Nations Elders, Knowledge Keepers and/or musicians to introduce music associated with round dance and various powwow dances (e.g., fancy dance, men’s and women’s traditional, jingle dress).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Discuss ways of knowing and learning (e.g., songs passed down/gifted, songs composed) that are applied to learning First Nations traditional and contemporary music.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Recognize how the work of contemporary musicians is influenced by traditional First Nationsmusic.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Examine how music and musicians, including current Saskatchewan musicians, influence and respond to social, political and cultural issues (e.g., treaty education outcome SI10 - examine the spirit and intent of Treaties and investigate [within the context of music] the extent to which they have been fulfilled).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Identify how First Nations music is used for different purposes (e.g., public songs, social songs, ceremonial songs).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Describe protocols for singing and drumming at powwows including different gender roles.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Explore the differences in music and protocols among First Nations.

outcomes.statement: Investigate and respond to the music of Saskatchewan Métis peoples.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Engage with Métis musicians to introduce characteristics of traditional Métis music.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Discuss ways of knowing and learning (e.g., songs passed down, songs composed) that are applied to learning traditional and contemporary Métis music.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Recognize how the work of contemporary Métis musicians is influenced by traditional music.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Describe various purposes for Métis music (e.g., celebration, storytelling, dance accompaniment, competition).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Examine how Métis music and musicians in Saskatchewan influence and respond to social, political and cultural issues.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Explore the regional and/or stylistic differences in Métis music (e.g., kitchen parties, reels, spoons, crooked tunes, jigging and other dances).

outcomes.statement: Listen and respond critically to own musical expressions and, with guidance, set short term goals for musical growth.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Examine own musical expressions, using teacher feedback and self-assessment, in order to improve.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Respond to qualities of musical elements such as tone, pitch, dynamics and rhythm as well as style, intonation and phrasing within own musical expressions.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: With guidance, generate technique-related inquiry questions and set short term goals for personal improvement based on the inquiry findings.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Apply methods to improve sound quality through care and maintenance of instruments and/or voices.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Identify equipment (e.g., instruments, accessories, amplification systems, acoustical designs, technologies) that impacts sound quality.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Conduct an inquiry into ways technology (e.g., microphones, software, pedals) and materials (e.g., drum heads, mutes, baffles, curtains) can manipulate sound.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Explain relationships between acoustics and sound, experiment with acoustics of various environments and discuss acoustic design considerations.

outcomes.statement: Listen and respond to musical expressions of others, differentiating between critical analysis and personal preference.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Express initial reactions, while listening to music, and conduct further analysis based on evidence in the work.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Examine and classify music representing various genres, styles, time periods, places, social groups, world cultures, composers and performers.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Respond critically (e.g., written, oral, arts expression) to music from various genres, styles, times, places, social groups and cultures using terminology specific to the music genre.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Analyse the characteristics of excellent performance through listening to and watching other performers.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Explain relationships between acoustics and sound.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Analyse and interpret music using evidence from the piece and/or performance including examination of the importance of musical text.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Make personal connections to the music and provide reasons for individual preferences.

outcomes.statement: Identify characteristics of the different eras, genres and styles through listening to and/or performing the representative music.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify musical, cultural, aural, textual clues that indicate the music’s place and time.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Investigate the influence of cultural and historical contexts on the creation of selected music.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Investigate the influence of personal experience and place on the creation of selected music.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Conduct an inquiry into how music from the past is recreated today, or how music of today can be reinterpreted in styles from the past.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Explore the evolution of instruments, voice and creative technologies and their use in various world cultures and time periods.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Identify protocols for audience and performer according to norms within the genre.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Respond as an audience member and perform in a manner appropriate to the genre (e.g., First Nations powwow, symphony, jazz, African or Latin percussion drum group, rock band) respecting cultural protocols and performance norms (e.g., deportment, attire, respect for local tradition, awaiting invitation to join jam session, bowing, encore).

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Anticipate and prepare for how audiences might react to the music performed in relation to, for example, venue, genre, demographics or type of event.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Investigate the origins of performance and audience etiquette (e.g., clapping following jazz solos, silence between symphonic movements) in different genres of music.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Examine ways in which audience responses in different musical genres affect the musician’s performance and the audience’s experience.

outcomes.statement: Describe the impact and role of music in own life and identify music careers and pathways for continuing engagement in music.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Investigate relationships between music and personal wellness including mental health (e.g., music therapy) and identify and discuss associated research.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Examine ways that different genres/styles of music influence one’s wellbeing (e.g., mood, anxiety, sense of peace) and examine how music is used in media and infused in daily life (e.g., to influence consumers via advertising, shopping environments).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Make connections between music and other areas of study (e.g., literature, math, science, social sciences, physical education, other arts).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explore opportunities and benefits for continuing lifelong engagement in music (e.g., community choirs, bands, musical theatre).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Conduct an inquiry into career opportunities in music and investigate opportunities (e.g., career avenues in specific disciplines, scholarships, entrepreneurial skills required, performance contract fees, licensing and financial compensation for digital distribution of recordings) for continuing the study of music.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Examine ways that First Nations musicians learn to sing and play in powwow drum groups.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Examine legalities (e.g., copyrighting, trademarking, First Nations traditional laws, contracts) and ethics (e.g., illegal downloading, sampling, cultural protocols, compensation from streaming services) related to creating and producing music.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Research supports for musicians such as unions, professional associations, agents, Elders and Knowledge Keepers, provincial and federal grants (e.g., funding for creation, touring and recording).

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Discuss entrepreneurship and personal qualities required for pursuing a career in music.

outcomes.statement: Explore the lives and work of local, Canadian and international musicians.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify, listen to and discuss the work of musicians who have made an impact on music.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Investigate why influential musicians (e.g., current, historical, community) and music educators (e.g., Kodaly, John-Baptiste Arcand, Orff, Buffy Sainte-Marie, Jose Antonio Abreu) and their work are/were influential.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Examine how music and musicians influence and respond to social, political and cultural issues(e.g., representing gender and sexual diversity, concern for environmental sustainability or human rights, world music activists).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Conduct an inquiry into how change (e.g., personal, social, technology) influences musical works.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Recognize and analyse how music is used in everyday life (e.g., video games, films, social media, apps).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Draw on the experience of local musicians and community members (e.g., community performances, collaborative workshops, adult musicians, guest artists from diverse cultures) to examine their work and careers and to improve own practice.

evidence.observation: The outcomes page groups the outcomes under 9 unit headings.

outcomes.statement: view, interact with, and experience the natural and constructed environments of the community.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: interacts with classmates and teacher respectfully during learning activities using the Nakawē language;

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: interacts with classmates in pairs or small groups to plan and complete class projects using the Nakawē language;

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: seeks and records information to further understanding of Nakawē concepts from Elders and other knowledge keepers within the community (by keeping a journal, transcribing encounters, videotaping interactions, creating a dictionary);

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: participates in developing language and culture during experiential learning opportunities, such as helping at community/cultural events, volunteering with day-care children, visiting and conversing with Elders in the community, planning cultural camps/activities and presents these experiences with classmates and teacher;

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: discusses and promotes positive interactions and relationships in the school by inviting (Elders into the classroom to share with students);

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: derives meaning from, and responds to a variety of text forms including storytelling in a variety of media (videotaped instructions or events by creating illustrations, respond in learning logs, or questioning the author); and,

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: responds to representation of ideas, events and information by creating a chart, illustrations or technology.

outcomes.statement: understand and interpret the Nakawē language as a connected set of ideas.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: explains electronically or in person, short and simple oral excerpts from the oral tradition of the people, relating to areas of local lifestyles in the past and present (histories, biographies, moral stories, songs, including entertainment stories);

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: presents oral forms of simple and short contemporary Nakawē reflections, such as songs, short entertaining films, short stories, recipes using land foods;

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: uses language for fun (e.g., express humor, figures of speech literally (illustrate or present short skits, perform songs, chants, dances, or short plays);

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: uses language creatively and for aesthetic purposes (write simple sentences creating situations in a different time or place);

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: uses language for personal enjoyment (create songs, chants, or word games);

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: shares and explains examples of short and simple excerpts using stories from the oral tradition;

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: responds to the main point and some supporting details of oral texts on a variety of familiar topics guided by the teacher using graphic organizer or flow chart or technology; and,

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: discusses selected topics providing some details to support main idea.

outcomes.statement: produce oral language that is understandable to others.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: identifies and uses terms related to kinship (e.g., sister, brother, mother, father, mother-in-law, father-in-law, etc.,);

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: expresses some emotions and feelings familiar to the classroom (by role-playing, talking circles;

indicators.label: c

items.text: Apply previous knowledge to a group project. Aboriginal worldviews are as diverse as they are complex. Aboriginal peoples in Saskatchewan, like all other Canadians, have divergent cultural backgrounds and innumerable experiences that shape the ways in which they see the world. Saskatchewan Education acknowledges the complexity of Aboriginal worldviews. However, it is important for teachers to explore and expand their understanding of Aboriginal worldviews because they are so closely linked to Aboriginal identity. Such knowledge aids in dispelling stereotypes and enhances our ability to empathize. Seeing the world from another person’s perspective is an invaluable skill that can enhance all the relationships we have in life. Teachers and students need a guide or benchmark from which to begin discussions and learning. Therefore, the following model of a traditional Aboriginal worldview is presented. It is important to remember that the Aboriginal students in Saskatchewan classrooms may or may not have this worldview and that their own is just as important as anyone else’s, even those expressed in this curriculum guide. Within Aboriginal philosophy, four dimensions of human nature (spiritual, mental, emotional and physical) are identified and viewed as interrelated.

If you are trying to access a curriculum, it might have been renewed. Please use the menu above to search for the updated version.'

Practical and Applied Arts (PAA) is a family of separate module-based curricula (Accounting, Information Processing, Welding, … — 35 of them are already in sk.json with their modules). The site's only general PAA page (PaaOverview) is 'Practical and Applied Arts 7-9: Guidelines for Middle Level Survey Courses', which refers to a 'Practical and Applied Arts Handbook'. There is no single 'Practical & Applied Arts 10/20/30' curriculum.

Recommendation: drop these three entries from the course list (or mark them 'no curriculum'); the importer currently reports them as 'No outcomes are published', which hides the fact that the site returned an error page.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text:
Debug a non-working circuit, following a step-by-step process and considering questions such as:
- Did you build the circuit as described in your circuit diagram or schematic?
- Is there power to your circuit?
- Have you exceeded the limitations of any component?
- Are all terminals receiving the correct voltage and polarity?
- Are there any short circuits?
- Is the logic of the circuit correct?

indicators.text: List and describe the advantages and disadvantages of different types of power sources (e.g., wall outlet, lab power supply, battery, solar and alternative) and their suitability for robotics and automation applications.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Compare different power sources in terms of power supply, current supply, power reliability and functionality.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Examine the difference between alternating current (AC) and direct current (DC) power sources and their suitability for robotics and automation applications

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Determine the suitability of various power sources for use in a robotics or automation application.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Select a power source for use in a robotics or automation application.

outcomes.statement: Evaluate wheels for suitability in robotics and automation applications.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 46: Wheels (Optional) · Suggested Time: 2-4 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify possible materials (e.g., foam, rubber, plastic and polyurethane) that can be used to construct wheels for robotic and automation applications.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Evaluate the use of different materials for a specific application of a wheel.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Identify the characteristics of different types of wheels (e.g., fixed, treaded, smooth, air tube, ball, Omni, Mecanum and solid) for robotic and automation applications.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Critique the use of different types of wheels for the functionality and purpose of a specific robotic or automation application

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Evaluate a chosen wheel for use in a specific robotic or automation application.

outcomes.statement: Experiment with the properties and capabilities of direct current (DC) motors.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 48: Motors (Optional) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify the components (e.g., shaft, commutator, brushes, case, leads, core and coils) of a brushed motor.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Build a DC motor using materials such as a battery, magnet, paper clips and enameled wire.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Evaluate the operation of a self-made direct-current (DC) motor.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explain the role of magnetism and electromagnetism in the operation of DC motors.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Provide examples of how DC motors are used in robotics and automation applications

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Build a testbed to test whether motors and servos work properly prior to device assembly.

outcomes.statement: Investigate applications of servos in robotics and automation applications.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 49: Servos (Optional) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Differentiate between servos and motors

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Recognize what type of signal controls a servo.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Attach and properly wire a servo to a device.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Compare the operation and function of continuous and positional rotation servos.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Determine the suitability of a servo for a specific application, considering factors such as type, physical size and speed.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Calibrate positional rotation servos.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Build a testbed to test whether motors and servos work properly prior to device assembly.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Construct a device that incorporates a standard servo.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Construct a device that incorporates a continuous rotation servo.

outcomes.statement: Experiment with the properties and capabilities of actuators.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 51A: Actuators A (Optional) · Suggested Time: 2-4 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 44, 49

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Describe the purpose and function of an actuator.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Differentiate between the characteristics of different types of actuators (e.g., DC brushed and brushless motors, linear actuators, solenoids, electromagnets and servos).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Match types of actuators with specific tasks (e.g., DC motor to drive and linear actuator to move arm).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Investigate how limit switches and diodes are used to restrict actuator motion.

outcomes.statement: Use motor controllers to power motors.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 52A: Motor Controllers A (Optional) · Suggested Time: 2-4 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Describe the role of a motor controller in robotics and automation applications

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Choose the correct motor controller for a stated motor size and type, considering factors such as current, voltage, number of motors and brushed versus brushless design.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Arrange the correct DIP switch or jumper wire orientation on a motor controller for desired usage.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Wire a motor controller to a receiver and to one or more motors.

outcomes.statement: Use fasteners and adhesives effectively in robotics and automation applications.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 56: Fasteners (Optional) · Suggested Time: 1-2 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Determine the characteristics of various types of nails, screws and bolts.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Select the best fasteners for a given task based on their characteristics.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Identify common glues and mastics to determine the appropriate product for a specific application

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Investigate the use of spot welding and riveting to determine which would be best for a given task.

outcomes.statement: Investigate techniques used to build mechanical structure for use in robotics and automation applications.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 57: Mechanical Structure (Core) · Suggested Time: 3-6 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Investigate the stability of various types of connections.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explore the suitability of various supports for overhanging structures and for mobile structures.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Critique the suitability of different structures for their ability to provide support and stability.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Construct stable and sturdy bases, including bases for moving parts, for robotics and automation applications.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Ensure proper fit and alignment of constructed components.

outcomes.statement: Modify existing parts for use in a device.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 58A: Fabricate A (Optional) · Suggested Time: 2-3 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Develop a plan to modify a pre-existing part for suitable use on a device.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Modify a pre-existing part appropriately for suitable use on a device (e.g., take an arm off of a mannequin and attach a motor to it to use in a project).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Install and use a modified part on a device.

outcomes.statement: Construct a simple automated device.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 63A: Automation A (Optional) · Suggested Time: 10-15 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Design a device to automatically perform a task using a single sensor (e.g., tactile, infrared and ultrasonic).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Construct a simple automated device using available materials.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Troubleshoot the functioning of a simple automated device.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Analyze the functionality and ease of use of a simple automated device.

outcomes.statement: Evaluate workspace organization for effectiveness and efficiency.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 65: Physical Space Management (Optional) · Suggested Time: 1-2 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Choose an appropriate workspace for a given task.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Maintain organization of tools and materials to prevent loss or damage.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Maintain a safe workspace environment.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Demonstrate consideration for other users of a shared space.

outcomes.statement: Create, follow and manage a basic project plan.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 66A: Project Management A (Optional) · Suggested Time: 1-2 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text:
Apply a basic project design including:
- identifying the tasks necessary to complete a simple project;
- assigning an approximate length of time to each task in a project; and,
- generating a timeline for task completion.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Monitor and adjust project timeline as needed.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Reflect on project plan at completion.

outcomes.statement: Construct an introductory level assigned or approved robotics or automation project.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 67A: Introductory Project (Optional) · Suggested Time: 10-20 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

outcomes.statement: Explore robotics and automation career paths in Saskatchewan, Canada and the world.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Research career options and trends in robotics and automation in Saskatchewan, Canada and the world.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Develop a list of career opportunities related to the fields of robotics and automation.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Communicate research findings related to occupations in robotics and automation through a display, brochure, video, presentation software, website or oral presentation.

outcomes.statement: Investigate career paths related to various branches and sub-branches of science.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Create a representation that demonstrates interrelationships between various branches and sub-branches of science. (STSE, S, A)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explore the breadth of science-related work roles and who is engaged in those work roles in the community. (STSE, S, A)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Develop a profile of a specific individual involved in a science career, addressing factors such as their educational and personal background, what drew them to their career, the focus of their work and their advice for others who wish to pursue a similar career. (STSE, S, A)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Research the range of science-related programs offered by post-secondary institutions in Saskatchewan and across the country. (STSE, S, A)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Identify the ways in which professional societies and organizations provide support to those engaged in science-related careers in Saskatchewan. (STSE, S, A)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Research the educational qualifications of people engaged in science-related careers. (STSE, S, A)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Attend a science-related career fair and analyze career choices based on information gathered. (STSE, S, A)

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Identify how personal activities and interests relate to topics in secondary science curricula. (STSE, S, A)

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Represent the range of career options available related to a specific branch or sub-branch of science. (STSE, S, A)

outcomes.statement: Assess the implications of human actions on the local and global climate and the sustainability of ecosystems.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Pose questions or problems relating to the effects of human actions on global climate change and the sustainability of ecosystems that arise from personal research. (A, S, STSE)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Reflect upon your personal view of humanity's relationship with the environment. (STSE, A)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Research how people from Aboriginal and other cultures view relationships between living organisms and their ecosystems, and the role of humans in those relationships. (STSE)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Examine the positions of First Nations and government agencies responsible for the stewardship and management of resources, including the duty to consult. (STSE, A)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Evaluate changes in the scientific worldview of sustainability and human's responsibility to protect ecosystems, considering key milestones and publications such as Our Common Future, Rio Declaration on Environment and Development, Agenda 21, Convention on Biological Diversity and the Bonn Declaration. (STSE, A)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Discuss why it is important to consider economic, social justice and environmental perspectives when examining sustainability. (STSE, A)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Select, integrate and analyze the validity of information from various human, print and electronic sources (e.g., government publications, community resources and personally collected data), with respect to sustainability, sustainable development and education for sustainable development. (S)

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Provide examples of human actions that have contributed to the anthropogenic greenhouse effect. (K, STSE)

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Research how scientists examine changes to the key indicators of climate change (e.g., CO2 concentration, global surface temperature, Arctic sea ice area, land ice mass and sea level) to support the scientific understanding of climate change. (K, STSE, A)

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Reflect upon individual and societal behavioural and lifestyle choices that can help to minimize anthropogenic sources of global climate change. (K, STSE)

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Develop, present and defend a position or course of action based on personal research related to mitigating the effects of global or local climate change or to enhancing the sustainability of an ecosystem, taking into account human and environmental needs. (S, A, STSE)

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Assess the current and potential future effects of ongoing changes to Earth's climate systems on the people and the environment in Saskatchewan and Canada's Arctic region. (K, STSE)

outcomes.statement: Investigate factors that influence Earth's climate system, including the role of the natural greenhouse effect.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Differentiate between weather and climate, and the impacts of each on daily life. (K, STSE)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Understand that Earth's climate system results from the exchange of thermal energy and moisture between the sun, ice sheets, oceans, solid earth and the biosphere over a range of timescales. (K, A)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Investigate how Earth's axial tilt, rotation and revolution around the sun cause uneven heating of Earth's surface, resulting in global convection currents, the Coriolis effect, jet streams, thermohaline circulation of the oceans and climate zones. (S, K)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Hypothesize how energy transfer, weather and climate might be different if Earth had a different axial tilt, diameter, period of rotation and/or period of revolution. (S, STSE, A)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Explain how greenhouse gases (e.g., water vapour, carbon dioxide, methane, nitrous oxide, sulphur dioxide and ozone), particles, clouds and surface albedo affect the amount of solar energy absorbed and re-radiated at various locations on Earth. (K)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Explain the role of natural sources (e.g., volcanoes, fire, evaporation and living organisms) of the primary greenhouse gases in Earth's atmosphere and how they contribute to the natural greenhouse effect. (K, A)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Design, construct and evaluate the effectiveness of a model used to illustrate the natural greenhouse effect, the reflectivity of Earth's surface or the relationship between Earth's axial tilt and the seasons. (S, STSE, A)

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Investigate, through laboratory activities or simulations, heat transfer in air and water, including heat involved in phase changes. (S, A)

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Examine how interactions between heat, pressure and the Coriolis Effect result in global wind patterns, ocean currents, jet streams and severe weather (e.g., hurricanes, tornadoes, blizzards and thunderstorms). (S, STSE)

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Analyze weather and atmospheric data to identify patterns in temperature and atmospheric pressure, and changes in those patterns locally, regionally and globally. (S)

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Provide examples of positive and negative feedback mechanisms in Earth's climate system. (K, STSE)

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Provide examples to show how scientific understanding may be refined in light of new evidence. (STSE)

outcomes.statement: Examine biodiversity through the analysis of interactions among populations within communities.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss the importance of biodiversity and maintaining biodiversity. (S, K)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Understand that scientists describe biomes as resulting from the interaction of biotic and abiotic factors such as temperature, precipitation, insolation, latitude, altitude and geography. (A, K)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Compare the biodiversity and climatic characteristics of several of Earth's major biomes. (S, K)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Estimate the abundance of organisms in a local ecosystem using random (e.g., quadrat), systematic (e.g., line transect and belt transect) and/or stratified sampling techniques. (S)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Determine the population density, percentage frequency and/or percentage cover of one or more organisms in an ecosystem using primary or secondary population data. (S)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Discuss ethical and cultural perspectives related to studying biotic components of ecosystems, including the potential benefits and consequences of technologies (e.g., radio collar) and techniques (e.g., mark and recapture) used to collect data. (K, STSE, A)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Examine ways in which scientists collaborate with Elders, knowledge keepers and other community members to gather and interpret data related to biotic components of ecosystems. (STSE, A)

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Construct and/or interpret graphs of population dynamics of humans and other species to determine population trends within an ecosystem. (S, A)

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Investigate various ways in which natural populations attempt to maintain equilibrium, and relate this equilibrium to the resource limits of an ecosystem with reference to concepts such as carrying capacity, natality, mortality, immigration and emigration. (S, K)

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Examine the relationship between the biodiversity of an ecosystem, its primary productivity and ecological resilience. (K, S)

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Examine how factors such as invasive species, habitat loss and climate change affect biodiversity within an ecosystem, and can result in species becoming at-risk (i.e., vulnerable, threatened and extirpated). (K, STSE)

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Analyze how the bioaccumulation and biomagnification of human-made substances can affect the viability and biodiversity of organisms and populations in an ecosystem. (K, STSE)

outcomes.statement: Investigate the role of feedback mechanisms in biogeochemical cycles and in maintaining stability in ecosystems.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explain systems in terms of their type (e.g., open, closed and isolated), equilibrium (e.g., dynamic, static, stable and unstable) and their associated feedbacks (e.g., positive and negative). (K)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Create a representation of a feedback mechanism that is relevant to a specific biogeochemical (e.g., carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus and water) cycle. (S)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explore Indigenous ways of understanding the role of matter and energy in the environment. (STSE, K)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Describe how human actions can affect the cycling of matter and flow of energy through ecosystems. (K, A, STSE)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Examine the role of photosynthesis, respiration and sinks in the cycling of carbon through the environment. (K, A)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Design and carry out an investigation to determine the effect of carbon dioxide levels on photosynthesis and/or to determine the effect of nitrogenous-based fertilizer on plant or algal growth. (S, A)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Compare the processes of nitrification and denitrification in terrestrial and aquatic ecosystems. (K)

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Research the short-term and long-term effects of small-scale and large-scale agricultural practices on the cycling of phosphorus, nitrogen and other nutrients in an ecosystem. (K, A, STSE)

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Analyze the interdependence between the water cycle and other biogeochemical cycles. (K, S)

outcomes.statement: Explore the properties of chemical reactions, including the role of energy changes, and applications of acids and bases.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Create a representation about the prevalence of chemistry in our lives. (A, S)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Research the ways in which people, including First Nations and Métis, from various times and cultures have applied their understanding of the transformation of materials to produce new substances. (STSE)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Observe and describe a variety of chemical reactions, including synthesis, decomposition, combustion, single replacement and double replacement. (S, K)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Demonstrate knowledge of Workplace Hazardous Materials Information System (WHMIS 2015) standards by selecting and applying proper techniques for handling and disposing of lab materials and interpreting Safety Data Sheets (SDSs). (K, STSE, A)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Explain why it can be difficult to classify changes as physical or chemical, including reference to the reversibility of the reaction. (K, A)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Differentiate between reactants and products in chemical reactions. (K)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Investigate the properties of endothermic and exothermic chemical reactions, including identifying where or how energy is absorbed or released in the reaction and identifying potential benefits and consequences of the reaction. (K, S)

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Research practical examples of chemical reactions involving acids and bases, including neutralization reactions such as those involved in chemical spills, soda-acid fire extinguishers and antacids. (S, STSE)

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Provide examples of the importance of pH measurements in areas such as biology, chemistry, food science, environmental science and water treatment. (K, STSE)

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Research the operation of technologies designed to monitor and manage pH in various applications such as swimming pools, consumer products, agriculture and horticulture. (K, S, STSE)

outcomes.statement: Name and write formulas for common ionic and molecular chemical compounds, including acids and bases.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Examine the relationship between an element's position on the periodic table, the number of its valence electrons and its chemical properties. (K, A)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Discuss the importance of valence electrons, and whether they are shared or transferred, in determining bond type in chemical compounds. (K)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Name and write formulas for common ionic compounds, including compounds involving polyatomic ions, using the periodic table and a list of common ions. (S)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Analyze the relationship between the structure of ionic compounds, their chemical formulas and their common names. (K)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Classify substances as ionic or molecular, based on their properties and the results of student conducted tests (e.g., melting/boiling point, electrical conductivity and solubility). (S)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Relate the properties (e.g., solubility, conductivity in solution or gaseous form, high melting point and brittleness) of ionic compounds to their uses. (STSE, K)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Name and write formulas for common molecular and organic compounds (e.g., methane, propane, butane, octane, methanol, ethanol and glucose), using the periodic table and a list of numerical Greek prefixes. (S)

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Design and carry out investigations to determine the properties of acids and bases, including selecting and using appropriate instruments for safely collecting evidence. (S, A)

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Classify substances as acids, bases or salts, based on observable properties, name and chemical formula. (S)

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Investigate how certain substances, including those traditional to First Nations and Métis cultures, can serve as acid-base indicators. (K, STSE, A)

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Describe how the pH scale is used to classify substances as acidic, basic or neutral. (S, STSE, A)

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Name and write formulas for common acids and bases, using the periodic table, a list of ions and rules for naming acids and bases. (S)

indicators.label: m
indicators.text: Explain the importance of scientific nomenclature systems such as the International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry (IUPAC) naming conventions in communicating information about chemical compounds. (STSE, A)

outcomes.statement: Represent chemical reactions and conservation of mass symbolically using models, word and skeleton equations and balanced chemical equations.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Design and safely carry out an experiment to confirm the law of conservation of mass, identifying and controlling major variables. (A, S)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explain the importance of the concept of conservation of mass in understanding, interpreting and predicting results of chemical reactions. (K, S)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Represent chemical reactions, organic compounds and conservation of mass using models and word equations. (S, K, A)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Represent chemical reactions and conservation of mass using skeleton equations and balanced equations. (S, K, A)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Translate word equations to balanced chemical equations and balanced chemical equations to word equations. (S, K)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Differentiate between the use of subscripts and coefficients in representing the numbers of atoms and molecules present in chemical reactions. (S)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Categorize chemical reactions as synthesis, decomposition, combustion, single replacement and double replacement, including acid base neutralization. (S, K, A)

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Verify whether a chemical equation is correctly balanced, and correct any errors. (S)

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Discuss the value of representing chemical reactions using models, word and skeleton equations and balanced chemical equations. (STSE)

outcomes.statement: Investigate the rates of chemical reactions, including factors that affect the rate.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Provide examples of chemical reactions that occur over a range of time scales. (K)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Predict how factors such as temperature of the reactant(s), concentration of the reactant(s), surface area of the reactant(s) and the presence or absence of catalysts or inhibitors might affect the rate of a chemical reaction. (S, A)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Formulate scientific questions about the rates of chemical reactions and the factors that affect rates of chemical reactions. (S, STSE)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Design and perform an experiment to determine how various factors affect chemical reaction rates, including identifying and controlling major variables. (S, STSE, A)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Compile and organize data, using appropriate formats and data treatments to facilitate interpretation of data related to rates of chemical reactions. (S, A)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Interpret patterns and trends in data, and infer or calculate linear and nonlinear relationships among variables related to chemical reaction rates. (S, A)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Reflect upon data collection and analysis procedures, and suggest improvements to increase precision and accuracy. (S, A, STSE)

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Use the collision model to explain differences in chemical reaction rates. (K, STSE)

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Value the processes for drawing conclusions in science. (A, STSE)

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Research how the rates of chemical reactions are controlled in everyday situations as well as in agricultural and industrial applications. (STSE)

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Work co-operatively with team members to develop and carry out a plan, and troubleshoot problems as they arise when investigating rates of reactions. (S, A)

outcomes.statement: Explore the development of motion-related technologies and their impacts on self and society.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Create a representation of different types of motion and motion-related technologies from various cultures, including First Nations and Métis. (S, STSE)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Describe how motion that may appear imperceptible to humans (e.g., continental drift, subatomic particles, light, blood circulating and galaxies) can be measured using appropriate technologies. (K, STSE)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Evaluate the historical development of a motion-related technology, including the role of continued testing in the development and improvement of the technology. (STSE)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Design, construct and evaluate a prototype of an object that meets a student-identified need related to motion. (STSE, S, A)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Evaluate the design and function of a motion-related technology using student-identified criteria such as safety, cost, availability and impact on everyday life and the environment. (STSE)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Describe examples of Canadian contributions to science and technology in motion-related fields such as transportation, sport science or space science. (STSE)

outcomes.statement: Investigate and represent the motion of objects that travel at a constant speed in a straight line.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Provide examples of objects that exhibit, or appear to exhibit, uniform motion. (K)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Discuss the concept of 'frame of reference' in determining whether an object is in motion and in constructing representations of an object's motion. (S, K, A)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Construct scale diagrams of displacement vectors (i.e., collinear, non-collinear [perpendicular], and non-collinear [non-perpendicular]) to represent changes in an object's position. (S, A)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Design and carry out experiments to determine the properties of uniform motion, using technologies such as photogates, motion detectors, ticker timers and stopwatches to collect distance and time data effectively and accurately. (S, STSE, A)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Discuss the importance of distinguishing between scalar (e.g., distance, speed and time) and vector (e.g., position, displacement, velocity and acceleration) quantities when studying motion. (K)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Construct and analyze graphs (i.e., distance-time, position-time, speed-time and velocity-time) using student-collected data obtained from objects undergoing uniform motion or through computer simulations. (S, A)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Describe quantitatively the relationship among distance, time and speed for everyday objects that undergo uniform motion. (K)

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Derive the relationship between speed, distance and time (i.e., $v={\Δd}/{\Δt}$) and between velocity, displacement and time (i.e., $v ↖ {→}={\Δd ↖ {→}}/{\Δt}$) using student-collected data from objects undergoing uniform motion.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Solve problems related to the motion of objects that travel at a constant speed in a straight line. (S)

notes: Indicator label (b) printed more than once on the official page.

outcomes.statement: Investigate and represent the motion of objects that undergo acceleration.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Develop and carry out experiments to determine the properties of accelerated motion, including identifying variables to be tested, developing appropriate sampling procedures for data collection, collecting and recording data and analyzing data to generate conclusions. (S, STSE)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Evaluate the relevance, reliability and adequacy of data and data collection methods, including identifying and explaining sources of error and uncertainty in measurements. (STSE, S)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Apply the concept of 'rate of change' to operationally define speed, velocity and acceleration. (K)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Demonstrate the importance of converting measurements to the same units when solving motion problems. (K)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Differentiate between the concepts of instantaneous and average as they relate to speed and velocity. (K)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Construct and analyze graphs (i.e., distance-time, position-time, speed-time and velocity-time) that represent the motion of objects that undergo acceleration. (S)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Solve problems related to acceleration using the equations of motion (e.g., $a^ ↖ {→}={\Δv ↖ {→}}/{\Δt}$, and $\Δd ↖ {→}=v ↖ {→}_it+1/2{a ↖ {→}\Δt^2}$). (S)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Value the role and contribution of science and technology in understanding phenomena that are directly observable and those that are not. (A)

notes: Indicator label (b) printed more than once on the official page.

outcomes.statement: Explore the relationship between force and motion for objects moving in one and two dimensions.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Pose and refine scientific questions about the ways in which forces cause objects to move or change their motion. (A, S)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Investigate the effects of applying constant forces to objects at rest and to objects moving at a constant velocity in a straight line. (S, A)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Add force vectors in one and two dimensions (i.e., collinear, non-collinear [perpendicular] and non-collinear [non-perpendicular]) using vector diagrams to determine the net force acting on an object. (S)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Demonstrate the role of friction in changing the position and/or motion of an object. (K, S)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Provide examples of technologies that have been developed to increase or decrease frictional forces between two or more surfaces. (STSE)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Analyze student-collected data to verify the relationship between the acceleration of an object and the net force acting on it. (S)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Describe and provide examples of Newton's three laws of motion in practical situations such as sports, flight and transportation. (K, A)

items.stem: The knowledge objectives are to help students:
items.heading: Foundational Objectives for the Course Social Organizations

items.text: understand that industrial societies are based on a complex system of political and economic organizations, which makes possible the production of goods and services;
items.stem: The knowledge objectives are to help students:
items.heading: Foundational Objectives for the Course Social Organizations

items.text: understand that whenever groups, societies, or nations interact, they do so according to patterns of beliefs and values which are both implicitly and explicitly accepted by the members of the group; and,
items.stem: The knowledge objectives are to help students:
items.heading: Foundational Objectives for the Course Social Organizations

items.text: understand that nations must live within a community of other nations in which the sovereignty of one nation must be reconciled with the sovereignty of another.
items.stem: The knowledge objectives are to help students:

items.stem: The skills/abilities objectives are to help students:

items.stem: The skills/abilities objectives are to help students:

items.stem: The skills/abilities objectives are to help students:
items.heading: Foundational Objectives for the Course Social Organizations

items.text: appreciate the necessity of interdependence within human relationships;
items.stem: The values objectives are to help students:
items.heading: Foundational Objectives for the Course Social Organizations

items.text: appreciate the legitimate constraints that interdependence places on the actions of individuals and nations; and,
items.stem: The values objectives are to help students:
items.heading: Foundational Objectives for the Course Social Organizations
