outcomes.statement: Explore the cultural, economic and social impact of tourism.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 1: Introduction to Tourism (Core) · Suggested Time: 3-7 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Describe what tourism is and what it means to be a tourist.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Discuss reasons (e.g., leisure, education, personal interests, disposable income and business) why people travel as tourists.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Differentiate among outbound (i.e., Saskatchewan residents travelling out of province), inbound (i.e., out-of-province tourists travelling to and within the province) and domestic (i.e., Saskatchewan residents travelling within the province).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Assess the relationship between culture and tourism.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Research what is meant by the term visitor economy.

indicators.label: f
g
indicators.text: Discuss reasons (e.g., economic and job opportunities) why tourism is important to an area and specifically the local area.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Explain potential negative impacts (e.g., wear and tear, pollution, rising costs for local residents and overcrowding) of tourism on a community.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Investigate the five industries (i.e., food and beverage, accommodation, recreation and entertainment, transportation, and travel services) within the tourism sector.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Identify examples of the five industries found within the community and the surrounding area.

outcomes.statement: Investigate types of tourism found within the local community, Saskatchewan and/or Canada.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 2: Types of Tourism (Core) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 1

indicators.label: a
b
indicators.text: Research the prevalence of, and provide examples for, each type of tourism found within the local community, Saskatchewan and/or Canada.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Reflect on personal preference for a specific type of tourism and how that preference may evolve and change over time.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Create a plan, including anticipated expenditures, for a vacation to a destination of choice within Canada that supports one’s preferred type of tourism and references the five industries of tourism.

outcomes.statement: Analyze the importance of environmental, economic, cultural and social sustainability to the tourism sector.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 3: Sustainable Tourism (Core) · Suggested Time: 8-12 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 2

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss what sustainability is and why it is an important consideration for all tourism industries at the local, provincial, national and global level.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Describe the four components (i.e., environmental, economic, cultural and social) of sustainable tourism.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Differentiate between mass and alternative tourism.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Investigate potential positive and negative impacts of mass and alternative tourism on the environment, economy, culture and society.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Research the origin, development and resulting impact of the Palau Pledge.

indicators.label: f

outcomes.statement: Explore the role and impact of tourism on the local community and surrounding area.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 4: Local Tourism (Core) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 2

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss the importance of tourism to the local community and surrounding area.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Research the connection and relationship of First Nations, Métis and Inuit peoples to the land in the local community and the surrounding area and the resulting impact on tourism.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Describe the local area, including ecosystems, landscape, climate, history, culture and people and their relationship to tourism.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Brainstorm reasons why tourists visit the local community and surrounding area.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Discuss common characteristics (e.g., families with young children, hunters, sports enthusiasts, adults, artisans, Saskatchewan residents and residents from other provinces or countries) of tourists who typically visit the local community and surrounding area.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Construct plans (i.e., for one and several days) for being a tourist within the local community and surrounding area, referencing all five industries in the tourism sector.

outcomes.statement: Examine the role and impact of tourism in Saskatchewan.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 5: Tourism in Saskatchewan (Core) · Suggested Time: 10-15 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 2

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Research the evolution of tourism in Saskatchewan.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Classify tourism businesses within the local community and surrounding area as family-owned and operated or as franchises.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Compare the advantages and disadvantages of owning and operating a family-owned and operated business to owning and operating a franchised business.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Discuss evolving expectations (e.g., experiencing nature and the outdoors, and enjoying local flavours and traditions) of travellers to the province and the resulting trends in tourism opportunities.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Analyze regional differences in tourism in Saskatchewan.

indicators.label: f
g
indicators.text: Assess the attitudes and habits of Saskatchewanians pertaining to tourism in Saskatchewan.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Propose factors (e.g., pandemic, economic downturn or economic boom) that may contribute to periods of growth and decline in the tourism sector in Saskatchewan.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: List examples of urban and rural tourism experiences in Saskatchewan for each of the five industries.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Explain strategies used by tourism industries to increase customer count.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Research how the tourism industry has capitalized, or could capitalize, on Saskatchewan’s natural capital (e.g., diversity, culture and natural landscape).

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Discuss the concept of competitive advantage.

indicators.label: m
indicators.text: Summarize Saskatchewan’s competitive advantage in the tourism sector compared to other provinces and neighbouring American states.

indicators.label: n
indicators.text: Investigate the connection and relationship of Métis, First Nations and Inuit peoples to the land in Saskatchewan and the resulting impact on tourism.

indicators.label: o

outcomes.statement: Explore the food and beverage industry and its interrelatedness to other industries within the tourism sector.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 8A: Food and Beverage Industry A (Core) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 2

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Describe common types of food service (e.g., fast food service, fine dining, drive through service, pick up and delivery, catering, cafeteria, buffet style and family style) and provide examples of when each might be used.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Classify examples of food establishments within the community and surrounding area or province according to market segments (e.g., banquet service, buffet and smorgasbord, haute cuisine; family, speciality and chain restaurants; franchise; catering; entertainment; and institutional food service).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Research characteristics of artisanal food (e.g., made locally using traditional methods and tools and local ingredients, and produced on a small-scale or in small batches).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Identify food artisans within the community and surrounding area or province.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Differentiate between commercial and non-commercial food service operations.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Discuss the interrelatedness among the food and beverage and other tourism industries (e.g., food and beverage as well as accommodation, transportation and/or travel services may be accessed by visitors attending an event).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Identify trends (e.g., plant-based meat alternatives, gluten-free diet and 100-mile diet) within the food and beverage industry.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Explain the potential impact (e.g., economic and human) of unforeseen events such as a global pandemic, natural disaster (e.g., earthquake or tornado) or man-made catastrophe (e.g., 9/11) on the food and beverage industry.

outcomes.statement: Explore the accommodation industry and its interrelatedness to other industries within the tourism sector.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 9A: Accommodation Industry A (Core) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 2

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Describe common types of accommodation (e.g., hotel, motel, cabin, bed and breakfast, guest ranch, hostel and camp/campground).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Classify examples of accommodation within the community and surrounding area and/or province according to the accommodation types.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explain the interrelatedness among the accommodation and other tourism industries.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Examine factors (e.g., ratings, purpose of travel, previous experiences— both positive and negative, price, location, accessibility and amenities) that influence an individual’s choice for accommodation.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Identify trends (e.g., sharing economy and self-service options) that may impact the accommodation industry.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Discuss the impact (e.g., economic and other) of unforeseen events such as a global pandemic, natural disaster (e.g., earthquake or tornado) or man- made catastrophe (e.g., 9/11) on the accommodation industry.

outcomes.statement: Explore the recreation and entertainment industry and its interrelatedness to other industries within the tourism sector.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 10A: Recreation and Entertainment Industry A (Core) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 2

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: List examples of the types of opportunities (e.g., attractions, museums, art galleries, sporting events, adventure tourism, nature-based tourism, outdoor/indoor recreation, festivals, cultural events, sporting events and dramatic/musical performances) within the recreation and entertainment industry.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify examples of the recreation and entertainment industry within the local community and/or province.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Examine the interrelatedness among the recreation and entertainment industry and other tourism industries.

indicators.label: d

courses.name: Treaty Education

evidence.observation: The curriculum document groups its outcomes under 3 headings: “Grade Ten: Examining the Canadian context for Treaties”, “Grade Eleven: Assessing Treaty Making from a Global Perspective”, “Grade Twelve: Applying Treaty Understandings to One’s Life”.

courses.problem: The site's outcomes page answers with its “Page Not Found” page (HTTP 200): “The page you are looking for does not exist. If you are trying to access a curriculum, it might have been renewed. Please use the menu above to search for the updated version.” Its curriculum document link (https://curriculum.gov.sk.ca/CurriculumFile?id=481) answers the same “Page Not Found” page; the outcomes are taken from the curriculum document the site's menus link (https://www.edonline.sk.ca/bbcswebdav/xid-8784654_1); see `document`.

units.name: Grade Ten: Examining the Canadian context for Treaties

items.text: Examine contemporary economic implications of Treaties for all the people of Saskatchewan and other Canadian jurisdictions.

Investigate the economic impact that First Nations have on the provincial and territorial economies and the resulting benefits for all people (e.g. natural resources; hunting, fishing and gathering; tourism; hospitality; gaming).
Evaluate the impact that First Nations have on local economies.
Investigate the cost of fulfilling treaties within Saskatchewan and other Canadian jurisdictions.
Analyze the spirit and intent of Treaties and investigate the extent to which they have been fulfilled.
Identify spirit and intent of the terms of treaty.

Imagine and describe what our society would look like today if all treaty obligations had been completely fulfilled and what it could look like into the future (e.g., Maori influence on New Zealand institutions).
Investigate opportunities and challenges faced by First Nations and the Government of Canada in relation to governance issues.
Examine the impact of federal, provincial, and municipal government policies on the fulfillment of Treaties.
Research public policy as it relates to self-government.
Investigate issues related to resource development and Treaties.
Research crown and private corporations that are involved in resource development to investigate the relationship they have with First Nations.
Investigate court rulings that have set the stage for resource development in Saskatchewan.
Examine the positions of First Nations and Government agencies responsible for the stewardship and management of resources (e.g., duty to consult process).

notes: Treaty Education is organised by grade (10, 11, 12), not by course level, and is meant to be taught within other subjects. `level` gives the matching course level (Grade 10 = 10-level, 11 = 20-level, 12 = 30-level) only so the course can sit beside the others.
Outcome codes are printed with a superscript goal number (TR¹, SI², HC³, TPP⁴, per the page's KEY); the superscript is kept in `superscript`, and `code` is the code as the Ministry CSV lists it.

The site's outcomes page for Treaty Education (https://curriculum.gov.sk.ca/CurriculumOutcomeContent?id=481) and its curriculum document link (https://curriculum.gov.sk.ca/CurriculumFile?id=481) both answer the site's “Page Not Found” page (checked 2026-11-21).
Every Grade 10–12 code matches the Ministry CSV (https://www.edonline.sk.ca/bbcswebdav/library/outcomes/csvFiles/481_Treaty_Education_.csv), which lists the codes with empty statements.

indicators.text: Investigate scholarship, grants, study and work opportunities available to Ukrainian-speaking students in Saskatchewan.

evidence.observation: The outcomes page groups the outcomes under 12 unit headings.

outcomes.statement: Initiate and develop ideas for art works that explore a variety of elements, design principles and image development strategies.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Examine sources of inspiration (e.g., research content from other subject areas, current events, life experiences, art movements, dreams, pop culture, the environment) to generate, develop and transform ideas into visual form.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text:
Review and examine, in the creation of art works, connections between the elements of art, principles of design and image development strategies, considering, for example: Elements of Art
- Colour
- Form
- Line
- Shape
- Space
- Texture
- Tone and Value
Principles of Design
- Balance
- Contrast and Variety
- Movement and Rhythm
- Pattern
- Harmony and Unity
- Emphasis
- Proportion and Scale
Sample Image Development Strategies
- abstract
- animate
- distort
- elaborate
- exaggerate
- fragment
- hybridize
- juxtapose
- layer
- magnify
- metamorphose
- miniaturize
- multiply
- point of view
- recontextualize
- reverse
- rotate
- simplify
- story
- stylize
- use of text

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Apply selected image development strategies to manipulate one or more elements of art or principles of design (e.g., elaborate by adding pattern to an image).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Manipulate and apply compositional strategies (e.g., rule of thirds, point of view/vantage point) to solve visual problems and communicate ideas.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Apply safe and proper use of tools, technologies, materials and work space.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Conduct an inquiry into artistic styles and apply image development strategies to create a work of art reflecting a selected style.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Collaborate on a work of art that explores various styles and image development strategies.

outcomes.statement: Demonstrate, through practice, a variety of drawing/mark making techniques, skills and compositional strategies using a range of media, to communicate ideas.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Use several methods (e.g., observation, memory, imagination) when practising 2D and 3D drawing/mark making and compositional strategies.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Research historical examples and experiment with methods of representing subject matter (e.g., nature studies, landscape, cityscape, interiors, portraits, still life, figure studies, hand and feet studies) and through drawing/mark making.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Employ a variety of drawing/mark making techniques (e.g., gesture, contour, perspective, grid) to demonstrate increased skills and visual impact.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Purposefully manipulate, through drawing/mark making techniques, selected elements of art and principles of design in own work.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Experiment with communicating ideas through drawing/mark making using various media (e.g., graphite, charcoal, paint, digital technologies, conté, pastels, wire, pen and ink, clay).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Apply safe and proper use of tools, technologies, materials and work space.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Discuss the difference between copying as a learning exercise versus representing other ideas as one’s own (e.g., intellectual copyright, appropriation).

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Demonstrate personal progress and experimentation with creative processes using a means of documentation such as a sketchbook, journal, portfolio or digital images and records.

outcomes.statement: Experiment with various art practices (e.g., drawing, painting, crafting, printmaking, digital technologies, sculpture, installation) to develop new or unique ideas.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Create an art work that has personal meaning and reflect on growth (e.g., How has your art changed you or how are you now seeing yourself differently?).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Use visual metaphor and/or symbols in art to express ideas and communicate meaning.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Transform ideas into visual form using creative processes (e.g., generating ideas, collecting images, taking photos, using visual references, working with media, revising, thumbnail sketching, seeking peer feedback).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Express new or unique ideas respecting intellectual property/copyright and appropriation.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Follow Workplace Hazardous Material Information System (WHMIS) and art classroom safety guidelines.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Take risks, build on unexpected results, and learn from mistakes.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Combine a variety of art practices to create a mixed media piece (e.g., sculpture installation, digital media, found objects, collage).

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Examine the practice of art-making in supporting one’s mental health and wellness.

outcomes.statement: Use inquiry to create a work of art inspired by the work of Saskatchewan artists.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text:
Create an art work based on individual or collaborative inquiry, including for example:
- generating questions for inquiry about the work of Saskatchewan artists (e.g., How do art works reflect a sense of place?)
- comparing and contrasting the work of urban and rural Saskatchewan artists
- researching and viewing works of recognized Saskatchewan artists
- experimenting with techniques and media used by Saskatchewan artists.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Engage with Elders, Knowledge Keepers, and/or Indigenous artists to examine traditional and contemporary visual art practices.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Engage with Indigenous and non-Indigenous artists to discuss sources of inspiration and art practices and apply new knowledge to own work.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Examine respectful ways of using sources of inspiration including issues of appropriation (e.g., What are the dynamics that make “borrowing” ideas appropriate or not?).

outcomes.statement: Assess to improve own art work using self-reflection, teacher and peer feedback.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Develop and use co-constructed criteria and assessment tools (e.g., rubric) to improve own work.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Assess own growth of visual art techniques and drawing skills using self-reflection and collaboratively-developed criteria.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Provide formative feedback on peers’ work.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Set goals to improve own work.

outcomes.statement: Examine how design and compositional strategies are used by Saskatchewan artists, including First Nations and Métis artists, to convey ideas.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Assess the use and impact of design and composition in others’ work to inform own practice.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Apply various historical and contemporary approaches for responding to an art work.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Research and analyse how materials, techniques, location/site and technologies can be used to represent ideas visually.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Examine and discuss art works that express personal and cultural identity, Métis and First Nations perspectives, and work from diverse Saskatchewan contexts (e.g., farming environments, urban pop culture, the far North, newcomer experiences).

outcomes.statement: Respond critically to art works of professional artists, including Indigenous artists, to explore intent.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Examine and discuss art works that represent perspectives of artists from underrepresented groups.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Collaborate with peers and teacher to identify artistic intent and evaluation criteria that are appropriate for the art work under discussion (e.g., architecture, beading, installation, finger weaving, painting, regalia, birch bark biting, creative technologies).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Respond personally (e.g., creative response, formal critique) to art works observed through gallery visits, studio visits, online supports or virtual tours.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Conduct research of a particular artist’s retrospective body of work to see how the artist’s ideas have changed.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Generate and select inquiry questions to examine the topic of art criticism (e.g., Who decides what is valued as art? How did Renaissance church patrons influence art practices? What is art?).

outcomes.statement: Investigate Saskatchewan art works that convey perspectives about topics related to treaties and/or building of relationships, including newcomer experiences.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: View and analyze works by Saskatchewan First Nations and Métis artists that convey perspectives on topics related to treaties and relationships (e.g., residential school experiences, this land and resource-related rights, treaty education outcome TPP10 – investigate issues related to resource development and treaties).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explore perspectives expressed in visual art (e.g., identity, sense of belonging, experiences of injustice, journeys, building relationships) by Saskatchewan newcomers.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explore, through examination of visual art works, differing perspectives on treaty promises and promises unfulfilled (e.g., treaty education outcome SI10 – analyze the spirit and intent of treaties and investigate the extent to which they have been fulfilled).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Discuss how ideas related to sense of belonging can be expressed in visual art.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Examine differing perspectives on relationships to this land and governance issues expressed in visual art (e.g., treaty education outcome HC10 – investigate opportunities and challenges faced by First Nations and the Government of Canada in relation to governance issues).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Examine and create art as a means of understanding complexities and social justice issues related to the process of reconciliation.

outcomes.statement: Investigate the impact of visual culture on students’ lives and the human condition.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Analyze and discuss the impact of visual expressions on self, culture and societies (e.g., expression of personal and cultural identity).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Examine and respond to the influence and meaning of visual designs (e.g., clothing, tattoos, beadwork, skateboards, ski logos, portraiture, web design, social media, gaming, graffiti) observed in daily life.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Conduct an inquiry on the use of visual imagery by corporations and others to promote differing perspectives and/or influence thought (e.g., social justice movements, advertising, propaganda and political imagery).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Analyze choices made in own visual expressions of self (e.g., choice of clothing, hairstyles, jewelry) and discuss the role of social media and other aspects of visual culture in influencing one’s choices.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Research visual literacy and its evolution (e.g., web design, rock concert staging, YouTube videos, powwows) and assess the personal and social value of visual literacy.

outcomes.statement: Research and share findings about opportunities to continue lifelong engagement and learning in visual art.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Conduct an inquiry into art making practices and traditions in First Nations communities in Saskatchewan.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Investigate the role of the arts in sustaining and teaching cultural heritage in Métis communities.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Engage with artists to explore creative processes and discover opportunities for ongoing participation in visual art.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Examine how visual art, and the other arts, contribute to social wellbeing in communities.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Generate a list of opportunities for accessing and engaging in visual art activities and related careers during and after high school.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Demonstrate awareness of arts community organizations and potential careers in visual art related fields (e.g., photographer, animator, curator, graphic designer, architect, illustrator).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Consider entering art shows in the community, collaborating with other schools, visiting galleries and reflect on what has been learned.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Research artist collectives, alternative gallery environments, artist-run centers, or studentrun art pop-up center, and consider opportunities for lifelong engagement and learning.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Seek out opportunities to contribute to an art project or exhibition in school and/or community (e.g., senior citizens’ home exhibition).

evidence.observation: The outcomes page groups the outcomes under 9 unit headings.

outcomes.statement: Impovising in a jazz style, exploring understanding of applicable jazz theory.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss understanding of jazz style and analyze musical events within a solo or composition(e.g. introduction, shout chorus, form, dynamics, pitches, changes, articulation).

indicators.label: b
c
d
e
indicators.text: Demonstrate improvement and growth in the presentation and construction of improvised solos in a performance setting.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Take personal and musical risks by trying new ways to express oneself in the jazz idiom, using new ides, new concepts and a variety of styles.

outcomes.statement: Recognize, with assistance as necessary, the importance of musical text in personal musical performance.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Prepare, rehearse and perform music in jazz style in solo, small group and/or large ensemble settings.

indicators.label: b
c
indicators.text: Explore text through creating original text to pre-existing melodies and improvisations (vocalese)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Examine the conventions regarding jazz articulation and use those conventions in performance.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Recognize jazz vocabulary and use this vocabulary to describe personal musical practise, learning, theory and performance.

outcomes.statement: Identify the elements of music and apply these to create a musical product.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Demonstrate the knowledge of standard notation conventions (e.g., note durations up to eighth notes, repeats, codas, D.S.s and dynamic markings). Identify jazz conventions that differ from traditional classical notation (e.g., falls, glisses, slides, inflection marks and hats).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Sing a variety of vocal jazz styles (e.g., swing, funk, ballad) accompanied and a cappella.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Describe the relationship of form and text in music, particularly blues and ABA, AABA song forms.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: In groups, design, implement and evaluate a plan to improve individual performance and to enhance the knowledge and uderstanding of vocal jazz. As part of this process of improvement, include recording and listening back to performances, practices and/or rehearsals.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Identify different elements of music such as articulation, rhythm, beat, metre, time placement and tone that help create a jazz style and apply this knowledge while music making.

outcomes.statement: Identify personal vocal techniques and apply these to create or show a musical product.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Recognize a vocal tone appropriate to the style and personal development.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Describe the connection betrween the breath and the voice.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Establish the key concepts related to singing expressively (e.g., work painting, phrasing, motion and dynamics). Show the knowledge of these concepts through singing.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Sing a known tune(e.g., O'Canada) a cappella maintaining key centre.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Sing a one octave chromatic scale, scending and descending, unaccompanied

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Sing the chord tones of major and minor triads and scale triads.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Sing a jazz standard (with recorded or live acoompaniment) exploring scat singin and other appropriate jazz stylings.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Sight-read a melodic line written in stepwise motions

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Compare and contrast vocal jazz style to other vocal styles.

outcomes.statement: Identify the skills and abilities required to listen and respond as a vocal jazz performer when singing jazz.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Respond to qualities of personal tone such as pitch, dynamics, style, colour, blend, rhythm, time, and consistent vowel use.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Respond to the rest of the ensemble (e.g., its tone, colour, pitch, dynamics, style, rhythm, time, balance, consistent vowel use and blend).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Immediately respond to the ensemble's response (e.g., When singing, does the student match and change vowel sounds and shapes to match the group?).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Respond to the conductor/leader, including gestures, cues, tempo, expressions and body language.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Listen to the acoustic properties of the performing space, including the sound, tone, loudness, and reverb of the room and adjust singing and microphone technique accordingly.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: React to the audience, their presence (or nor), body language, expressions and reaction to the music (e.g., applause, cheering, being asked to sing louder or quieter).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Know the history, culture, style, form and tempo of the music being performed and respond to the music by reading it and/or performing the notes and/or changes appropriately

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Recall previous experiences and knowledge (in music and in life) and integrate these into solo group vocal jazz performances.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Know any special emotional context that may apply to the music, generate the appropriate emotional feeling or energy and/or synchronize the personal emotional state of the performer with the emotional context of the music being performed.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Know, predict and/or anticipate what is next or might bve next in the music and prepare for that while performing in the moment of the music.

outcomes.statement: Identify skills and abilities necessary to listen to a jazz performer.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Listen to jazz music and with assistance analyze form, tone, style, era, dynamics, articulation, time signature, characteristic rhythms, time, balance, blend, key, monde and/or pitch.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text:
Analyze the development of the jazz music(melody, arrangement, changes, or improvisation) as a whole or in smaller sections.
;

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: In groups, analyze the characteristic sounds, licks, tone and other elements of well-known singers and/or groups. Identify these singers and/or groups. Identify these singers and/or groups on recordings aurally, only by listening to the characteristic sounds or ideas presented in the music.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Analyze and reflect on just one voice or instrument from the beginning to the end of a musical selection (e.g., Does the singer or player perform the same way all the way through? How was it different or the same? What did he/she sing or play that the student also might be able to sing or play?)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Listen to music analyzing and reflecting on the melody, other voices, bass line, drums and percussion, background lines, background vocals, roots and chord progression and sing with the recording.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Discuss the history, cultural heritage and effect of current events as these apply to the musical selection.

outcomes.statement: Identify the skills and abilities to analyze vocal jazz music in real time while making or listening to the music.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: In groups, identify, discuss and apply strategies to solve different challenges related to music making.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Examine common chord structures such as triads in music performed and/or listened to.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Create strategies to identify the time signature on first hearing a piece of music, in simpler time signatures such as 2/4, 3/4, 4/4.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Develop strategies to identify the types of scales being used (pentatonic, blues, major, etc.) in music performed and/or listened to.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Develp strategies for hearing 2 and 4 on first hearing a piece of music in an appropriate time signature.

outcomes.statement: Listen to performances of vocal jazz music and with assistance, develop and apply critical criteria to use in critical exaluation of one's own work and other's work.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Listen to the music of the great jazz and vocal jazz performers.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Generate criteria of excellence through listening to the music of the great performers (e.g., What is it that makes the music great? what do the great performers do that the student or student's ensemble does no do?)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: In groups, design and implement a plan for improvement (personal and ensemble) based on the criteria generated from listening to the great performers.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: When listening to a musical selection, as a group develop the ability to describe and classify the music using appropriate jazz language (e.g., style, period, compose, culture and performer).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Explore the skills and components of listening actively, continue to develop these listening skill and recognize that listening contributes to the authenticity of performances.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Recognize and discuss the value of original thought, technical proficiency, place, era and other concepts in the music of the great jazz performers.

outcomes.statement: Describe the skills, techniques and attitudes necessary for successful ensemble performace.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explore the role of each of the parts within the student's ensemble by demonstrating the ability to perform those specific tasks that are particular to the vocal part or instrument that the student sings or plays in the ensemble (e.g., bass part in the choir, comping for guitar and piano, walking lines for the bass, solo parts in the choir and position in a section).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: With assistance, identify the importance of and begin to implement, melodic phrasing, rhythmic accuracy and articulation in perparation and performance of vocal jazz.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Discuss the challenges and importance of singing in tune with good balance and tone and learn the capabilities of the student's own voice (e.g., range, where the break in the student's voice is).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Identify the components of a professional attitude towards conduct, focus and communication skills in rehearsal, preparation of materials and presentation of products.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Begin to apply the learned characteristics of different styles, eras, etc. to the performance of the student's music.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Show respect for the personal work of self and others through appropriate critique.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: With assistance, critically examine and assess the student's individual work and personal contribution to group projects/performances.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Know the value of individual practive, know how to practice, conduct an ongoing evaluation of the student;s personal practice skills and implement a plan for improvement.

outcomes.statement: Explore the different eras, genres, styles and feels of vocal jazz through listening to and.or performing the representative music.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: As a group, listen to recording of vocal jazz, develop a list or understanding of the basic characteristics of different jazz styles, genres, periods and place and implement that knowledge into practice and performance.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Discuss aspects of vocal jazz such as history, performers, styles and eras through a variety of media, with a focus on Canadian or Saskatchewan jazz artists.

outcomes.statement: Demonstrate an awareness of key historical and artist developments and trends as the relate to the eras and styles of vocal jazz.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Develop a jaz history timeline from about 1890 through the present, including developments in jazz music, major figures and styles along with important world historical events.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify the most influential jazz sings (e.g., Ella Fitzgerald, Frank Sinatra). Investigate why these performers are identified as influentional and listen to their music.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: A number of vocal jazz artists have First Nations or America Indian heritage (e.g., Mildred Bailey, Lena Horne, Joe Williams and Juila Keefe). Discuss possible resons why their heritage is not widely known.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Discuss the influence of jazz (and other musics) on contemporary First Nations music.

outcomes.statement: Discuss the influence of vocal jass on other types of music, with an emphasis on the music of Canada and Saskatchewan and assess possible careers in vocal jazz and music.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify the influence of vocal jazz in Canadian musical culture (e.g., Was jazz ever the "pop" music in Canada?).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Describe the different peoples that made up the culture of New Orleans at the start of the 20th century and the ways that these cultures influenced the development of jazz. Are there parallels in Canada?

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Research career pathways in vocal jazz and music in general.

evidence.observation: The outcomes page groups the outcomes under 3 unit headings.

outcomes.statement: Apply principles and techniques for unintentional injury prevention to ensure safe work performance in the welding area.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 1: General Shop Safety (Core) · Suggested Time: 2-3 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify the purpose and demonstrate the proper use and fit of personal protective equipment (PPE) including eye protection (lens shades), clothing, hearing protection, and footwear while identifying the hazards from which they protect individuals.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Analyze potential risk situations and solutions that apply specifically to slips and falls, as well as lifting heavy material, and identify safe solutions.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Recognize hazards associated with oxy-acetylene welding equipment (i.e., tanks, hoses, gauges) and take the necessary measures to avoid unintentional injuries, including those caused by flashback and backfire.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Recognize hazards associated with electric welding processes and take necessary measures to avoid unintentional injuries.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Evaluate the fire plan for the shop, including components such as fire alarms, fire extinguishers, exits, and procedures; and make recommendations for improvements.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Demonstrate the proper procedures to follow when reporting an unintentional injury.

outcomes.statement: Demonstrate and explain the correct procedures for the safe use, care, and handling of the hand tools and power equipment used in a welding shop.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 3: Hand and Power Tools (Core) · Suggested Time: 3-15 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify and define the safe use of hand tools such as hammers, pliers, wire brushes, strikers, anvils, files, tip cleaners, hand shears, hacksaws, clamps, vices, and marking tools.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Demonstrate and articulate the correct procedures for operating power tools such as grinders (stationary and portable), buffers (stationary and portable), power shear, power hacksaw, band saw, and drill press.

outcomes.statement: Develop and apply a systematic routine for setting up and putting away oxy-acetylene equipment.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 5: Oxy-acetylene Start-up, Shut-down, and Cutting (Core) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Describe and perform the accepted start-up and shut-down procedures for the oxy-acetylene system which includes valves, regulators, torches, tips, types of flames, and safety precautions.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Understand and describe how to cut 3⁄8” mild steel including the correct flame, flame distance, angle of the tip, direction of travel, speed of travel, and motion of tip.

outcomes.statement: Demonstrate safe and effective cutting using an oxy-acetylene torch after determining the proper tip size and gas pressure for the gauge of metal.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 6: Introduction to Oxy-acetylene Cutting (Core) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 5

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify precautionary procedures to limit the danger to others in the shop.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Describe the relationship between the tip size, metal thickness, and gas pressures.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Demonstrate the specified cuts on the provided material using an oxy-acetylene cutting torch.

outcomes.statement: Use oxy-acetylene equipment to complete the specified welds and analyze the results.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 9: Oxy-acetylene Welding (Core) · Suggested Time: 5-6 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 5

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Run lines of fusion without the use of filler rod in the flat position on gauge mild steel.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Assess the quality of personal work on practical assignments including butt weld, edge weld, and lines of fusion.

outcomes.statement: Demonstrate an increasingly high quality of both welding skill and self-assessment of that skill while using oxy-acetylene equipment.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 11A: Oxy-acetylene Welding Practice (Core) · Suggested Time: 10-12 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 10

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Create examples of basic oxy-acetylene welding practices, including beads with no filler, edge weld, corner weld, beads with filler, butt weld, and lap weld.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Perform an outside corner weld, no filler rod, in the flat position, on gauge mild steel.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Run lines of fusion using filler rod, in the flat position, on gauge mild steel.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Perform a butt weld using filler rod, in the flat position, on gauge mild steel.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Assess personal technique and results in consultation with the instructor.

outcomes.statement: Demonstrate a knowledge of and expertise with electric arc welding equipment including common types of electrodes, currents, and welding positions while using the correct terminology.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 14: Shielded Metal Arc Welding Procedures and Equipment (Core) · Suggested Time: 3-4 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Define and appropriately use terminology related to electric arc welding including alternating current, ampere, anode, arc, backing or backup, backhand welding, backstep welding, base metal, bead, bevel, brazing, capillary attraction, cathode, chipping, circuit, complete penetration, contraction, constant current, cover glass, crater, direct current, distortion, downhand welding, ductility, duty cycle, elasticity, electrode circuit, expansion, ferrous, finished bead, finished surface, flux, forehand welding, fusion welding, gaseous shield, generator, kerf, non-ferrous, parent metal, peening, penetration, polarity, porosity, rectifier, root opening, slag, solder, spatter, strain, stress, tensile strength, transformer, uphand welding, voltage, warping, yield point, and yield strength.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Describe the differences in welding electrodes such as 6011, 6013, 7014, and 7018.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Categorize and explain the uses of direct current with straight and reverse polarity.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Categorize and explain the difference between alternating current and direct current with straight and reverse polarity.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Demonstrate start-up and shut-down procedures as well as striking the arc, setting and adjusting amperage, correct electrode angle, and appropriate rate of travel.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Compile a list of specialty electrodes including those used for stainless steel, aluminium, nickel, and hard surfacing.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Identify situations where flat, horizontal, vertical, and overhead positions would be used.

outcomes.statement: Identify, diagnose, and provide remedies for common arc welding faults.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 15: Electric Arc Welding: Welding Faults (Core) · Suggested Time: 1-2 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify faults such as crater-cracking, gas pockets, porosity, and undercutting.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Justify and demonstrate corrections for electric arc faults.

outcomes.statement: Demonstrate the proper techniques for striking an arc and running a bead using four types of welds in flat and horizontal positions.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 16: Electric Arc Welding (Core) · Suggested Time: 1-2 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Compose a list of uses for common welds including butt, flat, corner, and fillet.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Run continuous weld beads on mild steel.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Demonstrate basic welding practices such as striking the arc, electrode angle, rate of travel, amperage settings, and electrode selection.

outcomes.statement: Describe critical aspects of electric arc welding such as types, uses, and characteristics of electrodes, types of current, polarity, joints, and welding positions.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 17: Electric Arc Welding Electrodes (Core) · Suggested Time: 1-2 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explain the significance of each position in the classification number for welding electrodes.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Categorize the following electrodes according to uses and weld characteristics such as penetration, slag, spatter, and application: 6010, 6011, 6013, 7014, 7018, and 7024.

outcomes.statement: Demonstrate increasing skill in running a continuous bead using arc welding equipment.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 18: Electric Arc Welding Skill Development - 7014, 7024, 7018, and 6010 (Core) · Suggested Time: 5-7 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 16 and 17

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Run individual beads using 7014, 6010, 7024, and 7018 electrodes.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Examine weld faults and identify causes and solutions.

outcomes.statement: Demonstrate increasing skill in running a continuous bead using arc welding equipment with 7014, 7024, 7018, and 6010 electrodes.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 19: Electric Arc Welding Skill Development - Padding and Butt Weld (Core) · Suggested Time: 15-20 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 18

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Perform a butt weld on mild steel using the four different electrodes while demonstrating the correct arc length, electrode angle, rate of travel, and amperage setting.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Demonstrate an ability to diagnose weld faults and causes.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Pad a plate with at least two layers on each side.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Compare and chart personal progress to identify increasing skill.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Assess personal technique and results in consultation with the instructor.

outcomes.statement: Apply safety principles and practices to the use of GMAW equipment.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 25A: Gas Metal Arc Welding (GMAW) Safety and Equipment (Core) · Suggested Time: 2-3 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Compile information related to the GMAW process including care and maintenance of equipment, GMAW equipment and process, shielding gases, types of wire, weld faults and causes, and advantages and disadvantages of GMAW.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Assess whether there are additional safety concerns for GMAW over oxy-acetylene and arc welding.

outcomes.statement: Develop increasing skill using GMAW equipment.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 27A: GMAW Procedures and Practice (Core) · Suggested Time: 15-20 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 25A

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Perform a forehand pad.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Perform a backhand pad.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Perform tack welding.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Perform a lap weld downhand on 14 gauge steel.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Perform a fillet weld downhand on 14 gauge steel.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Perform a butt weld downhand on 14 gauge steel.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Compare and chart personal progress to identify increasing skill.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Assess personal technique and results in consultation with the instructor.

outcomes.statement: Determine personal skills and interests that could lead to a career in the welding trade through an apprenticeship, technical school training, or paid work.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 34: Careers in Welding (Optional) · Suggested Time: 2-5 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Compare the transition from high school to apprenticeship to that of high school to further classroom instruction at university or college.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Develop a list of career opportunities related to the field of welding.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Identify entrepreneurial opportunities available to people in the welding profession.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Appraise a list of personal skills and traits that could lead to a career in the welding industry.
