outcomes.statement: Evaluate one's understanding of wellness while participating in various learning opportunities that balance the dimensions of wellness (i.e., physical, psychological, social, spiritual, environmental).

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Participate in a variety of learning experiences that positively influence and balance one's well-being (e.g., exercising, smudging, recycling, gardening).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Reflect on personal beliefs (e.g., being healthy takes work) while addressing common misconceptions about wellness (e.g., if one is not sick, then one must be well).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Employ appropriate and increasingly sophisticated strategies (including technology) to gather, interpret, and evaluate wellness information (e.g., interview community wellness experts, evaluate source of information, reflect on personal biases, discuss alternative perspectives).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Compare traditional (e.g., medicine wheel), contemporary (e.g., networked teams of health providers), and evolving information (e.g., technological advances, ongoing research) about wellness.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Analyze and communicate the dimensions of wellness in terms of their interconnectedness (i.e., connections), interdependence (i.e., mutual benefits), and interactions (i.e., effects of one on another).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Examine the consequences of neglecting or over-emphasizing any of the dimensions of wellness.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Investigate the multitude of factors that exert influences on life balance (e.g., relationships, gender, culture, stress, sense of belonging, leisure, traditions, socio-economic factors, physical and mental fitness, technology use).

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Critique community and societal norms (e.g., expectations regarding gender roles, norms regarding alcohol consumption) that influence the well-being of self, family, and community.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Assess one's motivations (e.g., appearance) and limitations (e.g., time management) that improve and/or impede one's personal wellness.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Analyze individual and civic responsibility in nurturing well-being and examine the social factors (including expectations of self and others) that influence personal wellness.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Examine available supports (both formal and informal) for attaining and maintaining optimal wellness and establish strategies to effectively access these supports.

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Analyze one's current level of wellness (e.g., wellness inventory).

indicators.label: m
indicators.text: Initiate an ongoing multi-dimensional (i.e., physical, psychological, social, spiritual, environmental) Personal Plan for Wellness based on a comprehensive analysis of personal well-being.

outcomes.statement: Assess, through participation in service learning opportunities and other means (e.g., interviews, discussions, observations), how service learning enhances the well-being of the volunteer and to the individual or organization/community.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Reflect on and discuss what is known about service learning (e.g., what volunteers do, where volunteering occurs, why people volunteer/ do not volunteer).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Investigate historical, contemporary, and evolving needs and opportunities (e.g., time, situations, programs, technology, and/or environments) in the community which might benefit from acts of service.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Determine a variety of community service opportunities that would benefit the well-being of one's community (e.g., meals on wheels, senior centres, canvasser, walking school bus, Special Olympics, coaching/officiating minor sports, Save the Planet, ditch picks, helping seniors who are housebound).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Investigate the impact of volunteering on the overall well-being of self and community (e.g., motivation and sense of accomplishment, sense of belonging, enhanced personal skills, career opportunities, advocacy, cleaner natural environment).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Analyze the contributions that young adults can make through service to their community.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Assess personal skills and aptitudes to find the most effective community service opportunities for self.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Set personal goals, that are documented in one's Personal Plan for Wellness, of what one wants to accomplish from service learning.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Evaluate, revise, and continue to implement Personal Plan for Wellness to be actively engaged in at least 12 hours of participation in service learning in the community (i.e., local community, global community).

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Document, monitor, and communicate, using a variety of technologies (e.g., photos, video), one's involvement in, and understanding of, service learning.

outcomes.statement:
Plan for and engage in movement activity to increase confidence, competence, and sustainability in self-selected individual and/or partner movement activities from each of the following categories:
- Body Management Activities (e.g., dance, yoga, pilates, martial arts, aerobics)
- Alternate Environment Activities (e.g., cycling, snowshoeing, cross-country skiing, swimming, hiking, skating, canoeing, trapping, weight lifting/going to a fitness centre)
- Target games (e.g., bowling, golf, archery, bocce ball)
- Net/Wall games (e.g., tennis, table tennis, racquetball, squash)
Reminder: Health-related fitness includes cardiovascular endurance, flexibility, muscular endurance, muscular strength, and body composition.
Skill-related fitness, includes power, agility, speed, reaction time, balance, and coordination.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Reflect on and make conclusions about one's own personal preference for participation in movement activities as based on the dimensions of wellness (i.e., physical, psychological, social, spiritual, environmental).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Assess own level of confidence and competence in participating, in each of the four basic physical environments (i.e., on the ground, in the water, on snow and ice, in the air).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Evaluate perceived and actual personal levels of confidence and competence when utilizing the required complex skills needed to participate in self-selected movement activities.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Analyze the impact that current personal strengths and weaknesses in health-related fitness have on personal performance of complex skills used in self-selected movement activities (e.g., I have good upper body strength so I am successful at swimming lengths in the pool).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Analyze a complex skill required in each self-selected movement activity to determine which Basic Movement Patterns/Skills require practice for enhancing sustainable performance of the skills.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Assess personal understanding of tactics (e.g., response to a specific moment in time such as what to do in the case of unexpected fatigue during long-distance running) and strategies (e.g., predetermined plan such as choosing a golf course based on your ability) in self-selected movement activities.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Apply relevant biomechanical principles (e.g., laws of motion, friction) to enhance complex skills required for competent participation in self-selected movement activities.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Analyze influences (e.g., fluid intake, commitment to practice, available technology, audience, nutrition) that affect optimal personal performance during participation in movement activities.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Locate, evaluate, and use resources (e.g., websites, people in the community, agencies in the province) to help support and build one's understanding of effective skill performance, tactics, and strategies to be used in individual/partner movement activities.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Analyze personal utilization of movement skills, tactics, and strategies utilizing technology (e.g., video motion analysis of self and others, pedometers, technological applications) and other means (e.g., checklists, rubrics).

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Analyze transferable skills, tactics, and strategies to be used in the performance of various other self-selected individual and/or partner movement activities.

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Utilize visualization and other mental preparation strategies to enhance performance in self-selected movement activities.

indicators.label: m
indicators.text: Critique, after participation in self-selected movement activities, decisions made regarding the utilization of skills, tactics, and strategies.

indicators.label: n
indicators.text: Evaluate, revise, and continue to implement a Personal Plan for Wellness to increase competency in complex skills and enhance participation in individual and/or partner movement activities that support sustainable wellness.

outcomes.statement: Assess the impact of mental health on overall well-being of self, family, and community.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Reflect on and discuss personal and community beliefs and biases about mental health.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Examine common misconceptions and negative stigmas/ connotations related to both the area of and the language of mental illness (e.g., misconception that an individual with a mental illness has a weak character or is inevitably dangerous).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Consider ways to reduce stigma, address discrimination, and eliminate structural barriers related to mental illness.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Describe, with information from a variety of mental health experts, the factors that contribute to positive mental health (e.g., involvement in extracurricular activities, belonging to a team/group).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Discuss prior understandings of how thoughts, actions, and behaviours are all connected to brain function.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Recognize that there is no single cause of any mental health problem or illness and no one is immune regardless of where they live, how young or old they are, or their social standing.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Examine evolving theories about the complex causes of mental illnesses (i.e., social, economic, psychological, biological, and genetic factors).

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Assess the influence of mental well-being on each of the dimensions of wellness (i.e., psychological, physical, social and environmental).

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Investigate various personal, environmental, biological, and social influences (e.g., sports competitions, use of cannabis, support networks) on mental health and determine one's relationship to these influences.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Determine why particular mental illnesses (e.g., anxiety disorders, depression, bipolar mood disorder, eating disorders, schizophrenia) are common in adolescence.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Investigate the relationships between personal mental health and personal wellness (e.g., feeling well, functioning well and being resilient, making positive changes, being physically fit).

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Examine the relationships among defense mechanisms, feelings, behaviours, and mental health (i.e., ways we protect ourselves from things we do not want to think about or deal with).

indicators.label: m
indicators.text: Examine the interconnectedness and interdependence of mental health and a variety of activities (e.g., leisure activities, competitive sports, physical activities, helping someone or some cause).

indicators.label: n
indicators.text: Analyze mental fitness factors (e.g., placing things in perspective, using stress management strategies, cultivating and maintaining a strong sense of humour) as they relate to personal well-being.

indicators.label: o
indicators.text: Evaluate, revise, and continue to implement a Personal Plan for Wellness based on new understandings about mental health.

outcomes.statement: Assess one's self-awareness (i.e., one's ability to perceive own emotions and tendencies) and self-management (i.e., ability to stay flexible and positively direct personal behaviour) for the purpose of enhancing well- being of self and others.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss personal standards, interests, abilities, and privileges, and how these influence one's well-being.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Complete a variety of personal inventories to analyze learnings about self.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Assess one's emotional intelligence (i.e., the ability to perceive, control, and evaluate emotions) using a variety of measurement tools.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Analyze how overall well-being is affected by biases and stereotyping (e.g., gender, physical abilities, culture, body composition).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Analyze own ability to manage physical fitness for a lifetime versus relying on others (e.g., a coach and a team).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Reflect on one's ability to recognize and manage emotions in self and in personal relationships.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Examine emotional and behavioural patterns of self and others and determine related impact on optimal wellness.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Practise and reflect on variety of self-awareness strategies (e.g., treat feelings as good or bad, identify triggers, seek feedback, keep a journal of emotions, observe others' reactions to your emotions).

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Reflect on and explain the 'what' and 'why' of one's own preference (e.g., alone, with a partner, in a group, on a team, competitive, recreational) for engagement in particular movement activity.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Examine internal (e.g., thinking patterns) and external (e.g., triggers) influences on one's emotional intelligence.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Analyze and practise effective identification and communication of feelings.

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Justify one's overall placement on the listening continuum (i.e., ignoring, pretending, selecting, attending, empathizing) and recognize opportunities for improvement.

indicators.label: m
indicators.text: Determine the benefits of proactive decision making in managing personal well-being.

indicators.label: n
indicators.text: Analyze one's preferred decision-making style in terms of its impact on well-being of self and others.

indicators.label: o
indicators.text: Evaluate, revise, and continue to implement a Personal Plan for Wellness based on new understandings about self.

outcomes.statement: Model and promote a local culture/norm of safety and injury prevention (i.e., physical safety, social safety, psychological safety, spiritual safety, environmental safety) to optimize well-being of self, family, community, and the environment.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Evaluate the norm/culture of safety in one's peer groups, family, and community.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Investigate (e.g., communicate with safety experts in the community) factors that influence safety norms.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Ask and investigate compelling questions about the local culture of safety (e.g., What can be the long-term impact of continuing to be physically active while injured? Are all injuries predictable and preventable? Are there occasions when an injured player should still be 'in the game'? How do you know if a risk is worth the potential consequences? What are personal responsibilities regarding safety in each dimension?).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Examine how the local culture of safety (i.e., physical safety, social safety, psychological safety, spiritual safety, environmental safety) has been established and nurtured while reflecting on its related impact on community and environmental well-being.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Evaluate risks and safety factors (i.e., physical safety, social safety, psychological safety, spiritual safety, environmental safety) that may affect activity choices (e.g., What are some physical activity options that are safe to participate in when one has a broken leg?) and preferences.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Investigate common safety risks (e.g., driving a motorized vehicle, participating in high-contact sports) for youth in local community and determine injury prevention opportunities.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Analyze common unintentional injuries (e.g., head injury from high jumping, death due to motor vehicle accidents, injury to hand while using a power tool) for youth in local community and discuss related impact on the overall well-being of self and others.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Demonstrate respect, responsibility, and caring for own wellness by applying understandings related to the identification, prevention (e.g., investigate facts, prepare basic first-aid kit, take time outs), and management of common safety risks (e.g., wearing personal protective equipment, following recommended guidelines and instruction for use of equipment).

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Analyze moral and ethical conduct in movement activities and sport (e.g., cheating, intentional fouls, performance-enhancing drugs) and their impact on the safety and well-being of self and others.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Evaluate, revise, and continue to implement Personal Plan for Wellness to address the local culture/norm of safety and injury prevention to enhance personal and/or community well-being.

outcomes.statement: Promote sustainable well-being by planning for and engaging in movement activities, alone and with others, that enhance the health-related (i.e., cardiovascular endurance, flexibility, muscular endurance, muscular strength, and body composition) and skill-related (i.e., power, agility, speed, reaction time, balance, and co-ordination) components of fitness.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Engage in, document, and analyze fitness benefits and sustainability potential of participation in 30 minutes of daily moderate to vigorous physical activity outside of class time over a four-week period.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Investigate opportunities (e.g. walking/running groups, recreation centres, green spaces, on-line opportunities) for engagement in movement activities for sustainable well-being at school, at home, and in the community.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Examine how technology (e.g., heart rate monitor, pedometer, fitness software, technological applications) may enhance and support one's health-related and skill-related components of fitness.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Create and justify the importance of the health-related and skill- related components of fitness (e.g., Is balance more important than muscular strength?).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Create and participate in a two-week cost-free FITT (i.e., Frequency, Intensity, Type of Activity, Time) plan that enhances all of the components of both health-related and skill-related fitness.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Investigate and evaluate, through participation in, a student selected pre-made fitness work-out.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Analyze the potential for preferred movement activities and achieved engagement level in those activities that may promote sustainable well-being and lifelong involvement.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Explain the direct correlation between committed engagement in cardiovascular endurance activities and calorie-burning potential.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Create and engage others in a fitness workout using items (e.g., towels, books, cans, rocks) and chores (e.g., sweeping, vacuuming, shoveling) and responsibilities (e.g., babysitting, walking pets) commonly found in and around the home and/community.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Examine factors (e.g., determinants of health, body composition, mental wellness, social wellness) that have an impact on one's commitment to achieving and maintaining recommended standards for health-related and skill-related components of fitness.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Evaluate fitness and activity guidelines and/or standards set by different agencies, organizations, or governments (including other countries) to determine suitability for self and community (e.g., Public Health Agency of Canada, ParticipACTION, Saskatchewan in motion, US Department of Health and Human Services, World Health Organization).

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Discuss why scientifically-based measures (e.g., skin-fold tests, BMI) used to determine body composition are not always accurate, effective, or complete indicators of physical fitness and level of well-being.

indicators.label: m
indicators.text: Examine the pressure and social implications placed on gender related to body composition and participation in movement activities.

indicators.label: n
indicators.text: Utilize the FITT (i.e., Frequency, Intensity, Type of activity, Time) principle and principles of training (i.e., overload, progressive resistance, specificity, use/disuse) in a plan for health-related and skill-related fitness.

indicators.label: o
indicators.text: Evaluate, revise, and continue to implement a Personal Plan for Wellness to include setting and achieving personal goals for health-related and skill-related fitness.

outcomes.statement:
Assess how relationships (e.g., with self, peers, family, teachers, teammates, opponents, coaches, employers) influence all dimensions of wellness.
Confrontation Model: Select a specific example that illustrates the behaviour/situation you want to change, describe your emotions re: behaviour/issue, clarify why this is important- what is at stake to gain/lose, identify your contribution to this problem, indicate your wish to resolve the issue, invite other(s) to respond. (Scott, 2002)

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Recognize that relationships are dynamic (i.e., variable) and change over time.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Ask and respond to important questions about relationships, such as: What matters most in relationships? Why is it important to step in or speak out in someone's defense? When is it important to keep silent? How do we maintain optimal wellness through our relationships with others? What is most effective for managing/ nurturing/embracing change in relationships?

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Analyze how relationships are developed and enhanced through an awareness of self, others, and by one's overall well-being.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Discuss and examine common challenges in relationships.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Determine own challenges in personal relationships.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Investigate ways in which relationships are initiated, maintained, and terminated and the related consequences to overall well- being.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Analyze negative interactions that may result during competitive participation in movement activities (e.g., a parent/adult yelling at an official, a coach who does not give equal playing time).

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Reflect on personal approaches to conflict and how these approaches enhance and/or impede wellness.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Discuss skills and behaviours that are effective in nurturing relationships and those that escalate conflict.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Evaluate and practise different ways to resolve a conflict including the "confrontation model".

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Examine the benefits (e.g., staying connected to a friend who has moved, enhanced opportunity to engage in social justice or political issues) and the harm (e.g., online bullying, inadequate sleep, scams) that may result from the use of social networking, online shopping, internet gambling, etc.

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Examine legal rights and responsibilities concerning relationships and how these rights and responsibilities are established to support overall well-being.

indicators.label: m
indicators.text: Demonstrate and evaluate personal commitment to responsible social behaviour (Hellison, 2011) while participating in and analyzing movement activities.

indicators.label: n
indicators.text: Reflect on and respond to relationship questions (e.g., Why would someone establish a positive relationship with an opponent in the context of participation in a competitive movement activity? How do I safely end or get out of relationships that are unsafe? How do relationships impact/influence one's wellness?).

indicators.label: o
indicators.text: Evaluate, revise, and continue to implement a Personal Plan for Wellness to demonstrate decision making that enhances relationships and overall well-being.

outcomes.statement: Assess challenges related to community well-being and take action to address these challenges.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Reflect on past, present, and evolving wellness challenges (e.g., physical inactivity, sexual health issues, bullying, drinking and driving, gambling, transportation, unemployment, suicide) in the local community.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Examine local community norms and practices that affect the well- being of self, family, community, and the environment.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Develop and ask critical questions of particular local wellness challenges while respecting facts, knowledge, and social and cultural contexts.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Critique various points of view concerning community wellness to better understand the influence of underlying values or assumptions.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Discuss the complexities of wellness issues within one's community and investigate possible opportunities to address these issues.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Access resources (e.g., community, provincial, national) and agencies (e.g., Saskatchewan in motion, Public Health Agency of Canada) to support and address community wellness challenges.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Conclude that real-life challenges to well-being often have more than one solution.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Describe personal challenges concerning community well-being.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Investigate legislation (i.e., local, provincial, and national) that relates to particular community wellness issues.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Determine the intent of legislation (see indictor i) and question if the intention is realized in the local community.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Initiate, in a variety of ways, community awareness and opportunities to address wellness issues.

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Evaluate, revise, and continue to implement a Personal Plan for Wellness to address self-selected community wellness challenges.

outcomes.statement:
Analyze, explain, and apply understandings, skills, tactics, and strategies that enhance confidence and competence in participating in recreational group/team movement activities through participation in various class-selected games from the following categories:
- Target games (e.g., curling)
- Net/Wall games (e.g., volleyball)
- Invasion/Territorial games (e.g., basketball, soccer, touch football, ultimate frisbee, lacrosse, double ball, street hockey)
- Striking/Fielding games (e.g., softball, slo-pitch, cricket).

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Co-construct and apply, as group/team, a list of criteria that exemplifies a recreational experience in a group/team movement activity and supports a positive experience for all participants.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Assess the sustainable wellness potential, for self and others, of participating in particular recreational group/team movement activities.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Reflect on and express personal thoughts on the potential positive and negative impacts of participation in recreational group/team movement activities on overall wellness.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Assess and explain personal level of confidence and competence in utilizing the required complex skills needed to participate in various recreational group/team movement activities.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Analyze group/team members' performance of complex skills, utilizing technology (e.g., video motion analysis of self and others, pedometers, technological applications) and other means (e.g., checklists, rubrics).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Develop and participate in practice opportunities that support all group/team members in enhanced utilization of complex skills.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Assess and explain/demonstrate personal understanding of tactics (e.g., what fake to use prior to shooting or passing) and strategies (e.g., using a zone or one-on-one defence) required for confident and competent participation in selected recreational group/team movement activities.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Locate, evaluate, and use resources (e.g., websites, people in the community, agencies in the province) to help support and build one's understanding of effective tactics and strategies to be used in selected team/group movement activities.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Support others in understanding and applying the tactics and strategies that enhance potential for positive participation in selected recreational group/team movement activities.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Co-develop and apply, group/team tactics and strategies to be used within the context of non-competitive participation in recreational group/team movement activities.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Analyze and discuss the transferable skills, tactics, and strategies to be used while participating in all selected recreational group/team movement activities.

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Evaluate, revise, and continue to implement a Personal Plan for Wellness to include participation in recreational group/team movement activities that support sustainable wellness.

outcomes.statement: Make informed decisions regarding personal healthy eating practices based on connections to wellness.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Compare eating practices (e.g., number of meals, snacking habits, time of day/night, fluid consumption, kinds of foods) of the past to those of the present.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Predict and justify what healthy eating might mean in the future.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explore some of the controversy that surrounds healthy eating practices and beliefs (e.g., nutrition supplements, digestive cleansing, mega vitamins, carbohydrate loading, vegetarianism, organic foods).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Investigate what is known about healthy eating practices (i.e., for children, teens, adults, athletes, pregnant mothers) from a variety of evaluated sources.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Examine the various nutrients (e.g., protein, fibre, calcium, omega-3 fat, vitamins) that should be considered for optimal well-being.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Examine cultural eating practices and determine their cultural significance and contribution to optimal wellness.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Examine what is known about sustainable eating practices (e.g., growing your own food, supporting local, using leftovers) and determine possible changes to personal eating practices.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Discuss food security and its impact on one's ability to make decisions about food practices.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Examine whether members of the community all have the same access to nutritious food, and determine how access influences wellness.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Examine and evaluate several different food guides or healthy eating recommendations related to personal eating practices.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Design a one-week plan for weight maintenance that balances physical output (i.e., calories burned through metabolism and activity) and food intake (i.e., calories consumed through food and drink).

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Predict the long-term impact, on overall wellness, of consuming more/less calories than one burns over a long period of time.

indicators.label: m
indicators.text: Analyze nutritional factors (e.g., hydration, pre-activity meal, sustainable eating habits) that affect optimal performance for selected movement activities.

indicators.label: n
indicators.text: Evaluate, revise, and continue to implement a Personal Plan for Wellness to incorporate healthy eating practices that enhance personal wellness.

outcomes.statement: Investigate the connection to and importance of spirituality on wellness.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Investigate various meanings of the concepts of spirit, soul, spiritual dimension, and spiritual development.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Examine diverse spiritual beliefs and traditions of individuals and cultures (including First Nations and Métis), past and present.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Analyze the relationships of vision, joy, struggle, and perseverance with regard to spiritual beliefs and practices.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Examine personal experience in relation to the larger questions of meaning (e.g., Who am I? What is human nature? Why do innocent people suffer?).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Examine how people have explored the larger questions of human existence (e.g., oral histories, literature, current events, celebrations, artwork) and represented own perspectives.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Investigate the value of silence, stillness, solitude, and an inward focus on one's overall wellness.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Examine the role individual activities (e.g., cooking, travelling, dancing, running) may have in one's spirituality and wellness.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Reflect on the concept of "sacred" (e.g., family, body) and its role in wellness.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Determine how one is influenced by norms, trends, images, and values in various cultures, communities, and groups.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Evaluate, revise, and continue to implement a Personal Plan for Wellness to purposefully enhance the spiritual dimension of one's wellness.

evidence.observation: The outcomes page groups the outcomes under 2 unit headings.

outcomes.statement: Explore the cultural, physical, mental, emotional and spiritual benefits of land-based learning.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 1: Benefits of Land-based Learning (Core) · Suggested Time: 6-10 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss the meaning of land-based learning and its effect on human interactions with the environment (e.g., respecting animals and taking only what is needed).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explore the Indigenous cultural learning opportunities (e.g., petroglyphs, pictographs, rubbing stones, tipi rings and traditional hunting grounds) in land-based learning.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explain the physical benefits of outdoor activities (e.g., improves overall well-being, increases vitamin D, lowers blood pressure and boosts immunity).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Investigate the mental benefits of being outside (e.g., helps prevent depression and reduces stress and anxiety).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Examine how time spent in nature contributes to managing emotions (e.g., reduces anger and promotes pleasure).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Discuss the spiritual benefits of spending time outdoors (e.g., connection to the land and sense of belonging).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Research the historical significance of the land upon which classroom excursions take place.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Maintain a journal (e.g., written, digital, photo journal or social media) to reflect on the cultural, physical, mental, emotional and spiritual benefits of outdoor experiences.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Explore outdoor pursuits that lead to personal growth and satisfaction.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Identify how benefits of nature are expressed through art (e.g., drama, literature, photography and paintings).

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Reflect on the cultural, physical, mental, emotional and spiritual benefits of land-based learning through outdoor solitude practices (e.g., sit-spot, sense of solitude and solo-time).

outcomes.statement: Investigate the connection between “Leave No Trace” principles and traditional ways of sustainably living on the land.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 2A: Leave No Trace - Fundamentals (Core) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
b
indicators.text:
Discuss how the “Leave No Trace” principles align with traditional Indigenous practices, including the ethics of:
- conservation (i.e., not to take more than is needed); and,
- reciprocity (i.e., offer acts of thankfulness).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explain how pre-excursion planning minimizes resource damage.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Describe how to leave the environment cleaner than found, such as picking up own and others' litter, including biodegradable material (e.g., sunflower seeds).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Explore opportunities for certification in “Leave No Trace” training.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Investigate how “Leave No Trace” guidelines may be applied in different geographical locations depending on population.

outcomes.statement: Explore general safety practices when engaging in wilderness activities.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 3A: Wilderness Safety - General (Core) · Suggested Time: 2-5 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explain the importance of establishing a trip plan and leaving it with someone before participating in a wilderness excursion.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify potential hazards unique to wilderness excursions.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Demonstrate safe practices (e.g., flagging, setting boundaries and carrying a whistle) when engaging in outdoor solitude.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Describe ways to reduce risk of personal injury (e.g., proper training, adhering to safety precautions and maintaining equipment) when participating in wilderness activities.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Investigate provincial and federal health and safety rules and guidelines for specific wilderness activities (e.g., hunting, fishing, trapping and camping).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Research opportunities for outdoor skill certification (e.g., Paddle Canada).

outcomes.statement: Explore basic and traditional navigational skills.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 5A: Basic Navigation (Optional) · Suggested Time: 4-8 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss Indigenous navigational skills and tools with an Elder or Knowledge Keeper.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Research different types of navigation techniques (e.g., natural, celestial, compass and technological).

indicators.label: c
d
indicators.text: Travel on a bearing without a map.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Determine individual pace length and use it to measure distances.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Explain the basic functionality of a Global Positioning System (GPS).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Use a GPS to navigate a given route and arrive at a destination (e.g., geocaching).

outcomes.statement: Demonstrate basic knot-tying skills.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 6A: Basic Ropes and Knots Skills (Optional) · Suggested Time: 3-6 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explore the materials (e.g., plant fibres and animal sources) used to make traditional Indigenous cordage.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Review the properties of familiar knots (e.g., tying shoes).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Identify the basic families of knots (e.g., loops, hitches, bends and lashings).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explain the properties of an effective knot (e.g., serves the purpose, easy to tie and easy to untie).

indicators.label: e

outcomes.statement: Explore traditional and contemporary shelters.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 7A: Shelters (Optional) · Suggested Time: 4-8 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss the cultural and traditional stories and teachings related to Indigenous shelters with an Elder or Knowledge Keeper.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Research traditional Indigenous shelters (e.g., tipi) and their purpose (e.g., housing, sweat and smudge).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explore opportunities to participate in a tipi-raising.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explain the significance of the parts (e.g., bottom, fire, flaps and poles) of a tipi.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Investigate the benefits and drawbacks of different styles of tents.

indicators.label: f
g
indicators.text: Investigate how to erect a tent and secure it using pegs and guy lines.

outcomes.statement: Explore ethical and traditional game harvesting practices.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 11: Game Harvesting (Core) · Suggested Time: 4-10 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
b
indicators.text: Investigate historical Indigenous tools and practices used for fishing (e.g., netting) and hunting (e.g., buffalo jump).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Compare and contrast commercial, sport, and Aboriginal and Treaty rightsprotected hunting, trapping and fishing.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Research the historical purpose (i.e., determine herd health and effectiveness of management practices) of scoring animals.

indicators.label: e
f
g
indicators.text: Investigate the hunter, trapper and angler's responsibilities and procedures used to report conditions (e.g., habitat abuse and neglect of wildlife laws) that may endanger wildlife.

outcomes.statement: Investigate the fundamentals of angling and fishing.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 12A: Angling and Fishing - Fundamentals (Core) · Suggested Time: 4-8 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 11

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explain the significance of access to fish in the context of Indigenous food sovereignty.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explain the differences between angling (i.e., uses a hook and line) and other types of fishing.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Investigate various types of fishing (e.g., jigging, casting, trolling, fly fishing and net).

indicators.label: d
e
indicators.text:
Describe common ways of classifying fish, such as:
- species relationship (e.g., salmonids, percids and minnows);
- water temperature preference (e.g., cold and warm); and,
- feeding habits (e.g., fish eaters, insect eaters and plant eaters).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Identify the distinguishing characteristics (e.g., physical features, habitat, spawning habits, feeding habits and angling techniques) of major game fish species in Saskatchewan.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Investigate the role of local fishing industries (e.g., fish farms and fish hatcheries) in Saskatchewan.

outcomes.statement: Investigate hunting regulations and safe hunting practices.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 13A: Hunting and Game - Safe Practices and Regulations (Core) · Suggested Time: 4-8 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 11

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explore Treaty and Métis Aboriginal hunting rights and where they may be exercised in Saskatchewan.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explain the significance of access to wild game in the context of Indigenous food sovereignty.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Investigate regulations and safety requirements contained in the annual Saskatchewan Hunters and Trappers Guide.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Describe the steps to obtain a hunting license.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Explain what it means to be drawn for big game.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text:
Research federal, provincial and municipal laws and regulations that prevent risk to Saskatchewan hunters, such as:
- lawful hunting hours;
- wearing high-visibility clothing when applicable; and,
- hunting prohibited from a vehicle without dispensation.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Discuss requirements and best practices for obtaining permission to access private property for hunting.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Explore provincial and federal regulations specific for youth hunters.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Describe safety procedures when hunting.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Identify common game animals in Saskatchewan using distinguishing characteristics.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Distinguish between threatening animal behaviours (e.g., pawing the ground and snarling) and normal behaviours (e.g., “escorting” humans away from a den) that do not pose a threat to humans.

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Explain precautions (e.g., sanitization, wearing gloves, bleed and remove intestines quickly and keep meat cool) that can be taken to minimize the risks (e.g., contamination) of consuming game meat.

outcomes.statement: Examine the relationship between wildlife and ecosystems.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 14: Wildlife and the Environment (Core) · Suggested Time: 4-8 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explain how wildlife can be used as a barometer of overall environmental health.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Examine the role biodiversity has in determining the health of an ecosystem.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Discuss reasons for differences in the diversity of wildlife in Saskatchewan, such as adaptation, environmental changes, biotic and abiotic factors and human influences.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explore how animals seek shelter in various landscapes (e.g., digging into snow and hiding under bushes).

indicators.label: e
f
g
indicators.text:
Explore how species have adapted to habitat changes, such as:
- introduction of racoons and white-tailed deer to the prairies; and,
- range of moose expanding from forest to agriculture ecosystems.

outcomes.statement: Investigate the impact that anthropogenic climate change has on habitat and wildlife populations.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 16: Climate Change (Core) · Suggested Time: 4-10 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss how climate changes over time through both natural and human processes.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Define the term anthropogenic and how it relates to climate change.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Examine the impact (e.g., relocation due to ice, water and forest fires) of climate change on Indigenous communities and culture.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Investigate the local and global impact climate change has on ecosystems (e.g., drought, fire and extreme weather).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text:
Analyze the effects climate change has on managing wildlife populations, such as:
- stocking with fish species that have a greater tolerance for higher temperatures;
- shifting hunting season to coincide with changes in rutting seasons; and,
- recording changes in migratory bird species.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Examine the impacts that increasing temperatures have on invasive species (e.g., ticks and mountain pine beetle) migrating through Saskatchewan.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Discuss how changing temperatures affect habitats (e.g., growing seasons, range of forest, algae blooms and expanding semi-arid areas).

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Examine the relationship between healthy ecosystems and carbon mitigation (e.g., role of peat bogs, marshland, grasslands and forests).

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Analyze how the implications of climate change on wildlife species and spaces may also indicate implications for humans.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Investigate the cost of climate change on wildlife-related industries (e.g., hunting, fishing and tourism).

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Discuss the long-term effects of climate change on wildlife and habitats.

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Review community science programs (e.g., Plantwatch) that engage the community and contribute to monitoring climate change.

indicators.label: m

outcomes.statement: Employ cooperative group living skills.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 20: Group Living and Leadership Skills (Core) · Suggested Time: 3-6 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explore examples of teamwork in nature (e.g., geese's flying formation).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Participate in a variety of team-building activities.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Discuss the importance of cooperative living in communities in different cultures (e.g., Indigenous, Asian and Nordic), including a shared sense of responsibility for the good of the collective.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explore examples of how group cooperation was employed in Indigenous ways of living (e.g., hide tanning, rope making and shelter building).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Describe the various roles required to work effectively as a group in outdoor living situations, such as meal preparation and shelter building.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Implement constructive problem-solving strategies, including eliciting input from each group member.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Identify rules and norms (e.g., sharing responsibility, contributing to the group’s activities and respecting others) for effective group living.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Analyze the importance of establishing group norms.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Exhibit cooperative behaviour in partner recreational activities (e.g., wall climbing and canoe paddling).

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Explain the importance of effective communication in group living.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Employ effective communication skills (e.g., active listening and positive body language) in various situations.

outcomes.statement: Plan and facilitate an outdoor excursion in the local community.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 21A: Outdoor Excursion - Local (Optional) · Suggested Time: 6-12 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Modules 1 and 2A

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss the importance of land acknowledgements (e.g., naming the traditional peoples of the area, identifying the treaty and partnerships with local Indigenous people) when participating in local excursions.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Reflect upon the traditional stories of the land where the local excursion will take place.

indicators.label: c
d
indicators.text: Investigate the principles of layering clothing and appropriate fabric choices depending on the season, weather conditions and activity.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Identify which supplies are required for the excursion.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Establish communication routines (e.g., whistle commands and carry contact information) in emergency situations both within and outside of cell phone range.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Identify the route, possible exit points and muster point for the excursion.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Evaluate possible risks (e.g., weather, terrain, animals and plants) that may be encountered.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Plan for hydration and nutrition requirements appropriate to the excursion.

outcomes.statement: Discuss the history and evolution of wildlife and habitat management.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 22A: Wildlife and Habitat Management - History (Core) · Suggested Time: 2-5 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explore how the historical philosophy of dominion over animals has evolved to a philosophy of managing resources.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Examine the impacts of historical uses of wildlife resources (e.g., bison and beaver) on Indigenous people's way of life.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Investigate the connection between treaties and the hunting, fishing and trapping rights of Indigenous people.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explain the purpose of the Treaty Land Sharing Network.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Describe the evolution of wildlife management practices to include the management of habitat and ecosystems.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Trace the evolution of natural resource responsibility in Saskatchewan from federal to provincial governments.

outcomes.statement: Explore career opportunities in the field of wildlife and habitat management.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 23A: Career Opportunities (Core) · Suggested Time: 4-8 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify careers in the area of wildlife and habitat management.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Create a list of personal interests, skills and traits that could lead to a career in wildlife and habitat management.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Develop a list of career opportunities (e.g., wildlife biologist, environmental technician and conservation officer) related to the field of wildlife and habitat management.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Research which wildlife and habitat management-related occupations are facing shortages and which are oversubscribed locally, regionally or provincially.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Examine the roles, responsibilities, educational qualifications and personal and professional qualities common in wildlife and habitat management careers.

indicators.label: f
g
indicators.text: Explore opportunities for underrepresented populations in the wildlife and habitat management field.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Research experience and qualifications for newcomers to enter the wildlife and habitat management field.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Present research findings regarding wildlife and habitat management-related occupations.

evidence.quote: All Practical and Applied Arts curricula are designed using modules, each with a single outcome for students to achieve.

allEvidence.quote: All Practical and Applied Arts curricula are designed using modules, each with a single outcome for students to achieve.
Each Practical and Applied Arts curriculum is composed of modules configured into courses, along with suggestions for modules that are suitable for middle or secondary level survey courses.

allEvidence.observation: Each entry on the course's outcomes page is one module: the entry is titled with the module name and shows a “Module Code” (the outcome code in sk.json); the module's own page prints one “Outcome” with its indicators. The site lists the course levels under “Course Configurations”.

outcomes.statement:
Demonstrate understanding of the preservation of equality including solving problems that involve the manipulation and application of formulas related to:
- perimeter
- area
- the Pythagorean Theorem
- primary trigonometric ratios
- income.
outcomes.printedWith: [C, CN, ME, PS, R, T]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Verify, using examples, and explain why different forms of the same formula are equivalent.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Verify if given forms of the same formula are equivalent and justify the conclusion.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Describe, using examples, how a given formula is used in a trade or an occupation.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Create, solve, and verify the reasonableness of solutions to situational questions relevant to self, family, or community that involve the use of a formula.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Analyze solutions to questions that involve formulae to verify the preservation of equality and correct, with explanation, if necessary.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text:
Solve situational questions that involve the application of a formula that:
- does not require manipulation
- does require manipulation.

guidance: (It is intended that this outcome be integrated with other outcomes throughout the course.)

outcomes.statement: Analyze puzzles and games that involve spatial reasoning using problem solving strategies.
outcomes.printedWith: [C, CN, PS, R]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text:
Determine, explain, and verify strategies to solve a puzzle or to win a game such as:
- guess and check
- look for a pattern
- make a systematic list
- draw or model
- eliminate possibilities
- solve a simpler problem
- work backwards
- develop alternative approaches.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Observe and analyze errors in a solution to a puzzle or in a strategy for winning a game and explain the reasoning.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Create a variation on a puzzle or a game, and describe a strategy for solving the puzzle or winning the game.

guidance: (It is intended that this outcome be integrated throughout the course by using sliding, rotation, construction, deconstruction, and puzzles and games such as Tetris, Rubik’s cube, Blokus, chess, checkers, Backgammon, Mastermind, Tic-Tac-Toe, Connect Four or Five, Battleship, and Cathedral World).

outcomes.statement:
Demonstrate using concrete, and pictorial models, and symbolic representations, understanding of measurement systems including:
- The Système International (SI)
- The British Imperial system
- The US customary system.
outcomes.printedWith: [C, CN, ME, T, V]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text:
Research and present about a topic related to measurement systems such as:
- how the SI system and the Imperial system were developed
- the adoption of the SI system in Canada
- development of the US customary system and the relationship between the units of this system and those of the Imperial measurement system (e.g., units for length and area are the same; there are differences, however, for mass, weight, and capacity)
- early systems of measurement in Canada and contexts in which some are still used today (e.g., hand span and thumbs for measuring horses from the ground to its withers).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Describe situations relevant to self, family, or community in which the SI and/or Imperial systems are used.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text:
Analyze the relationships between:
- the base units of the metric system of measurement and the base ten number system
- the prefixes used in the metric system and powers of ten
- the related units for length, area, volume, capacity, mass, and temperature for each of the two systems of measurement.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text:
Explain, using examples, how and why:
- decimal numbers are usually used for SI units
- fractions are usually used for Imperial units.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text:
Provide an approximate measurement in:
- SI units for a measure given in Imperial units (e.g., 1 inch is approximately 2.5 cm, 1 kg is a little more than 2 lbs)
- Imperial units for a measurement given in SI units (e.g., 1 litre is approximately 1/4 US gallon, 250 mL is approximately 1 cup).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text:
Develop (using proportional reasoning), generalize, explain, and apply strategies (including formulas) to convert measurements from:
- SI to Imperial units (e.g., Celsius to Fahrenheit, centimetres to inches, kilograms to pounds, litres to quarts)
- Imperial to SI units (e.g., Fahrenheit to Celsius, inches to centimetres, pounds to kilograms, quarts to litres).

guidance:
It is intended that students explore, analyze for patterns, and develop understanding of many units in all three systems of measurements. The units used should be those that are appropriate to the workplace or apprenticeship context being considered. These units include:
- metres, grams, litres, and seconds along with appropriate prefixes such as kilo, hecto, deci, centi, and milli, as well as hectare, tonne, and degrees Celsius (SI system).
- inch, foot, board foot, yard, mile, acre, teaspoon, tablespoon, cup, pint, quart, gallon, bushel, ton, and degrees Fahrenheit (British and US systems where appropriate).

outcomes.statement: Demonstrate, using concrete and pictorial models, and symbolic representations, understanding of linear measurement, including units in the SI and Imperial systems of measurement.
outcomes.printedWith: [CN, ME, PS, R, T, V]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Justify the choice of referents for units in both the SI system and the Imperial system (e.g, the width of the thumb for an inch and the width of the little finger for 1 centimetre).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Estimate, using personal referents for SI and Imperial units, linear measurements such as the dimensions of regular 3-D objects or 2-D shapes found in the classroom, at home, or in the community.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text:
Explain why and how the same linear measurement can be expressed using:
- equivalent SI units (e.g., 10 centimetres, 0.1 metres, and 100 millimetres)
- equivalent Imperial units (e.g., 6 inches, $1/2$ foot, $6/36$ or $1/6$ yard).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text:
Measure and record (using Canadian spelling and abbreviations for SI or Imperial units) using a variety of instruments such as trundle or surveyor’s wheels, height gauges, metric and Imperial tapes and rulers, carpenter’s squares, micrometers, fractional or electronic callipers, and pedometers:
- distances at school, at home, and in the community
- inside diameters, outside diameters, lengths, and widths of personally relevant 3-D objects.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Develop, generalize, explain, and apply strategies to convert units of linear measurements within the same system (e.g., feet to yards, or metres to millimetres).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Apply knowledge and skills with linear measurement to create and solve or verify the reasonableness of solutions to situational questions relevant to self, family, or community (including perimeter, circumference, and the length + width + height measurement used in shipping and air travel).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Determine the operation that should be used to solve a linear measurement problem and explain the reasoning (e.g., Write the equation that could be used to determine how many lengths of $1/3$ of a yard can be cut out of a log measuring $5 1/2$ yards).

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Develop, generalize, explain, and apply strategies to determine the midpoint of a linear measurement, such as the length, width, height, depth, diagonal length, or diameter of a 3-D object (e.g., A wall measures 5 yards and $6 7/8$ inches. If a painting is to be hung centered on the wall, how far is the centre of the painting from each of the adjacent walls?).

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Critique the statement “the distance between Regina and Saskatoon is 2 hours”.

guidance: It is intended that contextual situations involve the four arithmetic operations on decimals or on fractions, and that students do not convert from one to the other when performing calculations unless required within the particular question.

outcomes.statement: Demonstrate using concrete and pictorial models, and symbolic representations, understanding of area of 2-D shapes and surface area of 3-D objects including units in SI and Imperial systems of measurement.
outcomes.printedWith: [CN, ME, PS, R, T, V]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Describe situations relevant to self, family, or community in which SI and/or Imperial units for area measurement are used.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Justify the choice of referents for area measurements in both the SI and Imperial units (e.g., a dime or a small fingernail is about one cm² and the thumb nail is about 1 in²).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Estimate, using strategies such as personal referents or grids, area and surface area measurements in SI or Imperial units including regular, composite, and irregular 2-D shapes and 3-D objects found in the classroom, at home, or in the community.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text:
Develop, generalize, explain, and apply strategies (including measuring and applying formulae) for determining areas and surface areas of:
- regular, composite, and irregular 2-D shapes, including circles.
- 3-D objects, including right cylinders and right cones.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text:
Create, solve, and verify the reasonableness of solutions to situational questions relevant to self, family, or community that involve area or surface area measurement of:
- regular or irregular 2-D shapes including circles.
- 3-D objects, including right cylinders and cones.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text:
Develop, generalize, explain, and apply strategies to convert, within the same system of measurement, area measurements expressed in:
- an SI unit squared to another SI unit squared
- an Imperial unit squared to another Imperial unit squared.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Analyze, with and without the use of dynamic geometry software, the effect of changing the measurement of one or more dimensions on area and perimeter of rectangles and surface area of rectangular prisms.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Critique the statement “Area involves one face of a 2-D object while surface area is the sum of the areas of all the faces of a 3-D object”.

outcomes.statement: Apply understanding of the Pythagorean Theorem to solve problems.
outcomes.printedWith: [C, CN, PS, T, V]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Model, including the use of drawing, concrete materials, and technology, the meaning, role, and use of the Pythagorean Theorem, using examples and non-examples.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Observe and analyze a set of triangles to judge if the Pythagorean Theorem could be used to determine an unknown side length and explain the reasoning.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Describe historical and contemporary applications of the Pythagorean Theorem, including the 3:4:5 ratio (e.g., Explain the relationship between a circle of string that has 13 equidistant knots or beads forming 12 spaces of equal length on it to the Pythagorean Theorem).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Relate, using examples, ratios equivalent to 3:4:5 and other Pythagorean Triples to the Pythagorean Theorem.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Develop, generalize, apply, and explain strategies to verify if a corner of a 3-D object is square (90°) or if a parallelogram is a rectangle.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Observe and analyze the lengths and intersections of diagonals of various quadrilaterals and draw conclusions.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Determine if given triangles are right triangles and explain the reasoning.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Create, solve, and verify the reasonableness of solutions to problems relevant to self, family, or community, for which the Pythagorean Theorem can be used.

outcomes.statement: Demonstrate understanding of similarity of convex polygons, including regular and irregular polygons.
outcomes.printedWith: [C, CN, PS, T, V]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text:
Analyze and generalize about the relationships between:
- the corresponding sides of two or more polygons that have corresponding angles of equal measure
- the corresponding angles of two or more polygons that have corresponding sides that are proportional.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Develop, generalize, explain, and apply strategies for determining if two or more convex polygons (regular or irregular) are similar.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Verify whether two or more given polygons are similar.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Draw polygons that are similar to a given polygon using measuring tools and technology, explain the strategies used, and justify why the polygons are similar.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Apply knowledge and skills related to similar polygons to solve situational questions relevant to self, family, or community that involve right triangles with a shared acute angle (e.g., determining the height of a tree).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Create and solve situational questions relevant to self, family, or community that involve similarity of polygons.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Critique the statement “All congruent polygons are similar and all similar polygons are congruent”.

outcomes.statement: Demonstrate an understanding of primary trigonometric ratios (sine, cosine, and tangent).
outcomes.printedWith: [CN, PS, R, T, V]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text:
Observe a set of similar right triangles and analyze and draw conclusions about the ratios of the lengths, with respect to one acute angle of the:
- side opposite to the side adjacent
- side opposite to the hypotenuse
- side adjacent to the hypotenuse.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify situations where the trigonometric ratios can be used for indirect measurement for angles and lengths.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Develop, generalize, explain, and apply formulae for the primary trigonometric ratios (cosine, tangent, and sine).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Analyze solutions to situational questions that involve primary trigonometric ratios to determine if they are reasonable and explain the reasoning.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Apply knowledge and skills related to the solving of right triangles using the primary trigonometric ratios to create and solve situational problems relevant to self, family, or community.

outcomes.statement:
Demonstrate understanding of angles including:
- drawing and sketching
- replicating and constructing
- bisecting
- relating to parallel, perpendicular, and transversal lines
- solving problems.
outcomes.printedWith: [C, ME, PS, T, V]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Justify the choice of personal referents for angles measuring $22.5°$, $30°$, $45°$, $60°$, $90°$, and $180°$ and use them to estimate angle measurements (e.g., a corner of a sheet of paper is $90°$ so $1/2$ of a corner is $45°$).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Sketch or draw angles of various measures, including acute, right, straight, obtuse, and reflex angles, and justify the choice of sketching or drawing in relation to the situation.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explain, using examples, how to measure angles in different orientations using a variety of instruments such as a protractor, carpenter’s square, or dynamic software.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explain and illustrate how angles can be replicated (e.g., Mira, protractor, compass and straightedge, carpenter’s square, and dynamic software).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Replicate angles in various orientations, with and without the use of technology.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Explain, using examples, the relationship between the bisecting of angles and axial symmetry.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Bisect angles in various orientations and explain the strategy used.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Observe and sort a set of pairs of lines as perpendicular, parallel, or neither, and justify.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Relate complementary and supplementary angles to parallel, perpendicular, and transversal lines.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Observe and identify in a situation relevant to self, family, or community adjacent angles that are complementary, supplementary, or neither, and explain the reasoning.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text:
Generalize, develop, explain, and apply relationships between pairs of angles formed by parallel lines and a transversal, inclu
- corresponding angles
- vertically opposite angles
- alternate interior angles
- alternate exterior angles
- interior angles on the same side of the transversal
- exterior angles on the same side of the transversal.

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Provide concrete and pictorial examples that show that there are no angle relationships (excluding vertically opposite angles) when two lines that are not parallel are crossed by a transversal.

indicators.label: m
indicators.text: Describe and apply strategies for determining if lines or planes are perpendicular or parallel in situations relevant to self, family, or community (e.g., are the walls perpendicular to the floor? Are the corners square? Are the seams on the duvet parallel? Are the joists parallel?).

indicators.label: n
indicators.text: Analyze personally relevant situations for the impact if lines or planes that are meant to be perpendicular or parallel are not (e.g., What would it be like if the stairs in a staircase were not parallel?).

indicators.label: o
indicators.text: Create and solve relevant situational questions that involve angles and/or parallel lines and transversals, including perpendicular transversals, and explain the reasoning.

indicators.label: p
indicators.text: Critique the statement “If two or more lines are perpendicular, then each is a transversal of the other and if two or more lines are transversals of each other, they are perpendicular”.

indicators.label: q
indicators.text: Critique the statement “All lines are either parallel or transversals”.

indicators.label: r
indicators.text: Analyze and describe the role of angles, parallel lines, perpendicular lines, and transversals in games and sports (e.g., chess, curling, pool, hockey, soccer, and basketball).

outcomes.statement: Apply proportional reasoning to solve problems involving unit pricing and currency exchange.
outcomes.printedWith: [CN, ME, PS, R, T]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Create and solve problems relevant to self, family, and community that involve best buy, and explain the solution in terms of the cost as well as other factors, such as quality and quantity.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Describe and analyze, using relevant examples taken from print and other media, different sales promotion techniques (e.g., deli meat at $2 per 100g seems less expensive than $20 per kilogram).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Determine the percent increase or decrease from an original price to a new price and explain the reasoning for the method

indicators.label: d
indicators.text:
Develop (using proportional reasoning), explain, and apply strategies for:
- comparing the unit price of two or more items
- solving situational problems involving currency exchange
- determining percent increase or decrease for a given situation.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Develop using proportional reasoning and mental mathematics strategies, explain, and apply strategies for estimating the cost of items or services in Canadian currency while in a foreign country or when making purchases via the Internet, and explain why this may be important.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Convert between Canadian currency and foreign currencies, such as Mexican or American currencies, using formulas, charts, or tables, and explain how to know if the solution is reasonable

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Analyze solutions to situational questions that involve unit pricing or conversions of currency to determine if they are reasonable and explain the reasoning.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Research advantages and disadvantages for individuals, groups, businesses, and communities of having differences in currency rates between Canada and the United States.

outcomes.statement:
Demonstrate understanding of income including:
- wages
- salary
- contracts
- commissions
- piecework
- self-employment
- gross pay
- net pay.
outcomes.printedWith: [C, CN, R, T]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Describe, using examples, various methods of earning income.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Research and record jobs that commonly use different methods of earning income, including hourly wage, wage and tips, salary, commission, contract, bonus, and shift premiums.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Describe the advantages and disadvantages for a variety of methods of earning income, such as hourly wage, tips, piecework, salary, commission, contract work, and self-employment.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Read and explain the information provided on pay stubs.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Determine in decimal form, from a time schedule, the total time worked in hours and minutes, including time and a half and/or double time and explain the strategies used.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text:
Determine gross pay for different situations, including:
- base hourly wage, with and without tips, from given or calculated hours worked
- base hourly wage, plus overtime (time and a half, double time) from given or calculated hours worked
- base wage, plus commission
- single commission rate
- graduated commission.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Determine the Canadian Pension Plan (CPP), Employment Insurance (EI), and income tax deductions for a given amount of gross pay.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Identify and describe deductions that may be relevant to self in the future which are used when calculating net pay (e.g., health plans, uniforms, union dues, charitable donations, payroll tax).

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Investigate, using technology, “what if ...” questions related to changes in income (e.g., “What if there is a change in the rate of pay?”, “What if there is a change in the method of earning income?”, “What if I can qualify for deductions?”, “What if I work 80% time instead of full time?” , “What if I am sick for a long period of time?”).

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Create, research, and solve situational questions relevant to self, family, and community that involve income.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Critique the statement “When planning for a budget, it is important to calculate net pay rather than rely only on gross pay”.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: participates in developing language and culture during experiential learning opportunities, such as helping at community/cultural events, volunteering with day-care children, visiting and conversing with kēhtē-ayak in the community, planning cultural camps/activities and presents these experiences with classmates and teacher

outcomes.statement: Demonstrate, when interpreting oral and written texts, knowledge of German language concepts including basic context-specific vocabulary, word order and linguistic conventions.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Comprehend simple context-appropriate vocabulary in personal texts and basic sight vocabulary (e.g., 250 basic words).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Apply knowledge of simple prefixes (e.g., “ge-” for past perfect tense and “un-” for negation) and suffixes (e.g., “-lich”, “-ig” and “-heit”) to construct meaning.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Identify related words in different forms (e.g., “Ich spiele” / “das Spiel” / “spielerisch”).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Recognize conventions specific to German (e.g., capitalization of nouns, gender of nouns and placement of verb in the sentence).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Analyze the correlation of sound-letter elements.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Investigate generalized patterns for word order and verb conjugations.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Interpret nuance expressed through present tense modal verbs (e.g., “I want to swim on Friday.” and “Ich will am Freitag schwimmen.”).

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Identify the use of formal voice (e.g., “Sie” / “Ihnen” as the formal “you”).

indicators.label: i
j

h

- “Ich habe einen Bruder.”; and,

Pose questions to clarify understanding, such as:
